Sports.title: What Max Verstappen will change after Red Bull’s poor F1 starts in Malaysia and Singapore
Sports.content:
The Singapore weekend is one of milestones for Verstappen. The Dutchman is contesting his 250th Formula 1 Grand Prix this weekend and has claimed his 50th pole position in the process.

Verstappen now belongs to an exclusive group of just five drivers – alongside Lewis Hamilton, Michael Schumacher, Ayrton Senna and Sebastian Vettel – who have secured 50 or more pole positions, but the Dutchman insists he does not pay much attention to such achievements.

"That's not why I do this. I take it one weekend at a time and always try to get the maximum out of it. Whether that's number 50, 55 or 45... The more, the better, of course, but it's not something I'm going to dwell on and pat myself on the back for, thinking, 'This is really good.' No, not at all."

Nevertheless, the first two days in Singapore have been special. Verstappen has topped every significant session so far – sprint qualifying, the sprint race and regular qualifying – despite the street circuit often proving to be Red Bull's Achilles' heel in recent years.

You might think that would be cause for satisfaction, but Verstappen is still not entirely happy when speaking to the Dutch media in the paddock.

"No, because of course it isn't perfect," Verstappen replied when asked by Autosport why he did not look 100% satisfied. "There's always more to be found and I always want to get more out of it. That's what we'll keep working on."

Extra focus on the start in Singapore

Two aspects were not optimal for Verstappen on Saturday in Singapore: the downshifts and – far more importantly – his start in the sprint race.

Immediately after the shortest race of the weekend, Verstappen described his start as “horrendous” and warned that a repeat on Sunday could cost Red Bull the race.

A closer look at the starting problems reveals two separate issues. Yes, Verstappen has generally struggled with poor and inconsistent starts on numerous occasions this year, but in the wet conditions at Sepang and Singapore, the problem was also partly related to the team's recommendation on which gear to use.

Verstappen got beaten off the line by George Russell during Saturday's sprint Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

Verstappen started in second gear on both occasions – something fairly common in F1 in wet conditions – but several rivals, including Russell, opted for first gear on both occasions, which helped them to spool the turbo and get off the line more effectively with the 2026 power units.

Read Also: Formula 1 Verstappen urges Red Bull to fix race starts problem

"In Malaysia, it was a different problem. That problem was added on top of everything else, which meant starting in second gear didn't work properly there.

"Then the team thought: if that problem doesn't happen here again, starting in second gear should work fine this time. But it still wasn't good enough. My start was actually quite okay compared to most of the others, just not compared to George and Lewis."

The start will therefore be under particular scrutiny again on Sunday, especially with two Ferraris lining up immediately behind Verstappen – on average, the best-starting cars this season.

"Yes, you just know they will have good starts. They've been like that all season. It's always an important factor in Singapore, and if you've had a few poor starts, then naturally there's even more focus on it."

When Autosport asked Verstappen whether he would approach a potentially wet start differently tomorrow, he first made it clear that he was not necessarily hoping for such conditions.

"Hopefully it'll be dry tomorrow, first of all. Otherwise, we'll just have to see whether it's good enough."

Should it be wet, however, Verstappen hinted that he would change his gear selection this time. "I think it's pretty clear that second gear isn't the right gear for us at the moment!" the four-time world champion laughed.

Verstappen knows a good start will be crucial to potentially winning the Singapore GP for the first time Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

How can Racing Bulls have better starts than Red Bull?

Remarkably, sister team Racing Bulls has often enjoyed better starts than the senior team this year, even though Verstappen stressed that the hardware and software are completely identical.

"Everything is the same, but of course you have engineers who can use different settings for the clutch, the engine and different procedures for warming up the tyres and so on. So there is a difference there, between different people and how they operate."

According to Verstappen, that is precisely where Red Bull needs to improve, although he stressed that the situation is no longer as disastrous as it was at the beginning of the year.

"No, at the beginning I really had a lot of problems. A lot of random issues that kept coming up, and they also kept happening on my side of the garage."

Now it is more about the details, but Verstappen knows better than anyone that those details could make the difference between victory and defeat as he chases his first win at the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

"You know there's a good chance you'll win this race if you get a good start. But yeah, if you lose it because of that, then of course it's painful, but you also have to accept it. That's just how it is. But, of course, we'll do everything we can on Sunday."

Sports.title: A "better job" or more engine power? Verstappen's Singapore pole unpicked
Sports.content:
There's many a slip twixt cup and lip – and the ifs, buts and maybes nag even more insistently when the gap between pole position and P2 is measured in the thousandths of a second.

"I think there was potential to be on pole today, but Max just did a better job," said Charles Leclerc after falling 0.054s short of Max Verstappen in final qualifying for the Singapore Grand Prix. Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton, who had topped the first two segments of qualifying, was a further 0.069s in arrears after making a setup change which he felt transformed his SF-26 for the worse.

Leclerc admitted to making "some mistakes", as evinced by looking at the scrappy evolution of his times through qualifying. Only in Q1 did he set a faster lap than Verstappen, and that was after a second bite at the cherry; Max only did one push lap in that session, and it was good enough. Charles went for a third lap but it was so scrappy he bailed out of it late on.

Verstappen's gains through qualifying were more linear, suggestive of a driver not only gaining confidence (given just one practice session before going into sprint business), but also judging the track evolution well. Hamilton went the other way: after going fastest of all through Q1 and Q2 he felt there was more to come from the car and dialled in a little more front wing.

Lewis was pre-empting the track evolution a little and it put his car too on those nose, so he bled out laptime with oversteer snaps through the opening corners, then again at the chicane at the close of the lap.

Still, comparing Leclerc's fastest Q3 lap with Verstappen's reveals a clear trend towards the Red Bull enjoying a higher top speed on every straight. That could steer you in the direction of concluding that Max enjoyed more power – well, the Red Bull/Ford internal combustion engine is supposedly the most powerful in F1, after all – or was carrying less downforce.

Hamilton was fastest in Q1 and Q2 but pre-empted track evolution with a front-wing tweak which damaged his car's balance Photo by: Clive Rose / Formula 1 via Getty Images

It's tricky to be definitive, given the Ferrari's known strengths in slow-speed corners and its small-compressor turbo configuration, which lends itself to better punch out of those turns.

What we can see from the data is that Max opened his lap with a small top-speed advantage, in the order of 6km/h, but had to lift and brake earlier for Turn 1. By carrying more speed to the apex, Leclerc eked out a tenth of a second by Turn 2, building to two tenths by the exit of Turn 3. The onboard footage indicates he had the confidence to be much more aggressive on the turn-in phase.

But despite similar throttle traces, the Red Bull was up to 18km/h faster throughout the run from there to Turn 5, where again Leclerc had the confidence to commit to the corner later and stay on the throttle for longer. That stemmed the laptime leak but, once again, Verstappen had a straightline speed advantage – albeit smaller this time, in the order of 4km/h. Easily in the noise of having less downforce or drag.

Perhaps the Red Bull had shot its electrical bolt earlier in the lap? It's reasonable to conclude this, since Verstappen lifted off far earlier before the entry to Turn 7, suggesting more lift-and-coast than the Ferrari required. From there, through Turns 8, 9 and 10, a pattern emerged of Leclerc being much faster through the corners but Verstappen then clawing back those gains on the straights.

From a more granular point of view, the offset of the speed traces suggests Max was compromising his entry speed slightly for a more aggressive throttle-on at the exit, so he could hustle the car without taking it too close to the barriers at the exit. Looking at the onboard confirms this: he got the car pointing straight much sooner, enabling him to be in the acceleration phase while the Ferrari was still slowing to its minimum corner speed.

At Turn 13, the light left-hander before the Anderson Bridge, Verstappen had his only scrappy moment of the lap, having to apply a flick of opposite lock as the back end stepped out, sending him wide of the apex – but, again, like a cat landing on all four paws, he got it pointing straight earlier than Leclerc and was faster towards Turn 14 and the end of the sector.

Verstappen (blue trace) enjoyed a straightline speed advantage while Leclerc clawed back laptime in slow corners; in the end, Max's fluency through the final chicane made the difference Photo by: Autosport

Again, at Turn 14, Leclerc was later off the throttle and carried more speed. Verstappen then enjoyed fractionally better acceleration off the corner but the gap between them was by this point hovering around a tenth of a second in Leclerc's favour. Even with the Red Bull's now fractional speed advantage down the back straight, Leclerc was still fractionally up on entry for the right/left chicane of turns 16 and 17, dethrottling less sharply and taking fractionally more kerb at the first apex.

But Leclerc then got a little too greedy between the corners, holding half-throttle as Verstappen lifted almost completely off, which induced a transient moment of understeer in the Ferrari. That gave Verstappen a better exit angle again and a cleaner path to full throttle. Small margins, but it inverted the laptime delta in his favour and he held it all the way to the line.

Whatever balance of virtues the different cars had over the lap, it was Verstappen's lighter touch through this chicane which proved decisive.

"I think the whole weekend already we've had a strong car," said Max afterwards.

"So I knew it was going to be a tight battle, and I think you could see that throughout qualifying.

"I think the car has been in the right window the whole weekend, so it was more just fine-tuning and tweaking tiny little bits."

What's becoming clear is that Red Bull have finally got the RB21 into a place where Verstappen can work with it. Some of the weaknesses are still there, but gains in other places have softened the impact: it may not have the Ferrari's slow-corner performance, for instance, or the theoretical low-down grunt, but its stability and traction on corner exit offsets that.

And in Max Verstappen, Red Bull has a champion street fighter well capable of locating and exploiting any scrap of advantage he can find.

Sports.title: McLaren to talk internally after "simply not acceptable" Norris-Piastri clash
Sports.content:
On the final lap of a wet 20-lap sprint, Lando Norris made a lunge on Oscar Piastri on the inside of Turn 5, unsuccessfully backing out of a closing gap and striking his McLarne team-mate's right-rear corner.

The tangle sent both cars into a spin, with Piastri eliminated and sustaining severe damage to the rear of his MCL40 and Norris dropping down to eighth at the finish. The stewards summoned both drivers, but decided not to take further action because "the stewards considered that both drivers had contributed to the incident and that neither driver was wholly or predominantly to blame for the collision.

Be that as it may, it was still a costly and avoidable incident for McLaren, which had to scramble to replace Piastri's gearbox and repair his car - facing a hefty repair bill and losing valuable championship points.

Coming after a series of incidents in 2025, which prompted McLaren to tighten up its rules of engagement, the so-called Papaya Rules, team principal Andrea Stella was not amused with the latest episode between his drivers.

"Seeing two McLarens making contact like that is simply not acceptable," Stella told Sky.

"This is something we will discuss with our drivers, we will do it in private, we will reiterate that team interest is far bigger than any of us. There’s no ego, there’s no person that is bigger than the interest of the McLaren Formula 1 team."

Piastri revealed that Norris had apologised to him and the team about the incident, and subsequently the Australian chose diplomacy when facing the media.

"The biggest thing obviously is we just can't have that happen in terms of the points and also the workload and money," Piastri said.

"It just wasn't a situation that needed to happen, really. So, Lando apologised and we moved on.

Lando Norris, McLaren, Oscar Piastri, McLaren Photo by: Michael Potts / LAT images via Getty Images

"Unfortunately, it's not our first coming together, but I think we're both very good at saying sorry when we need to and moving on, and I think that's what makes us strong as a team."

Norris followed the stewards' reasoning, maintaining that both he and Piastri could have done something differently. "As you probably expect, no one's very happy. I'm not happy. Oscar wasn't happy," Norris said. "None of us wanted to go that way. There were things both of us could have done better. And yeah, we spoke about it and we moved on."

When put to Piastri that the stewards felt he also played a role in the incident, he replied: "I mean, I don't think there was anything massively out of line, but at the same time it's not very smart to try and get each other penalties, is it?"

Sports.title: Russell bemoans "very bad" Saturday at Singapore GP
Sports.content:
Mercedes Formula 1 driver George Russell conceded it was his own mistake that led to him crashing out of the Singapore Grand Prix sprint race – an accident which may have hindered his performance in qualifying.

Front-row starter Russell surged into the lead on a wet Marina Bay track with a much better getaway than polesitter Max Verstappen, but lost control as he ran ever so slightly wide on the exit of the last corner. The Briton spun into the inside wall and retired from the race.

As shown by his second place on the grid, Russell had been quick in sprint qualifying, but he couldn’t do better than sixth in the main qualifying session, which he believes is down to his mechanics having to hastily rebuild his W17.

“Obviously a very bad day all in all, and stemming from my own mistake,” Russell commented.

“The car didn't feel quite the same. I was struggling with the rear end and then I was overheating the tyres and it was just a bit of a downward spiral, whereas yesterday it all just clicked and it was all working well, so we need to see why that was.

“[This] is not, sometimes, a surprise when the whole team is putting it back together so quickly and it's obviously been in the wall. Yesterday we were competitive every lap we did, and today it was not the case.”

George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

That’s a theory that Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff can get behind, even though the squad still needs to look into it.

“With George, the car was only finished at the very last minute,” Wolff told Sky Germany. “The floor is probably not quite as it should be. So all in all, it was a good performance.”

Asked what he could aim for in the race, Russell was indecisive, with a power unit penalty – ensuing from his Sepang engine failure – relegating him to the back of the grid.

The 28-year-old is aware that while Kimi Antonelli stormed to victory from 19th in the Italian Grand Prix, in Azerbaijan it took him 17 laps to climb from 16th on the grid back into the top 10; admittedly the youngster was ‘driving like his grandmother’ in the streets of Baku.

“It's going to be very challenging,” said Russell, when asked by Autosport for what is possible on Sunday. “Kimi obviously had one race starting in 19th and won, and another race in 16th and was only up to P10 with 10 laps remaining or whatever.

"Same driver, same car, but very different outcomes. So to answer your question, I really don't know.”

Sports.title: F1 Singapore GP: Verstappen continues recent dominance with pole
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen clinched pole position for Formula 1’s Singapore Grand Prix, outpacing the Ferraris of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton as Mercedes struggled.

Championship leader Kimi Antonelli and George Russell finished just fourth and sixth, while Verstappen’s Red Bull team-mate, Isack Hadjar, will start from the back of the grid.

Q1 – Hadjar failed by his Red Bull

Laurent Mekies, Red Bull Racing Team Principal, Isack Hadjar, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Mark Thompson / Getty Images

The first qualifying segment got off to a poor start for Esteban Ocon, who locked up and appeared to graze the wall in Turn 13. Moments later, Lance Stroll suffered a similar fate in Turn 7. Both seemingly escaped those errors without damage.

Hadjar also had an off but ended up stopping out on track. “The engine is off,” he reported; the Red Bull driver eventually managing to restart his car and pitted without a time on the board.

Hours after colliding with Oscar Piastri in the sprint race, Lando Norris set the early pace in 1m33.047s, 0.029s quicker than his team-mate. Verstappen and Hamilton were 0.194s and 0.264s down respectively, with Mercedes duo Antonelli and Russell over half a second adrift.

With five minutes remaining, Arvid Lindblad, Alex Albon, Sergio Perez, Valtteri Bottas, Gabriel Bortoleto and Hadjar were the bottom six drivers; Stroll was just 0.04s clear of the 17th-placed Racing Bulls. Things weren’t going any better for Hadjar: “Same issue, I lost the gears,” he said. The Frenchman returned to the pitlane and never emerged back out.

As Hamilton took the lead with a 1m32.680s and improved upon it in 1m32.429s, three tenths faster than Leclerc and Norris after their respective improvements, Antonelli and Russell ended up 12th and 13th, nearly 1.2s adrift.

Further down the classification, major progress from Lindblad and Bortoleto kicked both Aston Martins out of the top 16; Alonso’s and Stroll’s day ended right there.

Out in Q1: Alonso, Albon, Stroll, Perez, Bottas, Hadjar

Q2 – Hamilton on top, albeit challenged by Verstappen

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Clive Rose / Formula 1 via Getty Images

Hamilton maintained a similar advantage on the opening runs of Q2, with his 1m31.766s putting him four tenths clear of Antonelli. Verstappen was over half a second adrift, complaining of “insanely bad” gear shifts, followed by Russell, Norris, Piastri and Leclerc – those five drivers within one-and-a-half tenth.

There were theoretically three Q3 spots for midfield teams, and with five minutes remaining, those were occupied by Liam Lawson, Lindblad and Nico Hulkenberg; Pierre Gasly was two tenths away from the German, in 11th.

Gasly actually improved by six tenths on his final attempt, jumping ahead of all his main rivals; the Racing Bulls managed to regain their advantage over the Alpine, but the Frenchman still clinched the final spot for the top-10 shootout, as Hulkenberg gained an insufficient two tenths late on.

Having clipped the wall in Turn 17, Franco Colapinto ended up down in 16th, a whopping 1.2s down on his team-mate.

Meanwhile, Hamilton perpetuated his dominance with a 1m31.529s, which only Verstappen came close to, in 1m31.639s. Norris and Leclerc were 0.366s and 0.424s down respectively. Antonelli and Russell, again, were more than half a second adrift.

Out in Q2: Hulkenberg, Bearman, Ocon, Sainz, Bortoleto, Colapinto

Q3 – Verstappen prevails in the final phase

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Lillian Suwanrumpha / AFP via Getty Images

It was actually Verstappen who set the pace early on in Q3 with a 1m31.373s, with Hamilton registering a 1m31.496s despite being nearly three tenths faster than the Dutchman in sector two.

Antonelli was up to an encouraging third place in 1m31.562s, with Leclerc, Norris and Russell all within four tenths of the leader. Piastri, however, was 0.820s adrift, having been slower than anyone but Lindblad in the final sector.

Both Verstappen and Hamilton failed to improve on their final attempts; the Briton was jumped by Ferrari team-mate Leclerc for second place, with the Monegasque 0.054s slower than Red Bull’s polesetter.

Piastri was the only other top team driver to improve, by some margin – over three tenths – but that was not enough for him to gain a position; he took seventh behind Antonelli, Norris and Russell.

Gasly was best of the rest for Alpine with a 1m32.225, while Lawson and Lindblad ended up 0.144s and 0.556s slower respectively to complete the top 10.

Sports.title: Verstappen urges Red Bull to fix race starts problem
Sports.content:
A day after topping a Formula 1 qualifying session at the Marina Bay Street Circuit for the first time, Max Verstappen has now added a victory at the same venue. Both sprint sessions underline that Red Bull has a more than competitive car in Singapore this year, although Verstappen himself still does not count these achievements.

When the four-time world champion was asked about the significance of this sprint victory, he immediately made it clear that it meant very little to him.

“I want to win tomorrow,” he said. “I don't see this as a win in terms of actually winning a grand prix.”

Verstappen has previously made it clear that he feels no emotion whatsoever when winning a sprint race, a format he is famously not a fan of. Nevertheless, it could be argued that victory in Singapore means slightly more given Red Bull's struggles at the street circuit in recent years.

However, when Motorsport.com put that to Verstappen, it turned out not to be the case. The sprint underlines that Red Bull is heading in the right direction with the RB22, but for Verstappen it means nothing more than that.

“My emotion is the same,” he added. “It doesn't matter to me if I have won on the track before or not.”

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: James Sutton / Formula 1 / Formula Motorsport Ltd via Getty Images

It means Verstappen's attention is entirely focused on Sunday's grand prix. Qualifying is naturally crucial, given how difficult overtaking is in Singapore, but Verstappen also points to another major concern for Red Bull: its starts.

In Malaysia, Verstappen saw both Mercedes cars surge past him, and the same thing happened with George Russell in Singapore on Saturday.

“The start was horrendous again, so that's definitely something that we need to improve on,” admitted Verstappen. “If you have something like that tomorrow, that's your race over, if nothing crazy happens.”

Asked what exactly went wrong, Verstappen responded: “As always, it just doesn't go off the line. The car just doesn't go, we don't accelerate off the line.”

Red Bull has been struggling with this for some time, raising the question of whether there are any potential solutions for Sunday or whether the team will simply have to hope for the best.

“We have a few limitations that we have to work on, and that is probably from our side as well,” said Verstappen. “We have to do a better job because Racing Bulls sometimes does better starts than us, so yeah, we just need to be better.”

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

On Saturday, the poor start ultimately did not prove costly, as Verstappen saw Russell crash out in front of him at the end of the opening lap.

“He was already sideways a few times in that first lap, so I think he was just pushing quite hard on the first lap,” said Verstappen. “And then in the last corner, he clipped the white line and, of course, it did send him into the wall. It’s an easy mistake to make, I guess, and unlucky at the same time.”

Verstappen himself tried to avoid taking such risks, knowing that overtaking is virtually impossible unless someone makes a mistake. That was even more the case on a partially wet track, as the drivers found out there was only one racing line.

“It was calm in a way, but at the same time, you need to be focused. If you relax, it’s easy to make a mistake or go wide, so it was more about paying attention,” Verstappen explained his mindset.

“Stay calm, but pay attention on the road ahead with your tyres degrading and the road becoming dry in some places and greasy in others. You just have to be patient.”

Verstappen managed to do just that, although he still has two more steps to take towards the victory that – unlike the sprint race – really matters to him: getting the second qualifying session of the weekend right and improving his start.

Sports.title: F1 Singapore GP: Verstappen wins chaotic wet sprint after Russell's crash
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen won the Singapore Grand Prix sprint race from pole position after ephemeral leader George Russell crashed out at the end of the very first lap.

A downpour soaked the grid 15 minutes before the scheduled start, while some parts of the Marina Bay Street Circuit remained dry. The race was delayed by half an hour due to the standing water in Turns 2 and 3.

By the time the sprint got under way, it still was a tale of two halves in terms of track conditions, and all cars started on intermediate tyres after two formation laps.

Front-row starter Russell had a much better getaway than Verstappen and took the lead even before Turn 1, with Lewis Hamilton up to third from sixth on the grid. Charles Leclerc, Oscar Piastri, Lando Norris, Kimi Antonelli, Liam Lawson and Pierre Gasly followed, with Isack Hadjar down to 11th.

Russell’s lead was short-lived, as he lost control of his W17 on the kerb at the exit of the last corner and spun into the inside wall at the end of lap one. Meanwhile, Lance Stroll and Sergio Perez collided at Turn 16, with the Aston Martin coming to a halt against the barriers, and Hadjar retired after reporting “the engine braking is dying”.

The safety car was called into action, with the race neutralised for five laps – during which Arvid Lindblad spun, rejoining in last place after driving the wrong way down the track, and Franco Colapinto’s race ended because of a technical issue.

Marshals before the delayed start Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

Verstappen maintained the lead at the restart, while Oliver Bearman snatched eighth place away from Gasly after wheel-to-wheel action throughout sector one. The Alpine driver lost another two positions over the following two laps; he complained of being pushed wide by Nico Hulkenberg, but the stewards took no further action.

Verstappen’s gap to Hamilton hovered between 0.7s and 1.4s from lap seven to lap 11 before the Red Bull racer significantly pulled away, with his advantage reaching three seconds at the end of lap 13 and five seconds by lap 16.

The intermediate compound was greatly suffering on the mostly dry track, so it was all about tyre management. Leclerc reported his front tyres were “destroyed”; the Ferrari driver was losing two seconds a lap to team-mate Hamilton and was caught by the McLarens and Antonelli with three laps remaining.

But Norris dove down the inside of Piastri on the final lap and the McLaren duo collided into a spin. The reigning world champion consequently dropped to eighth, while his Australian team-mate retired.

Meanwhile, Verstappen romped to victory with a reduced but healthy 2.6s-second lead over Hamilton, as Leclerc completed the podium in third. Antonelli inherited fourth ahead of Lawson, Bearman and Hulkenberg, with Norris taking the final points position.

Sports.title: Featured Comment: F1’s latest technical glitch shows its power unit rules are too intrusive | Briefs
Sports.content:
Five days after the embarrassment of multiple cars stopping on the formation lap in Sepang, Formula 1 was struck by another technical glitch in Singapore.

This time a “human error” meant some drivers had less power than their rivals during the first round of qualifying for the sprint race. The FIA admitted this resulted in some drivers being left at a disadvantage

Reader @Salty says this shows Formula 1’s electronics systems are too intrusive and power delivery should be exclusively under the control of the drivers and teams:

Energy deployment needs to be solely the provenance of the driver’s right foot. I don’t want the circuit mapping skills of an errant piece of software to continue impinging on F1. That is not racing. It isn’t better, smarter or more capable than any one of the 22 drivers on the grid at the moment. It does not ‘improve the show’, it has made it look stilted and awkward. If some manufacturers won’t race without electric assisted systems, they shouldn’t be looking at F1. There are plenty of car categories for driving with active suspension, battery recovery and deployment and non-driver power deployment. Bumper car and driverless taxi companies need not apply. We have seen multiple instances this season of the driver being left in the cockpit of an F1 car without full control of the throttle. Bin it before it makes another stupid decision and someone dies.

Sports.title: Hamilton admits set-up change spoiled car balance after missing out on pole position | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton revealed a last-minute set-up change was the reason he struggled in the final part of qualifying in Singapore.

The Ferrari driver was quickest in the first two rounds of qualifying but fell to third place in Q3.

“It’s just balance,” Hamilton explained after qualifying. “The car felt good. I think my team, the engineers, did a fantastic job, as well as the mechanics, between the sessions.

“The car felt amazing in Q1 and Q2, and when I finished the laps, I was like, “She’s got more in her.” And the only way in order to try and extract that is to try and add wing.

“In doing so, I think it just tipped it over the edge. It was only like one hole [of front wing angle] or something like that, but it was just on the knife point, and after that then the car was just snappy, and none of the laps in Q3 are any good. So, I’m grateful to be third, to be honest, given that those laps weren’t very good.”

Hamilton made a strong start in Saturday’s sprint race, jumping from sixth on the grid to third. With Charles Leclerc starting in front of him in the other Ferrari and Max Verstappen on pole position, Hamilton says he and his team mate can co-operate to attack the Red Bull.

“The right side is hopefully a little bit better to start on,” he said. “It’s obviously a short start, the start that I had was obviously in the wet, so it’s much different when it’s dry. And I think tomorrow is [supposed to be] dry.

Sports.title: Russell aiming for sixth from back of grid in Singapore | Formula 1
Sports.content:
George Russell hopes he can salvage a top-six finish starting from the back of the grid in Sunday’s Singapore Grand Prix.

The Mercedes driver has to start from the rear of the grid after exceeding his maximum allocation of power unit components this weekend. His latest engine change was triggered by the failure which put him out of last week’s race in Malaysia.

“It’s going to be challenging, for sure,” said Russell. “When you look at Kimi [Antonelli] he started 19th in Monza and won, and then in Baku he was in 16th and got up to P10 with about 15 laps remaining. So same driver, similar track and two very different circumstances.

“So I hope I can get into the points, I hope I can [reach] P7, P6 depending on whether Hadjar’s got a penalty or not.”

Russell is running Mercedes’ older aerodynamic specification this weekend as the team investigates the differences between it and the new components it introduced to mixed results a week ago.

He crashed while leading the sprint race in Singapore and said his car hasn’t felt the same since. Russell said he completed several laps in qualifying “mainly just to make sure the car was feeling as it did yesterday after the crash this morning, but it didn’t quite feel the same in all honesty.”

“I had great pace yesterday, we were in the top three almost every lap that I competed. Today I wasn’t even in the top five at any point throughout the session. So I need to try and understand why that was.”

Sports.title: Collision between Norris and Piastri was “simply not acceptable” – Stella | Formula 1
Sports.content:
McLaren team principal Andrea Stella says the team cannot accept the collision between its drivers in today’s sprint race.

Lando Norris knocked team mate Oscar Piastri into a spin while trying to pass him for fourth place at turn five on the final lap. Having been on course to score nine points the team took just one, as Norris finished eighth.

The stewards issued no penalty after ruling neither driver was predominantly to blame but Stella made it clear the incident should not have happened.

“The sprint race was a race that was giving us some good points,” Stella told Sky. “In a moment in which we are not in condition to win, still we were in condition to score good points, and we saw two McLarens having contact.

“Basically [they went] out of the race. Lando could score one point, but definitely that’s not enough.

“Seeing two McLarens making contact like that is simply not acceptable.”

Norris and Piastri have clashed previously, notably last year in the Canadian and Singapore grands prix. Stella said he will remind the pair of their obligations towards the team.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“This is something that we will discuss with our drivers,” he said. “We will do it in private. We will reiterate that the team interest is far bigger than any of us.

“There’s no ego, there’s no person that is bigger than the interest of the McLaren Formula 1 team. This will be reiterated. I’m sure, like always, these will be conversations that will lead to the team being more united and even stronger.”

Norris revealed he apologised to he team for the collision. “You have two sides,” he said. “One is what the stewards say and I think that’s just a fair reasoning of what happened, no one’s to blame.

“But I did apologise because it was still me that was the one attacking, as I have the right to do – if I just sat there and was boring like I should be then nothing would have happened. So really it’s still my fault but I deserve to go for the space and I still believe I had the right for it.”

Piastri said “it was clear that those kind of things can’t happen.”

Sports.title: Verstappen takes second pole position in Singapore ahead of the Ferraris | 2026 Singapore Grand Prix qualifying report
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen claimed his second pole position of the Singapore Grand Prix weekend ahead of the Ferrari drivers.

Having taken pole position for the sprint race, which he won earlier today, Verstappen produced a lap of 1’31.373 to put his Red Bull at the front of the field again.

Lewis Hamilton looked a serious threat for pole position but the Ferrari driver faded in Q3. Having set the second-fastest time on his first run, Hamilton was unable to improve on his last lap, struggling with oversteer in the final corners, and fell to third place.

Charles Leclerc therefore joins Verstappen on the front row of the grid. Andrea Kimi Antonelli will start fourth.

The McLaren pair with share the third row of the grid. George Russell qualified sixth but will start from the back of the grid due to his power unit change penalty.

Pierre Gasly was the only Alpine driver to reach Q3 after Franco Colapinto smacked the barrier at the exit of turn 17. Gasly led the Racing Bulls drivers in Q3.

The Haas pair also went out in the second round, Esteban Ocon being relieved to get that far after skidding to a stop at turn 13 in the first session. Nico Hulkenberg took 11th on the grid but the stewards will investigate him for potentially impeding Carlos Sainz Jnr, who also dropped out in Q2. Alexander Albon did not get beyond the first round in his Williams.

Isack Hadjar’s grim day continued. Having retired from the sprint race with a technical problem he was quick to thank his team for repairing his car as SQ1 began. But his RB22 came to a stop again within minutes. Hadjar was able to drive it back to the pits but he took no further part in the session.

The Aston Martin and Cadillac drivers also dropped out in the first round. Lance Stroll chased Valtteri Bottas across the line then slowed sharply, locking his brakes.

Sports.title: Verstappen: F1 shouldn’t hold sprint races on tracks where you can’t pass | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen criticised Formula 1’s decision to hold a sprint race in Singapore.

The Red Bull driver, who won the first sprint race at the Marina Bay circuit today, said “wou can’t pass” on the track.

Verstappen lost his lead from pole position at the start of the race to George Russell. However the Mercedes driver crashed out at the end of the first lap and Verstappen led the rest of the race until the end.

Afterwards Verstappen said Singapore is a poor choice of venue for a sprint race. F1 will increase the number of sprint races from six to ten next year and hold them at other circuits where overtaking is renowned for being difficult, such as Monaco.

“We shouldn’t host a sprint where you can’t pass,” said Verstappen. “You have tracks where you can race and can overtake, but of course, in some places you cannot pass and we are going to have sprints there also next year.”

Verstappen has been one of the most vocal critics of F1’s sprint race format, which has proved divisive among fans. He has also repeatedly drawn attention to the shortcomings of F1’s current power units, which he says make it even harder to pass in Singapore.

“I’m fine, I just do my thing, but it’s not what I like,” he said. “Also the problem we have at the moment is with the Overtake Mode, it barely does anything here. You don’t really gain a lot on the straights.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“So also that with how all the rules are at the moment with our lovely batteries, it just doesn’t do much. You can’t even get super-close or have a massive overspeed at the moment.”

Although Verstappen said “the track is great” he also suggested the layout needs changes to encourage better racing. “I of course fully agree we need to have a longer straight or more of a proper hairpin to overtake,” he said. “But even with that also, we need a bigger delta [between speeds] on the straight.”

Lewis Hamilton said Saturday’s race would have lacked action if it hadn’t been held in wet conditions.

“I thought it was fun,” he said. “But if it was dry, that would have been probably the most boring race for you to have watched.

“It was the wet, the rain, that made it exciting. So if you can always make it rain, then it’s always going to be a great sprint race. But otherwise, it would probably just have been straightforward tyre management, everyone sticking behind each other.”

Hamilton’s team mate Charles Leclerc also questioned the wisdom of holding sprint races on street tracks. “I don’t think it makes sense to have any sprint races on city tracks in general,” he said.

“We probably should use these sprints to have them on tracks where it’s easy to overtake, where you can have a lot of racing action and it actually adds something to the weekend. Whereas here or Monaco, I don’t think it adds anything to the weekend.”

Sports.title: Vergil Ortiz Jr. Prioritizes Activity Over Opponent Quality
Sports.content:
Robert Garcia wants Vergil Ortiz Jr. back in the ring, even if that means accepting an opponent who does little to satisfy fans waiting for the Jaron Ennis fight.

Keith Thurman is the likely opponent for Ortiz’s proposed December 5 return on the David Benavidez card. Talks appear promising, though the fight has yet to be finalized. Ortiz is scheduled to begin training camp next week.

“I don’t care whatever people say. I just need Vergil back in,” Garcia said. “He’s been out for a year. … It’s going to be 13 months basically. So, that’s too much.”

That explains the willingness to take Thurman. Garcia’s priority is getting Ortiz through a training camp and into a fight. Looking for someone who offers more prestige could bring another delay, leaving Vergil inactive into next year.

Thurman would give Ortiz a recognizable opponent, but beating him would leave the bigger questions unanswered. Fans want to see Vergil against the strongest fighters around his weight. A return bout can restore activity without delivering that test.

Garcia accepts the criticism. He believes the cost of waiting has become greater than the benefit of holding out for a better opponent.

“If we try to switch up, find somebody else or maybe a bigger fight, a fight that means a little bit more, then it might take longer,” he said.

The same frustration is behind the team’s decision to campaign at 160 pounds. Garcia expects Ennis to pursue Josh Kelly and then potentially Sebastian Fundora, a sequence he believes could leave Ortiz waiting another year.

He understands Ennis’s interest in unification, while maintaining that Vergil would present a harder fight. Ortiz’s team is choosing to move forward rather than keep cutting to 154 for an opportunity Garcia cannot count on.

Getting Ortiz active is a reasonable immediate goal. After that, the urgency needs to extend to finding stronger opposition. Thurman can end the layoff; he cannot replace the fights that made fans eager to see Vergil return.

Sports.title: Fabio Wardley Believes He Can Break Daniel Dubois
Sports.content:
Fabio Wardley believes Daniel Dubois’ decision to take a knee in their first fight revealed a weakness he could exploit again, saying that he needed to inflict enough punishment to bring it out.

Wardley pointed to the third-round knockdown, when Dubois backed up before dropping to one knee after taking an overhand right. He viewed that sequence differently from the first knockdown, where he felt his punch connected more cleanly.

“He started to kind of back up and then chose to take a knee. It was just an overhand right. It was the same one I did in the first round,” said Wardley to DAZN.

That right hand gives Wardley something more concrete to work with than questions about Dubois’ heart. Dubois has a strong jab, but Wardley described using the overhand counter to make him think twice about throwing it.

“A way to take away someone’s jab is to let them know that a shot will be coming straight behind it,” Wardley said.

If Dubois hesitates with his jab, he could give Wardley more opportunities to close the distance. The challenge for Dubois is to keep using that weapon without leaving himself open to the same right hand. Abandoning it would make it harder to control where the fight takes place.

Wardley’s interpretation of the knee is more debatable. A hurt fighter can take a count to recover without wanting out of the contest. Wardley nevertheless believes there is a point at which Dubois can be persuaded to surrender.

“I just knew I needed to do enough to bring it out. But that still wasn’t enough for me. I still needed a bit more,” said Wardley.

The practical task is reproducing the punishment that led to that moment. Wardley has identified a punch that worked and a reaction he believes he can force again. Dubois needs an answer to the counter before he can prevent Wardley from testing that theory.

Sports.title: Naoya Inoue Prepares With Bam Rodriguez In Mind
Sports.content:
Naoya Inoue says he is preparing with Jesse “Bam” Rodriguez in mind, keeping attention on a potential fight between two of boxing’s leading pound-for-pound fighters.

“Yes, I’m preparing with Jesse ‘Bam’ Rodriguez in mind,” Inoue said, according to a quote shared by Source of Boxing.

That falls short of a fight announcement, but it gives fans something more concrete than another expression of interest. Inoue is thinking about Bam as an opponent while preparing for his next appearance.

The appeal is easy to understand. Neither bantamweight nor super bantamweight has an abundance of big names, leaving these two as the obvious pairing for a fight capable of drawing attention beyond followers of the lighter divisions.

Inoue has already cleaned out the 122-pound division, collecting all four belts and beating the opponents put in front of him. Bam is working toward doing the same at 118. Bringing them together would give Inoue a fresh challenge and Rodriguez an opportunity to turn his success across the lower weights into the biggest victory of his career.

There are still questions about the timing. Inoue’s agent previously identified March 2027 as the deadline for the fight, with a move to featherweight an alternative if it cannot be arranged. That timetable predates this latest quote.

For Bam, the challenge extends beyond adding four pounds. His footwork and ability to attack from changing angles could make Inoue work harder to find his target. However, Rodriguez would need to maintain that approach against a bigger puncher who can punish him whenever he stays within range too long.

That is what makes the pairing interesting. Bam has the skill to give Inoue something different to solve, while Inoue would test whether Rodriguez’s offense remains as effective against an elite fighter at 122.

Fans have good reason to want this one. Another defense against a lesser-known challenger would be difficult to sell with Bam available. Inoue’s comments keep the possibility alive, but an agreement is still needed before anticipation becomes a date on the calendar.

Sports.title: Jack Catterall Demands His Turn Against Teofimo Lopez
Sports.content:
Jack Catterall insists his title fight with Teofimo Lopez must come next, while Teofimo’s manager Keith Connolly left the outcome open with a brief response on X: “Let’s see how it all plays out.”

The comments follow FazSportz’s report that Teofimo has appealed the WBA’s September 22 order to face Catterall, seeking permission to pursue bigger fights. The October 22 negotiation deadline is approaching.

“Was awarded a voluntary title shot coming off a loss. Im next,” Catterall wrote. “I’ve got no doubts the WBA will honour what they said and agreed before I boxed Giyasov. More waiting around but it is what it is.”

Connolly’s response stopped short of promising that Catterall would get the fight. It also offered no explanation of how Teofimo’s team expects the dispute to end, leaving Catterall waiting while the champion pursues an exception.

The WBA’s published ruling supports Catterall’s account of the arrangement. When Rolando Romero was elevated to super champion at welterweight, the organization allowed him one optional defense, with the Giyasov-Catterall winner due to face him afterward. Teofimo defeated Romero on August 22 and inherited that obligation.

Teofimo’s appeal seeks permission to pursue bigger fights. That may make commercial sense for his team, but Catterall completed the route the WBA established. Allowing another opponent would mean extending his wait after the optional defense had already been used.

Catterall’s reference to Teofimo receiving a title shot coming off a loss sharpens his complaint. Teofimo received an opportunity without having to rebuild first. Catterall now wants the opportunity attached to his own win over Giyasov.

The sides have until close of business, Eastern Time, on October 22 to reach an agreement. If negotiations fail or either side withdraws, the WBA Championship Committee may order a purse bid with its president’s approval. That is a possible next step, rather than an automatic event on deadline day.

Teofimo could relinquish the belt to pursue another opponent. Keeping it while avoiding Catterall, however, would require the WBA to change the conditions it had already attached to the title.

Sports.title: Osleys Iglesias Wants Canelo Or Mbilli Winner
Sports.content:
Osleys Iglesias wants a unification against the winner of Canelo Alvarez’s October 31 fight with Christian Mbilli. Getting that fight could prove harder than defending his IBF title. Canelo has bigger commercial options, while Mbilli could be drawn into a lucrative rematch if he wins.

“I hope the winner [of Canelo-Mbilli] faces me. I’d like my next fight to be a unification,” Iglesias said after stopping Oliver Zaren in Quebec on Thursday.

The seventh-round stoppage lifted Iglesias to 16-0 with 15 knockouts. Those numbers help explain the difficulty of finding a willing opponent. He brings a world title, southpaw skills and heavy power, but lacks the name recognition that would turn a Canelo fight into a major event.

Canelo would be risking more than another points defeat. Iglesias has the power to hurt him and force a punishing fight, with a stoppage a serious possibility. Another belt might not be enough compensation when better-known opponents could offer more money and a better chance of winning.

Hamzah Sheeraz and Chris Eubank Jr. would give Canelo fresh opponents with British interest behind them. Neither is a guaranteed victory, but his team could view both as less dangerous choices than Iglesias.

Canelo also has a remaining fight under his agreement with Turki Alalshikh’s boxing operation. What Alalshikh wants to fund will influence the selection, leaving Iglesias competing against names that could sell a bigger show.

Mbilli appears more likely to accept a unification, but beating Canelo could change his immediate plans. A rematch would be difficult to turn down financially, provided Canelo wanted another attempt. His defeats against Floyd Mayweather and Dmitry Bivol did not produce second meetings.

If Canelo moves on, Mbilli against Iglesias would offer plenty in the ring. Mbilli’s relentless pressure would test the Cuban, while also bringing him within range of dangerous southpaw counters.

That is Iglesias’ best opening. A Canelo victory could leave him making another defense while the Mexican pursues a more profitable opponent.

Sports.title: Amir Khan Rules Out December Manny Pacquiao Fight
Sports.content:
Amir Khan is interested in facing Manny Pacquiao, but says he would not be ready for December 11. His admission leaves the proposed comeback dependent on more than agreeing on a payday, with the former light welterweight champion approaching five years out of the ring.

“That’s a rumor,” Khan told Metro about appearing on the Tyson Fury–Anthony Joshua undercard. “Even if it was for that fight night, I wouldn’t be ready for it, and I don’t think Manny would be either. “We’ve both been traveling, and we’re obviously not back in camp. It’s only about nine weeks away. I don’t know where that came from.”

Khan says talks are taking place and that he is happy with the money and location discussed. That establishes interest, but no signed fight or date has been announced.

The preparation question is particularly significant for Khan. He has not fought since Kell Brook stopped him in February 2022, and his last victory over a leading opponent came against Chris Algieri in 2015.

A longer camp could help Khan recover his conditioning. Whether he can regain the timing and reactions needed against Pacquiao is harder to judge. His best boxing depended on fast combinations and getting out before opponents could answer. Returning after years away would test both parts of that approach.

Pacquiao has been inactive too, but his July 2025 draw with Mario Barrios provides more recent evidence that he can compete over 12 rounds. Khan would enter negotiations without a comparable performance to point to since his retirement.

That difference makes a return fight worth considering before Khan commits to Pacquiao. Sparring can help him prepare, but an actual bout would offer a clearer picture of what remains.

Khan has always wanted the matchup, and the proposed terms appear attractive. His decision to dismiss December is sensible. The next question is whether additional time produces a prepared fighter or simply delays a difficult comeback.

Adding Pacquiao against Khan, who hasn’t fought since Brook stopped him in 2022, would turn the Cardiff card into an expensive nostalgia show. Fury–Joshua is already years overdue, and the proposed Jai Opetaia–Deontay Wilder fight features a faded former champion who turns 41 before December 11. Another pairing built around aging stars would leave the event trading heavily on what these fighters used to be.

Sports.title: Joshua-Fury Needs Promotion as Dana White and Eddie Hearn Bicker
Sports.content:
Dana White now describes himself as one of the promoters of Anthony Joshua’s December 11 fight with Tyson Fury, saying that his team will produce the event that night.

White’s latest comments put him alongside Eddie Hearn and Frank Warren in his description of the operation, although his clearest commitment concerns production.

“I’m producing the fight. Me and my team will be producing the fight that night. And I guess we’ll call me one of the promoters of the event because you do have Frank Warren and Eddie Hearn that are both promoters too, promoting the event,” White told BBC 5 Live.

The heavyweight fight is scheduled for Cardiff’s Principality Stadium. White also credited Hearn with securing the UK location during his interview with Steve Bunce.

The wording deserves attention. “I guess we’ll call me” sounds like White describing how he sees his involvement rather than announcing a newly agreed contractual position. It leaves the formal promotional arrangements unresolved, but makes clear that he expects a substantial role when the fighters enter the ring.

White and Hearn’s continuing argument over their roles is becoming tiresome. Every interview spent discussing who gets to call himself a promoter is another opportunity lost to explain why Joshua-Fury is still worth watching in December.

The names are familiar, but that does not mean the fight sells itself. Many fans see Joshua and Fury as two former champions meeting years after the contest should have happened. The promotion needs to address that skepticism rather than assume their past achievements will be enough.

There is still a fight to sell: the rivalry, the contrasting styles and the consequences of defeat for both men. Fans want to know what Joshua and Fury have left and whether either can produce something better than their recent performances suggest.

White and Hearn arguing over credit gives those viewers little reason to get excited. They need to spend more time promoting the fighters and less time promoting their own involvement.

Ghana News.title: MamaCare CEO warns unresolved conflicts among health workers could undermine maternal and neonatal care
Ghana News.content:
Maternal and Child Health Expert and Chief Executive Officer of MamaCare by Racheal, Mrs Racheal Hesse Matey, has warned that unresolved conflicts among obstetric care providers can undermine teamwork and compromise care for pregnant women and newborns.

Speaking at the Annual Health Conference at the Korle-Bu Nursing and Midwifery Training College, she said disagreements among health workers and failure to follow agreed clinical protocols could lead to misdiagnosis, inappropriate interventions and poor coordination.

“Sometimes, if there is conflict among the internal people and it is not resolved, the protocols that are supposed to guide us are not followed. This person is saying this, that person is saying that, and we are not coming to one agreement,” she said.

Mrs Hesse Matey said tensions among staff working the same shift could affect patient care, urging health facilities and training institutions to prioritise teamwork, communication and prompt conflict resolution.

She also called on midwives to continually improve their professional knowledge and skills to meet the expectations of increasingly informed patients.

She noted that many women research pregnancy and childbirth throughout their pregnancies, making it important for health professionals to have the knowledge and competence required to provide appropriate care.

“Before they come to the hospital, they know the condition they are going through. Right from pregnancy, the woman is already reading about what is happening from week to week, month to month. So she is well informed,” she said.

“And if you don't have the knowledge to care for your patients, then we are talking about maternal mortality.”

Mrs Hesse Matey further stressed that quality healthcare should not depend on a patient’s social background, financial status or appearance, insisting that every patient deserves appropriate and respectful care.

She also cautioned midwives and trainees against excessive mobile phone and social media use while on duty, stressing the importance of remaining attentive to patients.

Her remarks formed part of discussions at the conference on maternal and neonatal mortality, with an emphasis on the role of clinical competence, professional conduct and teamwork in improving outcomes for mothers and newborns.

Ghana News.title: Health professionals urged to translate medical knowledge into practice to save mothers
Ghana News.content:
Obstetrician-gynaecologist Dr Elikem Oklu has raised concerns about the continued loss of mothers and newborns to preventable causes, saying gaps between medical knowledge and clinical practice remain a challenge in Ghana’s healthcare system.

Speaking at an annual health conference at the Korle Bu Nursing and Midwifery Training College, he questioned why maternal and neonatal deaths persist despite the availability of medical expertise, drugs and health facilities.

“Why are women still dying in the midst of all this knowledge? It's because for most of us, we do not make a connection between what we know and what we do,” Dr Oklu said.

His comments come as Ghana continues to grapple with maternal mortality and concerns about the quality of care provided to pregnant women and nursing mothers.

Figures from the Ministry of Health put Ghana’s maternal mortality ratio at approximately 234 deaths per 100,000 live births, while institutional maternal deaths stood at 965 in 2025.

Dr Oklu said improving outcomes requires health professionals to apply their training consistently, particularly when responding to emergencies.

He also highlighted the importance of attitude and institutional culture, noting that empathy and communication can make a difference even when treatment does not result in a positive outcome.

He urged health workers to communicate openly on the wards, make appropriate referrals and renew their commitment to professional duty.

University of Ghana School of Law lecturer Rachel Haizel has meanwhile argued that medical facilities and health professionals are not sued often enough over alleged medical negligence.

She said limited litigation could weaken accountability for poor professional conduct in some health facilities.

“We are not suing them enough. If you see the kind of treatment that some of these health practitioners give to their patients, it's horrible,” she said.

Ms Haizel stressed that healthcare professionals owe patients a duty of care and must exercise reasonable care and skill in line with the standards expected of their profession.

The concerns raised at the conference place renewed attention on clinical practice, patient safety and accountability as Ghana works to reduce preventable maternal and neonatal deaths.

Ghana News.title: Conflicts among care providers linked to maternal, neonatal deaths – Expert
Ghana News.content:
Maternal and child health expert and Chief Executive Officer of MamaCare by Racheal, Mrs Racheal Hesse Matey, has warned that unresolved conflicts among obstetric care providers are indirectly contributing to maternal and neonatal deaths.

Speaking at the Annual Health Conference on Maternal and Neonatal Mortality at the Korle-Bu Nursing and Midwifery Training College, she explained that internal disagreements and failure to adhere to agreed protocols among caregivers on duty could result in misdiagnosis, inappropriate interventions and poor coordination, with patients bearing the consequences.

“Sometimes, if there is conflict among the internal people and it is not resolved, the protocols that are supposed to guide us are not followed. This person is saying this, that person is saying that, and we are not coming to one agreement,” she said.

She explained that when staff working the same shift are not on good terms, patient care suffers, stressing that interpersonal conflicts must be resolved promptly.

She therefore called on health facilities and training institutions to prioritise teamwork, communication and conflict resolution as part of efforts to reduce preventable maternal deaths.

Mrs Hesse Matey also underscored the need for midwives to strengthen their professional knowledge and skills to meet the expectations of increasingly informed patients.

“Before they come to the hospital, they know the condition they are going through. Right from pregnancy, the woman is already reading about what is happening from week to week, month to month. So she is well informed. She is even reading about what is going to happen in labour,” she said.

“And if you don't have the knowledge to care for your patients, then we are talking about maternal mortality,” she added.

She further stressed the need for equitable healthcare delivery, insisting that every patient deserves quality care regardless of their social background, financial status, or appearance.

Mrs Hesse Matey also cautioned trainees against excessive use of mobile phones and social media while on duty, stressing that every moment spent with a patient counts.

Ghana News.title: GIS marks 10th TIME conference, champions improved teaching practices
Ghana News.content:
The Ghana International School (GIS) has marked the 10th anniversary of its TIME Educators’ Conference, an initiative aimed at strengthening teaching practices and improving learning outcomes.

Held on Saturday, October 10, 2026, at the GIS Secondary School campus in Cantonments, Accra, the conference was organised under the theme, “10 Years of Impact: Transforming Education, One Teacher at a TIME.”

TIME stands for Transform, Inspire, Motivate and Educate. The initiative brings educators together to share practical teaching methods, exchange ideas and strengthen their professional skills.

Delivering the keynote address, founding dean of the University of Ghana’s School of Education and Leadership, Professor Jonathan Fletcher, highlighted improvements in teaching standards over the past decade.

“In 2017, when we developed National Teachers’ Standards, at that time I could not say that more than 10% of teachers could actually teach to those standards. At least 68% of our teachers can do that,” he said.

Professor Fletcher credited the conference with helping to spread improved teaching practices across the country.

“The idea of TIME is a great thing… the way teaching is done in this school is being propagated and so gradually teachers in this institution are actually infecting, as it were, teachers in this country,” he said.

On the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI), Professor Fletcher described it as a valuable tool for teaching and learning but stressed the need for ethical use and academic integrity.

He said educators must ensure that learners understand work produced with AI rather than simply presenting it as their own.

The Principal and Head of School at GIS, Nadia O. Bruce-Müller, said the conference began in October 2016 as an in-house initiative designed to give teachers an opportunity to learn from one another.

She explained that the initiative was created partly because not every teacher could travel abroad to attend professional development conferences.

The conference started with about 30 presenters from GIS but has since grown to attract more than 1,000 participants and nearly 100 presenters, including educators from other parts of Ghana and abroad. This year’s programme also featured two senior student presenters.

Mrs Bruce-Müller said the changing needs of learners and developments in education make continuous professional development essential.

“Our students are changing; the educational landscape ecosystem is changing. We can’t do it the same way we used to do it,” she said.

She explained that the theme, “Transforming Education, One Teacher at a TIME,” reflects the belief that every teacher can take at least one practical lesson from the conference back to the classroom and use it to improve learning.

GIS also provides about 100 to 200 free registrations or sponsored places for teachers from public and private schools to participate in the annual conference.

The 10th edition reaffirmed the conference’s focus on lifelong learning, collaboration and the adoption of effective teaching methods to meet the changing demands of education.

Ghana News.title: BRICS Or Balance? What Ghana’s bid really means
Ghana News.content:
Ghana’s decision to apply to join BRICS is not a diplomatic footnote; it is a strategic signal.

On October 6, 2026, Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa announced that Cabinet had decided to pursue membership, saying the objective was to diversify partnerships, widen economic opportunities and deepen cooperation with the Global South.

.India, whose foreign minister was visiting Accra, has been approached to help Ghana navigate the application.

The World Bank puts Ghana’s 2025 GDP at $114.2 billion, with 6.0 percent growth, while its population stands at 35.1 million.

Ghana is not a great power seeking to rewrite the international system or dictate the rules of global commerce. It is a middle-sized African state seeking more room to manoeuvre within it.

BRICS has grown considerably beyond the original Brazil-Russia-India-China grouping. Its current membership comprises 11 states, representing about 49 percent of the world’s population, 39 percent of global GDP and 23 percent of international trade.

Its expanding economic and geopolitical weight offers Accra a platform for trade, investment and diplomatic coalition-building.

Membership could provide another channel for engaging major emerging economies, reducing excessive dependence on traditional Western partners and broadening Ghana’s strategic options.

The attraction is not ideological alignment with every member, but the opportunity to operate in a wider economic and diplomatic ecosystem as global power becomes more dispersed.

Membership, however, is not automatic. Ghana has announced a bid, not secured a seat.

BRICS says accession moves from formal interest to potential membership and then full membership, with Sherpas, foreign ministers and ultimately leaders deciding by consensus.

Accra must demonstrate that its application can win political support from members.

The bid is therefore the opening move in a consequential geopolitical negotiation, not a guaranteed victory.

The test is whether Ghana can convert its interest into gains without damaging longstanding relationships with the United States, European Union and other Western partners.

The Economic Logic Is Powerful, But Not Magical

Ghana already trades heavily with BRICS economies, China and India. Ghana-China trade reached a record $14.1 billion in 2025, up 19.3 percent. In 2024, China supplied 45.9 percent of Ghana’s imports from Asia, while India supplied 13.7 percent.

This concentration creates opportunity and vulnerability.

A formal BRICS relationship could help Ghana move beyond buying manufactured goods and exporting raw commodities, supporting investment in processing, infrastructure, digital technology, energy and transport.

The New Development Bank makes the prospect relevant. It has $52.7 billion in paid-in capital and supports development projects across member countries.

For a country seeking infrastructure and industrial financing, engagement with the BRICS ecosystem could open additional channels of capital and development cooperation.

But BRICS cannot substitute for economic reform.

Ghana’s debt problems, currency risks, productivity constraints and dependence on commodities will not disappear because Accra sits at the table.

Diplomatic access is not guaranteed investment, and every proposed project must still meet Ghana’s needs, affordability tests and transparency standards.

The strategic prize is bargaining power.

Ghana could use closer ties with China, India, Brazil, the Gulf and other emerging economies to negotiate from a broader base with Western partners.

The objective should not be to replace one sphere of dependence with another, but to expand Ghana’s room for manoeuvre.

Membership can strengthen that position if Accra treats it as an instrument of diversification and strategic autonomy.

The Security Question Is More Complicated

BRICS is not a military alliance and offers no Article 5-style collective-defence commitment.

Its significance is political: it provides a forum for coordinating positions on global governance, sanctions, development and the international order.

Joining would not give Ghana a BRICS security guarantee against jihadist violence spilling south from the Sahel, maritime insecurity in the Gulf of Guinea or cyber threats.

Ghana’s existing Western security relationships remain substantial.

In August 2026, the Defence Ministry said US cooperation included joint exercises, intelligence sharing, counter-terrorism support, maritime security and plans involving drone-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance.

In September, Ghana reaffirmed its defence and security partnership with Washington, including logistics, institutional development, peacekeeping, cyber defence and maritime security.

Strategic balance is essential. Accra should not allow BRICS membership to undermine interoperability with the United States, European partners or African security institutions.

The objective should be diversification rather than substitution: add partnerships, markets and diplomatic options without trading one dependency for another.

The Geopolitical Price of Greater Autonomy

The deeper consequence is diplomatic. Ghana’s bid would place it more visibly in the debate over whether the international system should remain predominantly Western-led or become more plural and representative.

BRICS says it seeks stronger Global South participation and reform of global governance.

A stronger voice within Global South coalitions could reinforce its calls to reform institutions whose voting structures often lag behind economic realities.

But autonomy has a cost. BRICS includes China and Russia, whose relations with the United States and its allies are marked by strategic rivalry and, in Russia’s case, war-related sanctions.

Ghana may face pressure to clarify positions on sanctions, conflicts, technology standards and contested international norms.

BRICS criteria emphasize good relations among members, support for governance reform and, for partners, avoiding unilateral sanctions not authorized by the UN Security Council. Accra must be disciplined.

Ghana should join only if it can preserve what has made its foreign policy effective: flexibility, credibility and the ability to work across competing blocs.

The objective is strategic autonomy, not bloc politics.

The smartest policy is conditional engagement.

Ghana should seek market access, investment, technology, development finance and diplomatic leverage from BRICS while maintaining US and European security partnerships, ECOWAS commitments and wider African obligations.

The test is simple: does membership expand Ghana’s choices?

If yes, the bid is strategically sound. If it merely replaces one external dependence with another, it is not diversification; it is dependency under a different flag.

Ghana’s geopolitical asset is not allegiance, but room to manoeuvre as rival powers compete for influence.

Ghana is not choosing between East and West.

It is trying to ensure that, in an increasingly fractured world, it has enough partners to choose for itself.

— The writer is a lecturer in journalism and media studies and the CEO of The International Lens (theinternationallens.com).

Ghana News.title: GPRTU wants full TRAFFITECH-GH implementation to start in 2027
Ghana News.content:
The Ghana Private Road Transport Union has asked the police to postpone the full implementation of TRAFFITECH-GH to 2027, citing concerns over inadequate preparation and public education ahead of the November 1 rollout.

The union's Deputy Public Relations Officer, Samuel Amoah, said the necessary infrastructure and enforcement equipment must be ready before the system is implemented.

Speaking in a television interview with Channel One News on Friday, [October 9], he acknowledged the system's potential to improve road discipline but questioned whether the authorities were adequately prepared.

"It is very good they are bringing it just to make sure that there will be sanity on our roads. Drivers will comply. Police will also not be disturbing drivers or taking money from drivers but the question is, the infrastructure they have to put in place, are they ready?" he questioned.

Mr Amoah said some police officers he had spoken to did not fully understand how the system would operate. "Trust me, I once spoke to some police personnel. They don't even understand the whole thing," he said.

He urged the authorities to use the remaining time to educate motorists and ensure officers were adequately prepared before enforcement begins.

"If the authorities can even push it to the end of the year so that we can start from next year, so that effective education and sensitisation will be done," he added.

Mr Amoah also called for the necessary devices to be made available to help police officers check drivers' licences and other documents.

He cautioned against focusing primarily on revenue from traffic offences, saying the system should prioritise road safety and compliance.

Ghana News.title: Mahama announces plans to import electric wheelchairs for PWDs
Ghana News.content:
President John Dramani Mahama has announced plans by the government to import rechargeable electric wheelchairs for persons with disabilities (PWDs).

He explained that the pilot project was intended to facilitate the mobility of PWDs and said the wheelchairs would be handed over to the National Council on Persons with Disability upon arrival.

The President made the announcement during a citizens’ engagement in Goaso at the end of his two-day Resetting Ghana Tour of the Ahafo Region.

He said the initiative would be replicated annually if the pilot project proved successful.

President Mahama said the allocation from the District Assemblies Common Fund (DACF) for persons with disabilities had been increased from three per cent to five per cent under his administration.

He also announced that the Persons with Disability Act, 2006 (Act 715), which seeks to protect and promote the rights of persons with disabilities, would be amended as part of efforts to improve their living conditions.

On health, President Mahama said the government had implemented the Free Primary Healthcare Programme to provide free healthcare services to the public.

He added that the Ghana Medical Trust Fund, also known as MahamaCares, had been established to reduce the financial burden of treating chronic diseases, including cancers and kidney disease requiring dialysis.

Ghana News.title: KGL U17 Colts 2026: Western beat Prempeh Elite Academy to set up final final with Greater Accra Region
Ghana News.content:
Western Region delivered a composed and disciplined performance to eliminate Prempeh Elite Academy on penalties and secure a place in the final of the 2026 KGL Foundation Inter-Regional U17 Colts Championship at the Ghanaman Soccer Centre of Excellence on Saturday, October 10.

The first semi-final ended in a pulsating 1-1 draw after 80 minutes of regulation time, forcing the contest to be decided from the penalty spot.

Western Region appeared to have done enough to secure victory after Emmanuel Nyankumi fired them ahead in the 44th minute. However, Prempeh Elite Academy refused to surrender, with Thomas Asante striking two minutes from the end of regulation time to restore parity and breathe new life into the contest.

With neither side able to find a decisive goal, the semi-final went to a penalty shootout, where Western Region held their nerve to claim a 4-2 victory and book their place in Sunday's final.

The result marked a significant achievement for Western Region, who produced a disciplined display to overcome one of the championship's most impressive and free-scoring sides. Their reward is a place in the title decider, scheduled for Sunday, October 11, 2026, at the same venue.

Western Region will face Greater Accra, who defeated Brong Ahafo Region, for the championship crown.

The defeat brings Prempeh Elite Academy's impressive campaign to an end and leaves them to contest third place after narrowly missing out on a place in the final.

Sponsored by the KGL Foundation, the Inter-Regional U17 Colts Championship forms part of the Ghana Football Association's Talent Development Scheme (TDS), which is dedicated to identifying, developing and nurturing the next generation of Ghanaian football talent.

The competition provides promising under-17 players with a valuable platform to showcase their technical ability, tactical awareness and potential while gaining vital competitive experience against some of the country's finest emerging talents.
