World.title: Africa: Guinean Entrepreneur Mariama Camara Promotes African Textiles Worldwide
World.content:
interview

Guinean textile entrepreneur Mariama Camara is moving from promoting African textiles globally to building the institutions behind the industry. Through the Institute of African Textiles, she is pushing for greater ownership, protection and commercial value for the knowledge held by African makers.

African textile designer Mariama Camara believes the next phase of Africa's textile industry must move beyond global recognition towards ownership, stronger institutions and greater economic value for the people who hold its knowledge.

Camara has spent more than two decades working with artisans across Africa and taking their textiles into global fashion. Her collaborations have included Tory Burch, Ulla Johnson, LemLem and EDUN, helping bring "Made in Africa" textiles into major international markets while keeping the women and artisans who make them at the centre of the story.



Now, her focus is on building the infrastructure around that knowledge. Through the Institute of African Textiles, the African Textile Academy, the IE3 Museum of African Textiles and IAT Magazine, she is working to document, preserve, teach and strengthen the continent's textile ecosystem.

In this conversation, Camara reflects on the knowledge she inherited growing up in Guinea, the global collaborations that shaped her work and why she believes Africa's next challenge is to value, protect and build its own textile heritage.

Kindly introduce yourself and tell us what did growing up around generations of women who knew how to make textiles teach you about the value of African textile knowledge?

I am Mariama Camara, originally from Guinea and based in New York City for 25 years. My work focuses on empowering women and girls, advocating for artisans, advancing sustainability and bringing Made-in-Africa textiles to global markets. I am a textile designer and founder of Mariama Fashion Production, the Institute of African Textile, the IE3 Museum of African Textile and IAT Magazine, and co-founder of There Is No Limit Foundation.

Textile has always been part of my life. I was introduced to it at four, watching my mother and aunt create textiles, a tradition passed down through generations. My great-great-grandmother came from the Ghana Empire, while my maternal great-grandmother was a renowned textile designer in Kindia, Guinea, who helped establish a government textile training centre and taught artisans across West Africa, including in Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire.

For us, textile is not fashion. It is identity.

In 2008, my younger sister, Aissata M. B. Camara, and I co-founded There Is No Limit Foundation with a US$250 loan to a woman maker, Fatoumata Banjoura. Since then, we have sponsored 300 women and empowered 37,000 people.

When did you realise that traditional African textiles could compete in global markets?

I saw what was possible through our first collaboration with designer Tory Burch in 2012. Through There Is No Limit Foundation, which I co-founded with my younger sister, Aïssata, we showcased textiles made by women artisans in Guinea, particularly in Kindia.

That year changed everything. Our textiles reached Tory Burch stores worldwide, as well as Bergdorf Goodman, Saks Fifth Avenue, Galeries Lafayette and Harrods. Michelle Obama wore our Blue Jasmine dress on live television during her Drink Up campaign. After she shared the campaign, interest grew and the dress sold out. Reese Witherspoon, Naomi Watts and fashion editors also wore it. Our work appeared in major magazines, including Vogue and Elle, within 24 hours of the fashion show, and was featured in Tory Burch's book, *Tory Burch in Color*, which recognised our organisation and the artisans behind the textiles.

I became one of the first African textile makers to present handmade African textiles, created with local artisans, at New York Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week. The collaboration also took the work of Guinean artisans to global markets.

Seeing this impact made me realise how much talent existed across Africa. Our foundation focused on empowering women artisans, but I wanted to take African textiles further. That led me to establish Mariama Fashion Production, with a clear mission to make Made-in-Africa textiles respected in global luxury. I had seen our fabrics dismissed, with some people even calling them "cheap fabrics."

Since then, I have worked with thousands of artisans across Africa, from Guinea to Côte d'Ivoire. During Guinea's Ebola outbreak, I relocated my production studio to Côte d'Ivoire, where I produced textiles for brands including Ulla Johnson, EDUN, TOAST and Lemlem.

By 2022, I had achieved nearly every goal I had set for myself, except one: creating more than one million jobs. I believe my latest work through the Institute of African Textile can help me pursue that ambition by documenting African textiles and tracing their sources and ownership.

There is still a gap between the value of handmade African textiles and what comparable international brands can command. Where do you think the biggest opportunity is to close that gap?

The gap still exists, and that's why I founded the Institute of African Textile.

From 2007 to 2022, my work with brands and the rise of the African creative industry changed how big brands see us. They no longer see African textiles as cheap.

The gap now is our own confidence, how we market, sell, and position ourselves.

I used to be offered US$10 for my textiles. Today, I wouldn't accept that. I had to accept many things in the past because I had a vision of where I wanted to take my work. I wanted to prove how good I could be. Today, I value my work as bigger than any other textile brand or market.

I just returned from Switzerland, where I participated in the 12th International Shibori Symposium in Basel, with sessions at the Museum der Kulturen Basel and opening ceremonies at the Museum of History in Basel.

During my panel discussion, I introduced the Institute of African Textile and the five pillars of its ecosystem. I shared the panel with Indian and Thai artisans, among others. They knew how to express their work. There was a father and son from Japan working together and showcasing their textile heritage. It was very impressive because they knew how to package and present their work.

These are some of the things we need to strengthen in Africa: passing knowledge between generations while bringing new ways to present our work. Our generation has tools our ancestors didn't have. We can now package our culture and communicate its value to the world.

The world comes to you when you know how to package your culture. That is the gap we need to close. Through the Institute of African Textile, we are working to empower the African textile ecosystem by strengthening knowledge, visibility, and opportunities for its makers.

Africa already has a strong foundation for sustainable textile production through natural dyes, traceable materials and traditional knowledge. What advantage does that give the continent today?

Historically, Africa had a strong sustainable textile heritage. Our ancestors used indigo to create adire and mud to make bogolan. But after more than 18 years in this field, I have seen synthetic dyes and counterfeit textiles spread across the continent. Africa has extraordinary biodiversity and natural resources, yet its textile industry remains fragile.

Our ecosystem lacked structure and a platform to bring people together. That is why I founded the Institute of African Textile.

The idea came to me in 2023, during a trip to Nigeria at the invitation of the French Embassy. Someone asked how I wanted to be remembered and whether I was documenting my work. I later thought about my great-grandmothers and countless Africans whose contributions have been forgotten. I had assumed an Institute of African Textile already existed, but my research showed otherwise. I immediately secured the name and registered the company.

Today, the Institute brings together five pillars: the Institute of African Textile, Àá¹¢À | African Textile Academy, IE3 Museum of African Textile, African Textile Alliance and IAT Magazine. Together, they support documentation, preservation, education, collaboration and visibility, connecting African makers with global textile communities.

Sustainability is central to this work. In 2019, I partnered with Dr. Theanne Schiros, a scientist and educator at the Fashion Institute of Technology and research scientist at Columbia University, to work with textile makers in Guinea and Côte d'Ivoire. We developed more than 100 natural colours using African plants and other sources, including onion skins, avocado skins, bissap and kola nuts.

We trained makers to move away from harmful synthetic dyes towards natural alternatives and responsible production. For me, sustainability also means protecting artisans' health, strengthening their knowledge and building on Africa's existing resources and textile heritage.

How can documentation of African textile knowledge lead to ownership, income and opportunities for the people who hold that knowledge?

Documentation must begin with the past. We cannot focus on the present without understanding what came before us.

Many historic African textiles are held in Western museums, including the Met, the British Museum and institutions in Basel and Paris. Our younger generation has limited access to them. We need to ask what existed before us, who created it and who holds that knowledge today, so we do not repeat past mistakes.

Our ancestors created beautiful things that were taken, sold without their consent or undervalued. Today, we have technology, global connections and opportunities they did not have. The diaspora can contribute from wherever they live. I live in New York, but I have been able to make an impact on the continent.

I am now speaking with museums about their African textile collections and how we can access, study and document them. We want to collaborate, whether through acquiring or borrowing textiles or photographing them. Without access, our documentation will remain incomplete.

This must be collaborative. Some museum records are outdated or incorrect. By tracing textiles to their makers, communities and living traditions, we can help correct those records and strengthen our own work at the Institute of African Textile and the IE3 Museum of African Textile.

I have seen historic African textiles labelled "unknown artist." Our first project, *Know Their Names*, aims to change that by documenting historic textiles alongside the people who make them and preserve their knowledge today.

Aboubakar Fofana is one example. He is a giant in African indigo dye knowledge, invited to teach around the world, from Japan to India and the United States. Knowledge like his must be recognised and valued.

Funding remains a major challenge in Africa's creative industries, as does ensuring that support reaches the people doing the work. Institutions such as Afreximbank, through CANEX, are funding creatives, but access remains an issue. We must work together to identify the people and institutions that need this support.

We must also address competition and jealousy among creators. We do not need to keep establishing institutions to compete with one another. We need to strengthen existing, well-structured institutions and work together to make progress.

Whenever I have a platform or a seat at the table, I remind people that it is not only for Mariama. It is for every young African, creative and immigrant with a dream. We need diverse voices in decision-making. I imagine a table where Hillary Clinton sits alongside an artisan from Côte d'Ivoire, with me and the press. We must create space for people to be heard and give them access to opportunities.

What do you want to change about who owns, controls and benefits from African textiles by the time your work is done?

I want this work to go beyond me. Just as I am continuing my family's textile lineage, I hope my daughter and her children will carry it forward, alongside future generations of Africans. I want to build an institution that gives them the knowledge, structure, and opportunities to continue this work. This cannot stop with me.

The Institute of African Textile is a Pan-African institution dedicated to documenting, preserving, teaching and advancing African textile knowledge. But I don't want people to see it only as a company. It is an ecosystem.

You cannot separate the textile from the maker, the community, the material, the dye, the loom, the knowledge, the economy, the designer who transforms it, the museum that preserves it, the school that teaches it, or the market that gives it value.

It is built on five pillars: the Institute of African Textile, Àá¹¢À | African Textile Academy, IE3 Museum of African Textile, African Textile Alliance and the editorial platform, IAT Magazine.

For too long, global media has covered Africa as a small story. It saddens me that our creatives sometimes feel their work is validated only when it appears in publications such as Vogue or Elle. With IAT Magazine, I am changing that perspective. We cover the global textile industry from an African perspective, bringing African creatives and textile practitioners from around the world into the same editorial conversation.

Close 

I want an African media platform to be a respected source of knowledge and recognition for textile work everywhere. Africa needs to build its own strong institutions and media platforms, with the confidence and capacity to cover both the continent and the world. We have the knowledge, talent, and perspective to contribute to global conversations and help shape them.

We just launched our global issue with almost 10,000 readers.

I love to think big or go home, as we say in New York. God did not call us to feel small. Africa is free today because of Kwame Nkrumah, Sékou Touré, and all who stood up and said "No more." I see my work as a modern continuation of that spirit: advocating for the continent, creating opportunities, and building institutions that will continue when I am no longer here.

I have always advocated for Africa and worked to set new precedents, including founding Kanafrik, Africa's first sustainable store. I want to continue creating those possibilities and inspire others to do the same.

How do you balance commercialisation with the responsibility to protect the meaning and techniques of the communities behind African textiles?

It is about boundaries, education and responsibility. People need to understand the difference between heritage textiles, artisan-made textiles and original designs developed by brands. Using a heritage textile does not mean a brand created the knowledge or tradition behind it.

Bogolanfini, for example, comes from Mali, where communities continue to preserve and practise that knowledge. We must find ways to acknowledge, empower and compensate the people behind these traditions. Even at the Institute of African Textile, we are working through these questions.

The recent discussion around NanaWax's use of a lépi-print scarf, customised with a client's name for a private sale in Guinea, brought this issue into focus. Léppi de Guinée is registered as a Protected Geographical Indication through the African Intellectual Property Organization (OAPI), recognising its specific origin and production tradition.

We need to educate brands and designers about textile heritage and the protections attached to it. That means understanding what we use, where it comes from, how it can be used and which communities should be involved.

African countries and institutions are paying greater attention to protecting textile heritage. As the industry evolves, African designers and brands must apply the same care we expect from international brands. We need to research origins, distinguish authentic heritage textiles from printed reproductions, acknowledge traditional knowledge and understand when permissions or partnerships are necessary.

The questions are how we create commercial value while protecting tradition, and how that value reaches the makers and families keeping the knowledge alive. Through the Institute of African Textile, we want to help build that understanding so creativity, commercial opportunity and respect for African textile heritage can grow together.

World.title: South Africa: Zuma Remains in Hospital as Conflicting Reports Emerge Over His Health
World.content:
Former South African president Jacob Zuma has remained at a private hospital in Pietermaritzburg. However, there have been conflicting accounts about his health following his admission.

The uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party said Zuma had attended a routine medical check-up, a procedure he undergoes twice a year, and reassured supporters that he was "healthy and in good spirits".

According to News24, his brother Khanya said that Zuma was unwell and remained in hospital. He said the situation was concerning and that the family was praying for Zuma's recovery.

The 84-year-old former president is set to testify before the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) cases inquiry in two weeks.

Zuma was president from 2009 to 2018.

He now leads the uMkhonto weSizwe Party. His hospitalisation comes as his party continues its campaign activities for the local government elections on 4 November.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 9, 2026
World.content:
press review

Home Affairs Withdraws Asylum Directive After Soweto, Durban Unrest

The Department of Home Affairs has withdrawn a directive on the intake of asylum applications following violent anti-immigration protests in Soweto and Durban, where at least 24 vehicles were torched and foreign-owned businesses were looted. The directive was introduced after a July Constitutional Court ruling that allowed asylum seekers to apply for protection regardless of how they entered South Africa or whether they missed immigration deadlines. However, mounting pressure on refugee reception offices, concerns over staff safety and threats to public order prompted the department to reconsider its approach. Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi welcomed the withdrawal, saying it creates an opportunity for further consultation without undermining the court judgment. The ruling remains in force, and asylum applications must still be assessed individually. Police are investigating cases of vandalism, assault and public violence as authorities remain on alert for further unrest.

Yemen Conflict Escalating, Endangering African Economies, Regional Stability

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Fears are mounting over Africa's economic stability, maritime trade and humanitarian situation due to the conflict involving Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. Fears of further disruption to world trade have been raised by the alleged seizure of Yemen's Perim Island by the Houthis. The island lies near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping route linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. If the strait becomes impassable, shipping companies may be forced to divert vessels around the southern tip of Africa, increasing transport costs, insurance premiums and consumer prices. African economies are already grappling with fuel and fertiliser shortages linked to disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict has also triggered a humanitarian crisis, with at least 3,700 refugees reportedly crossing from Yemen into Djibouti since September 10, mostly women and children. Djibouti faces additional pressure because of limited water resources, while neighbouring Ethiopia is particularly vulnerable because it relies on Djibouti's ports for about 95% of its imports and exports. Renewed fighting in Ethiopia's Tigray region and escalating tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea could further destabilise the Horn of Africa and threaten shipping through the strait. African countries have called for a United Nations-led diplomatic solution. Ports in Kenya and Tanzania could benefit from increased shipping activity if vessels continue to avoid the Red Sea.

Ethiopia's Humanitarian and Food Crisis Worsens as Tigray Conflict Flairs

Renewed fighting in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region is exacerbating an already dire humanitarian crisis that has seen millions of people face food shortages after years of conflict, displacement and drought. Four years after a peace deal was signed in 2022, communities are still struggling to recover from the effects of the unresolved territorial disputes, limited reconstruction and reduced international aid. About 44% of Tigray's prime agricultural land remains inaccessible to displaced residents, and erratic rainfall and prolonged dry spells have wiped out crops and grazed away livestock grazing areas. Regional assessments have reported the destruction of over 252,500 hectares of planted crops, dire conditions in 140 districts, and the threat of starvation and disease to over 3.5 million livestock. Some 3.9 million people require urgent food assistance, with millions more still in need of adequate support. Renewed hostilities since late September have further disrupted humanitarian operations through air strikes, damage to infrastructure, telecommunications blackouts, and closure or seizure of regional airports. Aid deliveries are either suspended or delayed, and the looting in Mekelle has destroyed the critical supplies, vehicles and medical equipment of humanitarian organizations. These losses have disrupted services for healthcare and support for displaced people and vulnerable children, including children living with HIV. Humanitarian workers are calling for an immediate pause in fighting and safe access for food, medicine, fuel and cash to reach affected communities, warning that continued disruption could push the region towards famine.

At Least 84 Kenyans Killed or Missing in Russia-Ukraine War

At least 84 Kenyans have been killed or remain missing in connection with the Russia-Ukraine war, according to figures released by Kenya's Ministry of Foreign and Diaspora Affairs. The government has identified 354 Kenyan nationals as having become involved in the conflict, including 77 reportedly on the front lines, 38 in military camps and 52 whose locations remain unknown or unclassified. Another 34 are hospitalised, 62 have been repatriated, and five are being held as prisoners of war in Ukraine. One Kenyan is in detention, while another has completed their military contract. Prime Cabinet Secretary and Foreign Affairs Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi said Ukrainian authorities confirmed the five prisoners of war on September 3, adding that Kenya is seeking to have them recognised as potential victims of human trafficking because some reportedly enlisted after receiving misleading employment offers. The government is pursuing their release and repatriation while investigating the deaths and disappearances of other nationals, including four whose remains are reportedly in Ukrainian custody. Kenya also says it secured Russia's inclusion of Kenyan nationals on a "Stop List" during a diplomatic visit in March, a measure intended to prevent further recruitment. Mudavadi has urged families to report missing relatives promptly to help authorities verify cases, trace their whereabouts and provide assistance. The government says it will continue diplomatic efforts and strengthen preventive measures against deceptive recruitment.

Guinea-Bissau Elections Face Delay

Guinea-Bissau's planned presidential and legislative elections, scheduled for December 6, could be delayed after Prime Minister Ilídio Vieira Té said the conditions necessary to hold the polls had not been met. Following a meeting with transitional President and junta leader General Horta N'Tam, Té said political parties were not adequately prepared to contest the elections and that several needed to renew their leadership structures. The National Electoral Commission also warned that organising the polls on the scheduled date would not be technically feasible, although no formal postponement has been announced. The elections form part of a 12-month transition programme introduced after the military seized power on November 26, 2025, just days after presidential and legislative elections were held but before their results were declared. The takeover halted the electoral process and led the junta to schedule new elections for December 2026. Political tensions have since intensified, particularly after the authorities barred former president Umaro Sissoco Embaló from returning from exile earlier this month, citing national security and public order concerns. Embaló had intended to contest the presidential election. The junta has also faced opposition over constitutional changes approved in an August 30 referendum that strengthen presidential powers and alter the country's political and electoral framework. With no new election date announced, uncertainty remains over the country's political transition and the restoration of civilian democratic rule.

Close 

Wajir Patient Tests Negative for Ebola, Positive for Malaria

Kenya's Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale has confirmed that a patient in Wajir County who was being assessed for a possible Ebola infection has tested negative for the virus and positive for malaria. The patient, who was receiving treatment at Habaswein Sub-County Hospital in Wajir South, was started on antimalarial medication after laboratory results confirmed the diagnosis. The findings have eased concerns about a possible second Ebola case as Kenya strengthens surveillance following its first confirmed imported case, involving a Kenyan citizen who had lived in the Democratic Republic of Congo for seven years and died in Nairobi on October 6. The deceased patient travelled from the DRC through Uganda before boarding Jambojet flight JM8523 to Nairobi on October 3, and laboratory tests confirmed Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease. Health authorities are tracing family members, healthcare workers and passengers who may have been exposed, while strengthening screening at points of entry and preparedness at designated treatment facilities. Wajir Governor Ahmed Abdullahi has called on residents to stay calm and not circulate unverified information. The Ministry of Health says Kenya is not experiencing an outbreak of Ebola on a large scale. Authorities continue to encourage good hygiene, prompt medical attention for concerning symptoms, and strict infection prevention measures among healthcare workers. Members of the public can access official health information through the Ministry's toll-free line, 719. The Wajir patient's negative result is separate from the confirmed imported case in Nairobi, and surveillance efforts remain ongoing.

World.title: South Africa: Home Affairs Withdraws Asylum Directive After Violent Anti-Immigration Protests
World.content:
Chaos erupted in Durban city centre during a march by hundreds of anti-immigrant protesters.

The Department of Home Affairs (DHA) has withdrawn a directive on the intake of asylum applications following violent anti-immigration protests in Durban and Soweto, as the government seeks to find a way to implement a Constitutional Court ruling without further escalating tensions.

The directive, issued on 28 September, followed a July judgment by the Constitutional Court in the Scalabrini Centre of Cape Town case. The ruling struck down provisions of the Refugees Act that prevented some asylum seekers from accessing the application process on procedural grounds before their claims could be assessed on their merits.

The judgment allows asylum seekers to apply for protection regardless of how they entered South Africa. However, it does not automatically grant applicants refugee status or permanent residence, as each claim must still be assessed in accordance with the law.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Home Affairs said the directive was introduced as an operational measure to implement the court order but was issued by the department’s director-general without the knowledge of the minister or other political office-bearers.

The department said the implementation process had presented unforeseen challenges, with Refugee Reception Offices overwhelmed by the number of people seeking to submit asylum applications within days of the directive being issued.

It also raised concerns about the safety of departmental officials and the potential impact on public safety and order.

The department will now develop a revised operational approach to ensure compliance with the Constitutional Court’s judgment while addressing the challenges experienced at its offices.

The withdrawal of the directive does not overturn the court ruling, and Home Affairs has yet to announce details of its revised approach.

The development follows violent protests in Durban and Soweto during which vehicles were torched, and businesses vandalised amid growing opposition to immigration and the processing of asylum applications.

Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi has welcomed the department's decision, describing it as a relief that creates an opportunity for further consultation.

World.title: South Africa: Four Killed in Germiston Shack Fire - South African News Briefs - October 9, 2026
World.content:
press review

Four Killed in Germiston Shack Fire

Four people, including three children aged two, five and seven, have died in a fire that destroyed 12 shacks at the Marathon informal settlement in Germiston, Gauteng, reports EWN. Ekurhuleni Emergency Management Services spokesperson William Ntladi said the victims' bodies were found beneath the rubble. Ntladi said the scene has been handed over to the South African Police Service (SAPS) for investigation, rehabilitation and the removal of the deceased. The cause of the fire remains unknown and is under investigation.

R10 Billion Bill Adopted to Help Stabilise Fuel Prices

The Standing Committee on Appropriations has adopted the Second Special Appropriations Bill, which proposes withdrawing R10 billion from the National Revenue Fund to help stabilise fuel prices amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, reports SABC News. Committee chairperson Mmusi Maimane said that consumers should receive immediate relief from fuel price volatility. The Bill will soon be tabled in the National Assembly for consideration.

Govt Warns Against Asylum System Abuse

The government has warned foreign nationals that those who do not qualify for asylum or refugee status will be deported, following the Department of Home Affairs' resumption of asylum application processing, reports EWN. Minister in the Presidency Khumbudzo Ntshavheni said the process would help identify undocumented migrants and those attempting to misuse the system. The announcement comes amid heightened tensions over immigration, with protests turning violent in Durban’s CBD and Soweto, leaving about 20 vehicles torched.

World.title: Nigeria: American Lobbying Firms Disagree Over $57m U.S. Lawsuit Against Tinubu
World.content:
DCI Group has rejected allegations in a $57 million US lawsuit against President Bola Tinubu and others, while Femi Fani-Kayode's office says he has not been formally served.

American lobbying firm DCI Group has rejected allegations made by Washington-based lobbyist Karl Von Batten in a $57 million lawsuit against President Bola Tinubu, the Federal Government of Nigeria, former aviation minister Femi Fani-Kayode and the firm.

DCI has been hired by the Nigerian government for lobbying activities in the United States, while Mr Von Batten is doing the same work for former Vice President Atiku Abubakar.

Mr Fani-Kayode's office also told PREMIUM TIMES that he had not been formally served with the court papers and maintained his earlier denial of the allegations.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The case, filed at the United States District Court for the District of Columbia on 28 September, concerns allegations of defamation and a conspiracy to kidnap and physically harm Mr Von Batten. The claims are disputed and have not been established by a court.

DCI, Fani-Kayode respond

In an email to PREMIUM TIMES on Wednesday, Craig Stevens of DCI Group dismissed the allegations.

"Mr. Von Batten's allegations are so far past unfounded that they reach the point of the absurd," Mr Stevens said.

He said DCI's work for the Nigerian government focused on strengthening relations between Nigeria and US policymakers and referred the newspaper to the firm's disclosures under the Foreign Agents Registration Act.

Mr Stevens did not address the specific allegations individually.

Mr Fani-Kayode's office, responding separately, answered "No" when asked whether the former minister had been formally served. It also confirmed that he stood by his earlier denial of the allegations.

Mr Fani-Kayode had previously indicated that he would pursue a $100 million counterclaim against Mr Von Batten.

Asked whether the counterclaim had been filed or lawyers instructed to commence proceedings, his office replied: "All in good time."

The response did not confirm any filing.

What the lawsuit alleges

The US federal court docket identifies the case as Von Batten v. Tinubu et al., No. 1:26-cv-03374, before Judge Randolph D. Moss.

The defendants include President Tinubu, the Federal Government of Nigeria, Mr Fani-Kayode, DCI Group AZ, LLC, and 10 unidentified persons.

In a public announcement, Von Batten-Montague-York said it was seeking $36 million jointly from President Tinubu and the Nigerian government, $3 million from Mr Fani-Kayode and $18 million from DCI.

The firm alleged that the defendants were involved in efforts to defame, kidnap or physically harm Mr Von Batten over his advocacy concerning US government records relating to President Tinubu.

Close 

The publicly accessible docket records the filing and issuance of summonses, although this does not establish that the defendants have been formally served.

PREMIUM TIMES has requested the complete file-stamped complaint and exhibits to examine the allegations and the damages sought.

Presidency, others yet to respond

PREMIUM TIMES contacted the Presidency through Bayo Onanuga, Special Adviser to President Tinubu on Information and Strategy, seeking its response to the allegations, confirmation of any formal service and its position on the court's jurisdiction.

The enquiries were sent by email and WhatsApp, followed by telephone contact and reminders.

The newspaper also contacted Mr Atiku's ADC campaign to establish whether the former vice president or his representatives knew about the lawsuit before it was filed and whether they endorsed its allegations.

The campaign was further asked about the status of Mr Atiku's $1.2 million lobbying agreement with Mr Von Batten's firm, payments made and their source.

Mr Von Batten was separately contacted for the full complaint, supporting documents and his response to the denials by DCI and Mr Fani-Kayode. PREMIUM TIMES also sought clarification on the alleged threats, the damages claimed and whether the incidents had been reported to US law-enforcement authorities.

During a telephone call to his firm's office on Thursday, an answering-service representative took the reporter's contact details and said the enquiry would be forwarded.

By the time this report was filed, the Presidency, the ADC campaign and Mr Von Batten had not provided substantive responses.

World.title: Kenya: U.S. Report Flags Kenya's Failure to Act On Officials Linked to Human Trafficking
World.content:
Nairobi — Kenya has failed to report meaningful enforcement action against public officials and recruitment agencies allegedly linked to human trafficking, with a new United States report warning that official complicity continues to undermine the country's efforts to prosecute the crime.

The 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report said Kenyan authorities investigated three Ministry of Labour officials suspected of accepting bribes to facilitate potential trafficking involving migrant workers travelling to the Middle East, but highlighted broader concerns over alleged collusion between public officials and recruitment networks.

The report also found that the government had not reported action against recruitment agencies allegedly owned by government employees and suspected of facilitating trafficking, with authorities frequently pursuing lesser offences such as failure to register recruitment companies.



"Corruption and official complicity in trafficking crimes remained significant concerns, inhibiting law enforcement action during the year," the report stated.

The findings raise questions about accountability within institutions responsible for regulating overseas recruitment and protecting Kenyans seeking employment abroad.

Media reports cited in the assessment indicated that more than 10 per cent of Kenyan government officials held ownership interests in private employment agencies, including firms recruiting migrant workers for jobs overseas, creating potential conflicts of interest.

Observers also alleged that criminal syndicates colluded with law enforcement and immigration departments at border checkpoints and airports to transport trafficking victims into and within Kenya.

The report further cited allegations that some Kenyan embassy officials in Saudi Arabia demanded sex or cash payments from women seeking government assistance to escape abusive employers and return home.

The allegations come against the backdrop of declining anti-trafficking prosecutions and convictions.

Kenya convicted six traffickers in 2025, down from 21 in 2024, while prosecutions fell from 44 cases to 14.

The government investigated 43 trafficking cases during the year, compared with 42 in 2024.

The report also detailed allegations involving the fraudulent recruitment of more than 1,000 Kenyan men to fight for the Russian military in the war against Ukraine, with officials reporting that Kenyan and Russian officials had colluded with illicit recruiters to facilitate the recruitment.

Despite the concerns, Kenya remained on Tier 2 in the US assessment, which recognises significant efforts to combat trafficking while finding that the government has not fully met the minimum standards for eliminating the crime.

Close 

The report credited Kenya with identifying more victims, repatriating citizens exploited in overseas online scam operations, and securing its first civil judgment against a fraudulent recruiter.

However, it said persistent concerns over official complicity continued to hamper law enforcement and victim identification, while protection services for adult survivors remained limited.

World.title: South Africa: Navi Pillay's Nobel Win Draws Attention To Her Work Defending Media Freedom And Beyond
World.content:
Navi Pillay speaking at the South African National EditorsÂ Forum (SANEF) Nat Nakasa Award for Courageous Journalism in 2022.

Recognised by the Norwegian Nobel Committee for her efforts to promote peace and international law, Navi Pillay is being celebrated by African media, legal and civil society voices for a career advancing justice, accountability and human rights — including the right to report freely and safely.

Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize, announced on Friday, 9 October, is drawing attention to her support for media freedom and a career spanning some of the most consequential developments in international human rights law.

The South African jurist has backed initiatives to strengthen legal protections for free expression and promote a free and pluralistic information space.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Pillay is the fifth South African to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, following Albert Luthuli, Desmond Tutu, Nelson Mandela and F. W. de Klerk.

Announcing the Nobel, Norwegian Nobel Committee chair Jørgen Watne Frydnes linked Pillay’s early legal work under apartheid to her later role in international justice, from defending Nelson Mandela and others who opposed apartheid to serving as a judge in major international cases.

The committee said she had helped strengthen the international legal order and institutions responsible for holding perpetrators of serious crimes accountable. It also highlighted the uneven application of international law and the ability of powerful states and leaders to evade responsibility.

“Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful co-existence," the committee said.

Pillay’s win is particularly being celebrated by the media fraternity in Africa, most of whom are citing her efforts in defending media freedom.

Reacting to the announcement, Moky Makura, executive director of Africa No Filter said Pillay “embodies African agency”.

“For decades, she has worked tirelessly to create the change she wants to see in the world. This Nobel Prize shines a well-deserved spotlight on her extraordinary contribution. It is a reminder that African progress is not always about what is happening, but also about what the world is failing to see,” Makura said.

Churchill Otieno, president of The African Editors Forum (TAEF), also said Pillay’s record held particular significance for journalists because of its emphasis on accountability and the right to report freely.

“From her struggle against apartheid to her work in international human rights and law, she has shown that peace cannot endure without accountability,” Otieno said.

“For us journalists and media workers, her record also speaks directly to the right to report freely and safely. As UN High Commissioner, she called for journalists to be protected from political interference and physical threats. Her recognition affirms that defending human dignity, press freedom and the rule of law takes courage, especially when powerful interests resist scrutiny.”

In February 2025, Pillay delivered the keynote address at the launch of South Africa’s Free Expression Legal Network in Johannesburg. Developed by the South African National Editors’ Forum (SANEF), the Press Council, the Campaign for Free Expression and other organisations and legal experts, the network connects journalists and others facing legal threats over their expression with support, including legal representation.

Information and digital rights activist Izak Minnaar notes that Pillay had actively supported the network and advanced media freedom initiatives internationally.

“As the only South African on the global Information and Democracy Commission, she has been spearheading initiatives to support media freedom in South Africa and beyond,” Minnaar explained.

Anton Harber, director of the Henry Nxumalo Foundation, said Pillay had been particularly consistent in defending independent journalism.

“Navi Pillay has stood firm on many human rights issues, but has had particularly clear, strong and consistent views in defence of media freedom and the importance of independent journalism.”

“Whenever called upon to defend the media, she has been quick to stand up and be counted, even when it was not an easy thing to do. Her prize will be celebrated by journalists,” Harber added.

At the network’s launch, Pillay stressed the value of collective action. “If you clap with a single hand, nobody yells for you. But if a lot of people form a network clap, they will be heard,” she said, according to SANEF.

In its statement congratulating her, SANEF recalled Pillay’s call for governments to promote a free press that can “combat disinformation, build public trust and advance the promotion and protection of human rights.”

She also emphasised the need to protect those who help journalists expose wrongdoing. “I would say that such action must also protect media sources and whistle-blowers,” she said, according to SANEF.

Pillay served on the International Commission on Information and Democracy, convened by Reporters Without Borders in 2018. The 25-member commission developed principles for protecting freedom of expression and democratic debate in the global information space. Its declaration described information and communication as a common good and called for freedom, pluralism and reliable information.

President Cyril Ramaphosa said the award recognised Pillay’s contributions to peace and human dignity in South Africa and internationally.

“She has served humanity with principle and the belief that the world can and should be a better place,” Ramaphosa said.

Mameltwe Sebei, president of the General Industries Workers Union of South Africa (Giwusa) and an attorney at Lawyers for Human Rights, described the Nobel as recognition of Pillay’s legal career serving oppressed and marginalised people.

Her work defending anti-apartheid activists and involvement in international cases concerning atrocities, including the Rwanda genocide and the occupied Palestinian territory, made the award a source of pride for South Africans, he said.

“Most importantly, this should affirm our commitment to the principles of justice that underpin the work of any lawyer who stands on the side of the oppressed,” Sebei said. “She represents that type of jurist, that type of lawyer, and this Nobel Peace Prize is a well-deserved recognition of that.”

South Africa’s parliamentary Portfolio Committee on International Relations and Cooperation also described the award as a source of national pride, citing Pillay’s contribution to international justice and accountability for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.

Na’eem Jeenah, Senior Researcher at Mapungubwe Institute for Strategic Reflection (MISTRA) and political analyst said the award carries significance beyond South Africa.

“This then is an honour not only for South Africa but for the whole of Africa, a continent that is battling with its own conflicts and violations of international law,” Jeenah said.

While he believes the Nobel Prize would not change conditions for Palestinians nor stop the violence in Gaza, it “adds to the body of moral and legal evidence against Israel, including several UN reports (including on genocide), and the ICJ genocide case”.

Born on 23 September 1941 in Clairwood, Durban, to a family of Indian Tamil descent, Pillay grew up under apartheid. She graduated from the University of Natal with a bachelor’s degree in 1963 and an LLB in 1965.

In 1967, she became the first Black woman to open her own law practice in Natal, now KwaZulu-Natal. She represented political detainees and exposed abuses including torture and solitary confinement. In 1973, she successfully challenged restrictions preventing political prisoners from accessing legal counsel, according to South African History Online.

After earning postgraduate law degrees at Harvard University, she became the first Black woman appointed to South Africa’s High Court in Natal in 1995. She also participated in the Women’s National Coalition during the country’s constitutional transition and co-founded Equality Now, an organisation campaigning for the rights of women and girls.

In 1995, Pillay joined the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, established to prosecute those responsible for the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi. She became its president in 1999, serving until 2003.

A landmark case during her time on the tribunal was the trial of Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former local official convicted of genocide and crimes against humanity. The tribunal’s 1998 judgment established that rape and other forms of sexual violence could constitute acts of genocide when committed with the intent to destroy a protected group, in whole or in part.

Pillay later served in the International Criminal Court’s Appeals Division from 2003 to 2008. She became United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights in 2008, serving until 2014, a period that included the Arab Spring uprisings and the Syrian civil war.

Close 

Her later work included international proceedings and investigations into alleged serious crimes. In December 2019, she was appointed an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice in the case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar over alleged genocide against the Rohingya minority. The court confirmed its jurisdiction and ruled the application admissible.

From 2021 to 2025, Pillay chaired the United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel.

In September 2025, the commission concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. Israel rejected the conclusion. The finding was made by a UN commission of inquiry, not a final judgment by an international court.

The commission’s work highlighted a central challenge for international law: translating findings of serious violations into consequences for those responsible, particularly when powerful states are involved.

The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) said the award underscored the importance of international law at a time when its institutions face growing pressure.

“Throughout her long career, Navi Pillay has set a high moral example, speaking out and standing up for justice, accountability and the rule of law,” said SIPRI director Karim Haggag.

Haggag said the award also recognised the institutions Pillay had served, warning that powerful states were increasingly resorting to power politics and transactionalism while international law and its institutions faced attack.

South African investigative organisation Open Secrets also welcomed the award, saying it affirmed the importance of international law and its promise of holding human rights abusers to account.

Pillay was a panellist at the first People’s Tribunal on Economic Crime in the arms trade, convened by Open Secrets and civil society partners in 2018. The tribunal sought accountability for arms companies and politicians in the aftermath of apartheid and State Capture.

The announcement also prompted a lighter moment. Reacting to the news in Nuremberg, Pillay joked with supporters, “If you clap a little bit louder, I may share this prize with Trump,” according to an amateur social media clip.

World.title: Tulsa's David Wells Jr. tips ball to himself for improbable touchdown in wild play against Navy
World.content:
Saturday's college football slate is headlined by two SEC matchups that are some of the best rivalries in the sport - but that doesn't mean there aren't eyebrow-raising plays elsewhere.

Tulsa visited Navy on Saturday, and the Golden Hurricane scored a touchdown that nobody could have drawn up.

With just under two minutes to play in the first quarter, the game was tied at seven when Tulsa was at the opposing 10-yard line.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Quarterback Baylor Hayes tossed a backwards pass to wide receiver Oran Singleton Jr., who was stuffed roughly seven yards behind the line of scrimmage.

However, he managed to escape a tackle and throw a floating prayer into coverage. But one of his fellow pass-catchers made an improbable rescue.

David Wells Jr. (not related to the former pitcher) tipped the ball backward to himself outside of the end zone, caught it, and then scampered back in for the score.

That wasn't the only action Singleton got - he would catch a touchdown of his own later on to give Tulsa a 26-14 lead early in the second half.

It has not been a pleasant season for the Midshipmen, who were nationally ranked and won the Commander-in-Chief's Trophy by defeating both Air Force and Army last year. Navy also won the Liberty Bowl to complete an 11-2 season.



But entering Saturday, they already had more losses than they did all of last season.

The weather also caused ESPN's "College Gameday" to record their show indoors at Coleman Coliseum on the campus of Alabama. That made for a far less raucous and smaller crowd. One thing that caught football fans eyes online was a photo shared by Daily Wire reporter Brecca Stoll, which showcased a disclaimer about what signs were allowed in "The Pit" during filming.

THE STORM IS HERE: GEORGIA-ALABAMA SET TO WRITE LATEST CHAPTER AFTER CHAOTIC WEEK AROUND HURRICANE ISAIAS

No Food or Drink

World.title: Veteran walked across four continents and just swam the English Channel to return home
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A British Army veteran has returned to his home country after a 28-year journey across four continents — but his trek isn't quite over.

Karl Bushby, a 57-year-old former paratrooper, reached England this week after swimming across the English Channel from France, marking the latest milestone in an around-the-world expedition that he embarked on in 1998.

Now, he has roughly 250 miles left to walk before reuniting with his mother, whom he hasn't seen in 11 years.

DIVERS BRAVE DEADLY 'MOUNT EVEREST OF SHIPWRECKS' AS FAMED WRECK BREAKS APART

Bushby spent about 20 hours swimming in the English Channel over three days before reaching Shakespeare Beach near Dover on Oct. 5, according to the BBC.

"Getting in the water that first day, I thought, 'Have I taken too much of a bite here?'" Bushby told the outlet. "But you dig deep. Keep on keeping on. You find a rhythm."

Bushby hadn't even trained for the last leg of the trip and after about an hour in the water, he was cramping and doubting whether he could finish, he told the BBC.

CLIMBER STRANDED ON 6-INCH LEDGE AT 11,000 FEET AS 46 MPH WINDS GROUND RESCUE HELICOPTER

But the Channel crossing was just the latest obstacle in an expedition spanning more than 30,000 miles and 29 countries.

Bushby set out from Chile on Nov. 1, 1998, and set two rules for himself: He would not use transportation including planes, trains, boats or cars to advance his expedition route and he would not return home to Hull until he had finished it.

His route took him the length of South America, through North America and across the Bering Strait between Alaska and Russia.

CLICK HERE TO 

Along the way, he trekked through the Darién Gap between Panama and Colombia and, in 2006, crossed the frozen Bering Strait on foot and over ice with Dimitri Kieffer, a French-American adventurer.

More recently, Bushby swam about 184 miles across the Caspian Sea before continuing west toward Europe.

His expedition faced delays related to visa restrictions, the loss of sponsors during the 2008 financial crisis, COVID-19 lockdowns and geopolitical turmoil, according to reports.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Bushby began his expedition with just $500 and no sponsors, relying over the years on book sales, speaking engagements, donations and corporate sponsorships to keep going. A documentary production company also provided support for the past 16 years, according to reports.

When Bushby finally reached France, he was hoping to cross into England on foot through the Channel Tunnel's service tunnel, which connects both countries, but his request was rejected over safety and maintenance concerns, according to the BBC, leaving him to swim the English Channel instead.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Bushby said floating on his back at night and looking at the stars offered a distraction from the physical pain he was in during the swim.

"You're far away from light pollution and have the whole night sky in front of you," he said. "It gave me something to think about and took my mind off the pain and aches. It was amazing."

The last leg of the journey will bring him to his mother, who he hasn't seen since 2015, in the port city of Hull, The Times of London reported. He is expected to arrive in early November.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I walked away from that place 28 years ago and that is where we are going to wrap it up," he told the outlet. "That’s about 400 kilometers from here, so I’ve got to get busy."

World.title: Bill Belichick earns first win against ranked opponent as UNC upsets No 25 Pitt on road
World.content:
Bill Belichick earned the biggest win of his college coaching career Saturday.

North Carolina defeated No. 25 Pitt 21-17 on the road Saturday at Acrisure Stadium, marking Belichick's first win over a ranked opponent as UNC's head coach. It was UNC's first win over a ranked opponent since beating No. 25 Miami in 2023 and its first road win over a ranked opponent since defeating No. 9 Miami in 2020.

World.title: 8 seriously annoying tasks you can hand off to an AI agent
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

I have a growing list of things I would gladly never do again. Checking the same airfare every morning is on it. Digging through an overflowing inbox is right up there too. And I would be perfectly happy never having to remember when some free trial is about to start charging me. This is where AI agents are starting to get genuinely useful.

A regular chatbot waits for you to ask a question. An AI agent can potentially keep working on something after that first conversation. It might monitor a price, watch for an opening or keep tabs on a task you would otherwise have to remember yourself. OpenAI, Meta and Google are all pushing further into this kind of AI. OpenAI now has Dots and ChatGPT Work, while Meta has Muse and Google has Gemini Spark.

That all sounds very impressive. But I am less interested in having an AI run my life than I am in having it take a few irritating chores off my hands. So if you are wondering what you would actually do with one of these agents, start here.

Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better healthcare. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist.

See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com

AI AGENT HACKS GYM SYSTEM TO MOVE UP WAITLIST

What are ChatGPT Dots, ChatGPT Work, Meta Muse and Gemini Spark?

ChatGPT Work is only one way to try an AI agent. OpenAI also offers Dots, which are more persistent. A Dot has its own cloud computer, can remember ongoing work and can keep making progress between conversations. Dots are currently rolling out to eligible ChatGPT Pro, Business Premium and Enterprise users. OpenAI says Dot usage will temporarily not count against eligible users' plan allowances during the introductory period, with longer-term usage terms still to come.

ChatGPT Work is built into ChatGPT and focuses on longer, multi-step tasks. On web and mobile, OpenAI says Work is available on eligible paid plans, including Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu, although access is still rolling out. Work can research, use connected apps and files, create finished materials and run scheduled or recurring tasks.

There are alternatives too. Meta Muse offers a free tier with usage limits, with a paid subscription available if you need more. Gemini Spark is Google's personal AI agent and is available to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in supported regions. It can manage ongoing tasks, use connected Google services and run scheduled workflows.

You do not need the most powerful or expensive agent to try the ideas in this article. Start with whichever service you already use, give it a low-risk task and see whether having AI continue the job actually saves you time.

How to get started with an AI agent in ChatGPT

If you have never used an AI agent, the first step is simply knowing where to find one. We will use ChatGPT Work as an example. OpenAI is rolling the feature out to eligible accounts, so what you see can vary depending on your plan and device. Before you get started, I recommend checking a few privacy settings so you have more control over what ChatGPT does with your information.

Check your ChatGPT privacy settings first

You can stop new ChatGPT conversations from being used to train OpenAI's models. Here's how:

Go to ChatGPT.com and sign in. If you do not have an account yet, choose the option to sign up and create one.

Click your profile icon.

Select Settings.

Click Data Controls.

Turn off Improve the model for everyone.

Your conversations can still appear in your chat history, but new chats will not be used to train OpenAI's models.

Next, review ChatGPT's memory settings:

Open Settings.

Select Personalization.

Find Memory.

Turn off Enable memory if you do not want ChatGPT using remembered information to personalize future conversations.

You can also use Temporary Chat for conversations you do not want saved in your history or used for model training. OpenAI may still retain these chats for up to 30 days for safety purposes. Finally, review your connected apps under Settings > Plugins. Remove any connections you no longer need. Keep in mind that turning off model training does not prevent ChatGPT from processing information you provide to complete a task.

Start using ChatGPT Work

Once you've reviewed those settings, you're ready to give an AI agent its first task. Here's how to get started:

Look near the top of the screen for Chat and Work .

Click Work .

Start a new chat .

In the message box, describe the task you want the agent to handle.

Add any useful files or information the task requires. If the job needs access to a supported app, ChatGPT may give you the option to connect it.

Be specific about what the agent can and cannot do. For example, you can tell it to research or draft something without sending, booking or buying anything.

Send your request and follow along as the agent works. Review its results before approving anything important.

You do not need to start by connecting your entire digital life. In fact, I would not. Try a simple task first, such as researching several products within a budget or comparing options for an upcoming trip. That lets you see how the agent works before you give it access to email, calendars or other personal information. Once you are comfortable with the basics, the eight ideas below show where an AI agent can start saving you some real time.

MALICIOUS BROWSER EXTENSIONS CAN HIJACK AI ASSISTANTS

1) Have AI prepare you for the day

I do not need another app demanding my attention first thing in the morning. What I would like is something that looks at the information I already have and tells me what I need to know. An AI agent with access to your calendar and other approved information could review what is coming up, flag a meeting you need to prepare for and surface something time-sensitive you might have missed. The key is asking for a briefing instead of another information dump.

Prompt to try:

"Review my calendar and relevant messages for today. Tell me what I need to prepare for, flag anything time-sensitive and point out any scheduling conflicts. Do not send messages or change my calendar without asking me first."

That last sentence would absolutely stay in my prompt. I want AI to tell me that my afternoon looks impossible. I do not want it quietly deciding which meeting gets moved.

2) Stop checking the same price over and over

You find a flight. It costs too much. So you check again tomorrow. Then you check again the next day. I have done this with airfare, hotels and products I was not in a hurry to buy. It gets old fast. This is almost a perfect AI agent task because there is very little value in you personally opening the same page 12 times. Give the agent the item and the price you are hoping to hit. Then let it tell you when something changes.

Prompt to try:

"Track the price of [item, flight or hotel]. Let me know if the total price drops below $___ or if you find a comparable option that costs less. Show me the details before taking any action."

You can even use this after a purchase. If the retailer offers price adjustments or you are still inside the return window, have the agent keep watching. I like this type of task because the AI does the watching while I keep control of the wallet.

3) Let AI sort the email you do not want to sort

There are days when opening my inbox feels like volunteering for another job. Some emails need an answer. Others are simply FYIs. Then you have the message you meant to answer two days ago sitting underneath six newsletters and a shipping notification. An AI agent connected to your inbox can help with that first pass. It can summarize what arrived, identify the messages that appear to need attention and prepare a reply for you to review.

Prompt to try:

"Review my unread email from the last 24 hours. Show me what needs my attention today and summarize the rest. Draft responses where appropriate. Do not send, delete or archive anything without my approval."

I would absolutely keep that approval requirement in place. Let AI write the first draft. Let AI tell you what looks urgent. But before something goes out under my name, I want to see it. That goes double if the recipient is my boss, my doctor or anybody who might interpret an AI hallucination as something I actually meant to say.

4) Make AI remember all the little deadlines you forget

Life is full of deadlines that are incredibly easy to miss because they do not feel urgent until suddenly they are. A subscription renews Friday. A rebate expires next week. Your insurance paperwork is due. Somewhere in your inbox there is a form you completely forgot existed. That is the kind of mental clutter I would love to hand off. An agent could keep track of deadlines you give it and remind you before something needs your attention.

Prompt to try:

"Keep track of the deadlines, renewals and appointments I give you. Tell me what is coming up this week and alert me early when I need to do something. Never renew, cancel or submit anything without my approval."

I would keep the agent in reminder mode when money is involved. Tell me the bill is due. Tell me the trial expires tomorrow. Then get out of the way and let me decide what happens next.

5) Let AI figure out what’s for dinner

I don't know about you, but deciding what to make for dinner every night gets old fast. You open the refrigerator, stare at what's inside and somehow still can't think of anything to eat. Why not hand that job to AI? Tell an AI agent what foods you like, what ingredients you already have and how much time you want to spend cooking. It can put together a weekly dinner plan, suggest simple recipes and even help you use up food before it goes bad.

Prompt to try:

"Every Sunday, prepare a dinner plan for the coming week with five easy meals. Use my food preferences and any ingredients I've told you I have. Keep each meal under 30 minutes. Include simple recipes and a grocery list of anything else I'll need. Don't order groceries without my approval."

You can schedule this as a weekly task so the agent prepares fresh dinner ideas without you having to ask each time. Just update it with what's in your refrigerator and pantry before it creates the next plan. That means fewer nights staring into the refrigerator wondering what to cook.

6) Put somebody else in charge of the household to-do list

Every home seems to have a list that nobody actually wrote down. The air filter needs replacing. The dog is running out of food. There is something in the garage you promised to fix about four months ago. Then, at exactly the wrong moment, somebody remembers it. An AI agent could become the place where all those loose ends go. Every time something pops into your head, give it to the agent and let the agent keep track of what is coming due.

Prompt to try:

"Keep a household task list based on the things I give you. Remind me when something needs attention and help me keep track of what is still unfinished. Ask me before adding anything to my calendar, ordering something or contacting anyone."

This is one of those uses that sounds almost too simple for AI. That may be exactly why I like it. If it remembers that I need a new refrigerator filter before the old one stops working, we are making progress.

7) Let AI remember who owes you an answer

This one drives me crazy. You send an email. You request a refund. You call somebody about a bill. They tell you they will get back to you. Then life happens. Two weeks later, you suddenly think, "Wait, did anybody ever answer me?" An AI agent could keep track of those loose ends for you. Tell it what you are waiting on and when you expect a response. If nothing arrives, have it remind you. Better yet, let it prepare the follow-up so you do not have to stare at a blank email trying to remember what happened in the first place.

Prompt to try:

"Keep track of the requests I am waiting on. If I have not received a response by the deadline I give you, remind me and draft a polite follow-up. Do not send it without my approval."

That could work for a contractor estimate, a disputed charge or a return you are still waiting to hear about. I like this because the agent becomes responsible for remembering that the conversation never actually ended.

8) Have AI watch for the opening you keep missing

Sometimes the issue is not the price. It is getting your hands on the thing at all. Maybe the restaurant you want is booked Saturday night. Your doctor has no opening for three weeks. The product you want keeps selling out. You could keep checking. Or you could make the AI check.

Prompt to try:

"Check [restaurant, appointment, event or product] for availability. Let me know when an opening appears that meets these conditions: ___. Do not book, buy or confirm anything without asking me first."

This will depend on the AI agent you are using and whether the website allows that kind of automated access. But the idea is exactly where agents become useful. I do not want to ask AI whether the table is available right now. I want it to tell me Friday afternoon when somebody cancels and suddenly it is.

CyberGuy pro tip: Make your AI agent earn its permissions

Here is the part I would pay close attention to. An AI agent becomes more useful as you give it more access. That can include your email, calendar and other accounts. More access also means there is more that can go wrong. So I would make the agent earn those permissions.

Start by letting it read something. See what it does with the information. If that goes well, maybe allow it to organize information or prepare drafts. Only then would I consider letting it perform a limited action, and even then I would keep approval turned on whenever something important could happen.

Think about email. Let the agent summarize messages first. Then maybe let it draft replies. Sending those replies is another level entirely.

The same thinking applies to shopping and your calendar. OpenAI says Dots can follow rules that determine which actions they can perform on their own and when they need your input. Meta says Muse asks for approval before certain critical actions, including purchases and sending emails. I would use those controls.

And I would never paste passwords, PINs or two-factor authentication codes into a chat window because an AI agent asks for them. If the service offers a secure way to connect an account, use that instead. Give AI what it needs to complete the task. Do not automatically give it everything it asks for.

Do you actually need an AI agent?

Here is an easy way to figure that out. Ask yourself whether the job ends when AI answers you. If you ask ChatGPT to help plan dinner tonight, you probably do not need an agent.

But suppose you say, "Keep watching the price of this flight and tell me when it drops below $300." Now the useful part of the job happens after you leave.

The same goes for appointments. Asking what appointments you have tomorrow can be a normal AI request. Asking AI to alert you when an earlier doctor's appointment becomes available requires something that keeps checking.

Agents make the most sense when the task has an unfinished part. That is where I see the real appeal.

What I still would not hand over to AI

There are some areas where convenience would not persuade me to give up control. I would not give an AI agent unrestricted access to move money or make major purchases. I also would not let one make medical decisions for me or handle a legal decision without a human involved.

Be careful with connected accounts too. If you connect an agent to your inbox or cloud storage for a particular task, check what it can see. Once you no longer need that connection, consider removing it. AI agents may get much better at taking action on our behalf. That does not mean every action should be theirs to take.

IDENTITY RESTORATION: WHAT TO DO AFTER IDENTITY THEFT

Kurt's key takeaways

I think AI agents get a lot more appealing when you forget the hype for a minute and ask one simple question: What am I tired of doing myself? For some people, that could be checking a price every morning. Others may want help remembering follow-ups or keeping track of household chores that always seem to surface at the worst possible time. Those are the kinds of tasks I would hand over first.

I become much more cautious when AI moves from watching and reminding to actually doing something in my name. I am happy to let an agent tell me that a restaurant table opened up. Before it books dinner for me, though, I want to know exactly what it is about to do. That is where I see the sweet spot with AI agents. Let them handle the annoying part while you stay in charge of anything that could cost you money, expose your information or create a mess you have to clean up later.

What is the one annoying task you would happily hand over to an AI agent tomorrow, and what is one thing you would never trust it to do for you? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

World.title: Starbucks hit with lawsuit over sugar content as experts reveal chain's most sugary drinks
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Starbucks is facing a lawsuit over its "sugar-free" protein drinks, with consumers alleging some contain nearly as much sugar as a candy bar.

The proposed class-action lawsuit, filed Oct. 2 in federal court in Washington state, targets eight hot and iced Starbucks protein beverages, including its Sugar-Free Vanilla Protein Latte, Sugar-Free Caramel Protein Latte and protein matcha drinks.

The beverages contain between 13 and 21 grams of sugar in a venti-sized serving, according to the lawsuit, which reportedly argues that "no reasonable consumer" would expect a drink called "sugar-free" to contain that amount.

POPULAR PANTRY PRODUCT CAN'T LEGALLY BE CALLED PEANUT BUTTER — HERE'S WHY

The suit was brought by three consumers who bought the drinks in California, New York and Washington. It asks the court to stop Starbucks from using "sugar-free" to describe products that contain sugar.

Starbucks is disputing the allegations.

"We believe these claims have no merit," a Starbucks spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

GROCERY SHOPPERS MAY BE RELYING ON A 'MISLEADING' CLUE WHEN CHOOSING HEALTHY FOODS

"Starbucks has consistently and clearly provided information about its protein beverages, sugar-free options, customization choices, and nutritional content across product announcements, menus, marketing materials, Starbucks.com and the Starbucks app, and we intend to vigorously defend ourselves in this matter."

The company says the sugar in the drinks comes naturally from protein-boosted milk rather than added sugar, and that sugar-free syrups are used for flavoring.

Nicolette Pace, a New York-based registered dietitian and certified diabetes educator, noted that lactose in milk is a naturally occurring sugar and is not counted as an added sugar, but "sugar-free" and "no added sugar" are not the same.

DIRTY SODA DRINKS ARE EVERYWHERE, BUT DOCTORS WARN OF HEALTH RISKS: 'METABOLIC DISASTER'

"Sugar-free" does not necessarily mean a product contains zero sugar, added Dr. Michael Aziz, an internist at Lenox Hill Hospital in New York City. Under FDA regulations, products labeled "sugar-free" generally must contain less than 0.5 gram of sugar per serving.

"No added sugar," meanwhile, means sugars or sugar-containing ingredients have not been added during processing or preparation, though a product can still contain naturally occurring sugar, as Starbucks says its protein drinks do. Naturally occurring sugars can still affect blood glucose levels, making the total carbohydrate content important for people with diabetes to consider.

JUST ONE SMALL SERVING OF ULTRA-PROCESSED FOOD A DAY LINKED TO HIGHER DISEASE RISK, MAJOR STUDY FINDS

The plaintiffs argue that they paid more for products advertised as sugar-free than they would have for comparable alternatives, said Danny Karon, an Ohio-based class-action attorney who is not involved in the case. "The challenge will be convincing the court — and then the jury — that consumers relied on Starbucks' alleged misrepresentations when making their purchases," Karon told Fox News Digital.

CLICK HERE TO 

Beyond the protein beverages cited in the lawsuit, Aziz and Pace warned that other Starbucks specialty drinks can pack significant amounts of sugar, underscoring the importance of considering nutrition information, serving size and add-ons such as whipped cream and drizzles.

A venti Java Chip Frappuccino can contain nearly 80 grams of sugar, or roughly 20 teaspoons, they said. They also pointed to the Caramel Ribbon Crunch Frappuccino and seasonal drinks such as the Peppermint Mocha and Pumpkin Spice Latte, which, depending on size and customization, can have almost as much sugar.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"That's massive amounts of sugar when we know that a soda has 63 grams of sugar," Aziz said, referring to standard 20-ounce bottles of popular regular sodas.

"Size does matter when it comes to these things at Starbucks," Pace said. The American Heart Association recommends limiting added sugar to about 6 teaspoons, or 25 grams, per day for most women and 9 teaspoons, or 36 grams, for men, she noted.

CLICK HERE TO 

She stressed, however, that those recommendations apply to added sugar, not naturally occurring lactose in milk.

For consumers looking to reduce their intake, she suggested keeping the order simple, and choosing a smaller size.
