Aziz recommends, "If you want to have a treat, maybe just have a simple latte or a cappuccino."

World.title: Indiana survives Nebraska in comeback win, extends nation's longest active winning streak
World.content:
The longest active winning streak in college football lives another week.

No. 7 Indiana was pushed to the brink by Nebraska, but ended up winning 20-17 on the road Saturday afternoon at Memorial Stadium. For a while, it looked like Nebraska was going to hand the defending national champions their first loss since the first round of the 2024 College Football Playoff, but a fourth quarter comeback prevented that.

Indiana hadn't even trailed in a game since the 2025 Big Ten Championship Game against Ohio State, eight games ago.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The win was Indiana's 27th straight against unranked teams, as Indiana's previous loss to an unranked opponent came Nov. 25, 2023, against Purdue. For Curt Cignetti, he improved to 33-2 as Indiana's head coach.

Indiana quarterback Josh Hoover did just enough in the win, completing 12 of his 22 passes for 263 yards and two touchdowns while wide receiver Nick Marsh was outstanding, catching six passes for 187 yards and two touchdowns.

While rallying late, the Indiana offense struggled in the first half. The Hoosiers ran just 17 plays and managed 115 yards of total offense, scoring their only three points on a 42-yard field goal by Nico Radicic in the first quarter.

Nebraska, on the other hand, started fast. The Huskers opened the scoring with a 28-yard field goal by Kyle Cunanan, capping a 13-play, 66-yard drive to take a 3-0 lead.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

After Indiana responded with a field goal of its own, the Nebraska offense went to work on another long drive.

Wide receiver Nyziah Hunter scored on a 10-yard end-around for his first touchdown of the season , putting Nebraska ahead 10-3 after a 10-play, 75-yard drive. The Huskers had an opportunity to add to their lead at the end of the first half, but Cunanan's 40-yard field goal attempt sailed wide right.

Nebraska held the ball for more than 22 minutes in the first half alone.

Indiana received the second-half kickoff and drove into Nebraska territory but was kept out of the end zone and forced to settle for another Radicic field goal, this time from 35 yards, making it 10-6.

After the Indiana field goal, the game turned into a field-position battle.

On the ensuing possession, the Huskers made their first mistake of the game. Facing third-and-16 from the Indiana 36-yard line, Nebraska quarterback Anthony Colandrea was forced out of the pocket and heaved a pass toward the end zone intended for Hunter. Instead, Indiana defensive back Jamari Sharpe leaped and intercepted the pass at his team's 2-yard line .

However, the Nebraska defense pinned Indiana deep in its own territory, forcing a three-and-out . After the punt, the Huskers took over at the Indiana 41-yard line.

The Nebraska offense squandered the opportunity, going three-and-out, but pinned Indiana at its own 1-yard line with an excellent punt. As the fourth quarter began, the Hoosiers were forced to punt again after the Nebraska defense kept them pinned deep inside their own territory.

Then, the floodgates opened.

Colandrea finally broke through the Indiana defense with a 39-yard touchdown run on third-and-5. On a read-option play, Colandrea kept the ball, picked up the first down, cut back upfield and turned the corner for Nebraska's second touchdown of the game, extending its lead to 17-6.

Just as the raucous Nebraska crowd erupted after Colandrea's score, Indiana quarterback Josh Hoover connected with wide receiver Nick Marsh on a 75-yard touchdown pass on the first play of the ensuing possession, silencing the Huskers faithful and cutting the deficit to 17-13.

The Nebraska offense couldn't respond, giving Indiana a chance to take its first lead of the day . On fourth-and-1 from the Nebraska 44-yard line, the Huskers defense bit on a play-action pass.

Hoover found a wide-open Marsh for a 44-yard touchdown, giving Indiana a 20-17 lead.

Nebraska, sensing the game was slipping away, went for it on fourth-and-9 from its own 44-yard line with just under five minutes remaining in the fourth quarter. The gamble failed, as Indiana forced an incompletion and took over on downs, despite Nebraska still having two timeouts and the two-minute warning.

However, the Nebraska defense forced a three-and-out, giving its offense another chance to mount a comeback. The Hoosiers defense held firm, forcing another turnover on downs with a sack of Colandrea.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Nebraska gave the defending national champions a run for their money, but Indiana proved too much to handle.

Nebraska fell to 5-1 with the loss and will look to bounce back against No. 13 Oregon next week.

Indiana has another big game next week against No. 5 Ohio State at home.

World.title: Trump says he’ll decide whether to livestream the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan
World.content:
President Donald Trump said Saturday that he hasn’t yet made a final decision on whether to livestream the execution of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan, who in 2009 killed 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas.

“There are two thoughts: don’t show it and show it. Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but I’ll make a decision,” the president told reporters at the White House.

He also spoke about Hasan’s crime, saying, “He’s a vicious killer — killed 13 people in cold blood, wounded over 20. Some of those people will never have their lives back in a true sense.”

Trump’s comments came a day after he told reporters that he “absolutely” approved the livestream plan announced earlier in the week, which has drawn skepticism and criticism from members of his own party.

Military officials said Monday that Hasan, who was sentenced to death in 2013, would be executed by firing squad in December. On Thursday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said that the execution would be livestreamed, raising concerns that Hasan could be viewed as a martyr by others seeking to commit mass violence.

00:38 Trump says he’ll decide on Fort Hood execution livestream 00:00 00:00

But Vice President JD Vance said Friday that he was not sure the federal government would livestream the execution, adding that if it did he would not watch the event.

That same day, several Republican lawmakers expressed concern about the idea of publicly broadcasting the killing.

Rep. Austin Scott, R-Ga., wrote in a post on X, “I absolutely support the sentence of death, but live-streaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that.”

Rep. Rob Bresnahan, R-Pa., said in a separate post on X that “an execution shouldn’t be a live-streamed spectacle. The focus should be on justice for the victims and their families, not turning an execution into entertainment. Their pain deserves respect, not a public show.”

Rep. Tom Barrett, R-Mich., wrote on X that “Secretary Hegseth should seriously reconsider this decision.”

Other Republican lawmakers have signaled support for the livestream plan. On Saturday, Rep. Matt Van Epps, R-Tenn., told NBC News that “Parents should not let their kids watch that. Just like they should have good parental guidance for social media and other things. This administration is focused on accountability.”

Earlier in the day on Truth Social, Trump reposted a Dallas Morning News article in which Robert Jeffress, a prominent Trump ally and the senior pastor of First Baptist Dallas, said that he supports the plan for a public killing.

World.title: Shooter kills 8 at family home in Pennsylvania before turning gun on self, Erie police say
World.content:
A man killed seven family members and a family friend at a home in Erie, Pennsylvania, on Friday night before dying of an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound, officials said.

The victims ranged in age from 22 months to 44 years old and included two children and a pregnant woman, Erie police said.

“It was the worst scene I have ever experienced,” said Police Chief Rick Lorah, who called it horrific.

Police responded to a home just before 5 p.m. on a ShotSpotter alert indicating two gunshots went off, Lorah said at a Saturday news conference.

When officers arrived, they found two women, ages 51 and 37, dead outside of the residence, the chief said.

Lorah said a neighbor’s Ring doorbell video showed those two women “arriving at the residence, appearing distressed, seeking assistance from neighbors and pounding on the door.”

Audio from video reviewed by investigators also “appears to capture muffled gunfire from inside the residence before the suspect emerged and fatally shot both women,” Lorah said.

The suspect then went back inside and witnesses reported hearing no further gunshots, Lorah said.

When officers arrived, they didn’t hear any movement inside the home and were unable to establish contact with anyone, Lorah said, adding it wasn’t clear whether someone was inside and posed a threat.

Ultimately, SWAT officers breached several doors and deployed a robot, which found multiple victims, and officers went in, the chief said.

Investigators determined the victims were killed and the suspect died by a self-inflicted gunshot wound before officers arrived.

Eight of the deceased, including the suspect, were related and one of the two women killed outside was a family friend, Lorah said. One of the victims found inside was eight months pregnant, he added.

“It’s a family,” Lorah said.

Two young children — a 5-year-old boy and a 22-month-old girl — were found on the first floor.

Four victims were found on the second floor in the stairwell: a 24-year-old woman, a 44-year-old woman, a 19-year-old man and a 21-year-old man.

The suspected shooter, 45, who was not publicly identified, was found dead on the second floor. A .40 caliber handgun that was registered to the suspect was recovered “on his person,” Lorah said.

The police chief said all the victims inside the home lived there, and the two women found outside did not.

The investigation into what precipitated the shooting is ongoing.

Lorah said “it’s too soon to talk about motive” but that he believed “mental health is at play here.”

He said investigators will look into what the two women found deceased outside the home knew when they arrived at the scene.

“We have to look at their cellphones. They knew something was going on at that house,” he said.

“We believe that the shooter comes out and calls towards the two females. They run towards and then he, then he shoots them,” Lorah said of the sequence of events.

Gov. Josh Shapiro said he had spoken with Erie Mayor Daria Devlin and offered his administration’s “full support.”

“My heart breaks for this family,” he wrote on X. “Lori and I are praying for their loved ones and the entire Erie community.”

Erie is about 128 miles north of Pittsburgh.

World.title: Mail ballot concerns are changing how Democrats vote
World.content:
Democrats are changing how they vote, requesting fewer mail ballots than in past elections but returning the ones they do request more quickly, according to a new NBC News Decision Desk analysis of the early vote conducted in coordination with the University of Pennsylvania.

The findings, which come less than four weeks before Election Day, reflect a midterm landscape shaped by concerns about mail-in voting and doubts about the reliability of the U.S. Postal Service. The shift among Democrats suggests they may be abandoning mail ballots in favor of in-person voting, or taking precautions to ensure their ballot arrives on time.

The implications could be significant. Since 2020, Democrats have been far more likely than Republicans to vote by mail, creating predictable patterns in how early election tallies shift as additional votes are counted. But if those habits are changing, it will be more difficult to gauge which party has more enthusiasm from early voting figures, while the now-familiar red and blue “mirages” seen on recent election nights could unfold differently.

For the analysis, we compared current and historical data on mail ballot requests and returns at the same point in time across four states: North Carolina, Georgia, Virginia and Pennsylvania. We gathered publicly available data from three states and sourced Virginia data from L2, a leading voter data firm.

Trump order supercharges concerns about the Postal Service

President Donald Trump has long attacked mail voting as rife with unfounded claims of fraud. Heading into the midterms, his administration exerted increased control over the Postal Service, whose slowed delivery times had already prompted voting rights groups and Democrats to push their voters to consider using other methods of voting.

Just months before the first mail ballots of the midterm elections were scheduled to go out, the Postal Service followed a Trump directive to impose new rules about how election officials could send those ballots to voters. The new requirements will ultimately not apply to this year’s midterm election, but the high-profile legal battle magnified worries about the reliability of the Postal Service.

Confidence that the Postal Service would deliver mail ballots on time plummeted among Democrats from 86% before the 2024 election to 60% now, according to polling conducted by Marist in September, just after the Supreme Court blocked the new Postal Service rules from going into effect. Confidence among Republicans remains unchanged. Meanwhile, more Democrats said they planned to vote in person this year than said the same at this time in 2024, according to NBC News polling.

The early vote data we examined suggests that what these Democratic voters may actually do is dependent on when voters may request mail ballots in each state.

In some states, voters may join a permanent list of mail voters or an annual list at the start of each year. If voters could request their ballot long before concerns about the Postal Service became national news, Democrats are still voting by mail, but taking steps to get those ballots back to election officials more quickly, the analysis shows.

But if Democrats face the choice about whether to request a mail ballot only after the Postal Service challenges, it’s more likely that ballot requests are down from previous election years.

Changing early voting patterns

In North Carolina, where the Senate race is poised to help decide control of the chamber, registrants typically apply for a mail ballot in the months before each particular election. As a result, few individuals had requested mail ballots for the upcoming midterm before the Postal Service attempted to impose its new rules.

So far, Democrats in the state are both less likely to request and more likely to return mail ballots compared to 2022, the most recent midterm election year. The decrease is larger among Democratic registered voters at 40% than among Republican registered voters or independent or third-party registrants at 18% and 23%, respectively. Further, the Democratic registrants who have requested mail ballots are more likely to have already returned them in 2026 (22%) than in 2022 (17%).

In Georgia, a state with competitive Senate and gubernatorial contests and a similar mail ballot request policy, we see the same pattern. While it’s not possible to directly replicate the North Carolina analysis because registrants in the state do not declare a party of registration and domestic mail ballots only went out this week, we can use how each precinct voted in 2024 as an approximation of the partisanship of voters.

As in North Carolina, the analysis shows that mail ballot requests are down more in precincts that overwhelmingly supported Kamala Harris (52%) than in precincts that overwhelmingly supported Donald Trump (39%).

The story is different in Virginia. Unlike North Carolina or Georgia, Virginia allows registrants to 

But as in Georgia and North Carolina, Democrats are returning their mail ballots faster. In the most Democratic precincts, 69% more ballots were returned at this point in the 2026 election compared to 2025, compared to 5% fewer returned ballots in the most Republican precincts.

One advantage of analyzing Virginia is that it is one of the few states with a significant amount of early in-person voting at this point in the electoral calendar.

Relative to 2025, there are more early in-person ballots already cast in precincts that overwhelmingly supported Harris (+10%) in 2024 than in precincts that overwhelmingly supported Trump (-14%). But only a small portion of this increase is caused by people shifting from voting by mail to voting early in person, so it does not explain most of the increase in early in-person voting.

Still, the relatively higher rate of people voting early in person in Democratic precincts compared to Republican precincts suggests that most Democrats who are shifting away from mail balloting, including in North Carolina and Georgia, may move to voting in person rather than not voting at all.

Finally, consider Pennsylvania, which maintains an annual list for mail ballot applications. Of the four states analyzed, it had the highest share of ballots cast by mail in the 2024 presidential election — 27%, versus Virginia at 11%, North Carolina at 5% and Georgia at 5%.

When registrants request a mail ballot in Pennsylvania, they are permitted to request a mail ballot for every subsequent election in that calendar year. Many registrants who request a mail ballot for the May primary election also request a mail ballot for the upcoming general election.

As in North Carolina and Georgia, there are fewer mail ballot requests from Democrats at this point in 2026 than in 2022. However, there is no difference among Democrats requesting mail ballots by May. Instead, the decline is concentrated among mail ballot requests after May, likely reflecting the increased uncertainty about the Postal Service since the summer.

Further, consistent with the other findings, Democrats are returning their mail ballots faster than in the past. A higher percentage of mail ballots requested by registered Democrats have already been returned (20%) than at this same point in 2022 (15%).

Why changing voting habits could complicate election night analysis

These changes in Democratic voting behavior present two challenges for election analysts: determining what the early vote data reveal about voter enthusiasm, and understanding what’s happening on election night as results are processed.

At this point, it is difficult to use the initial mail ballot data to gauge each party’s likelihood of success.

The relative decline in mail ballot requests could be interpreted as a sign that Democrats have less momentum heading into the midterm election than current polling indicates. But Democrats may also be shifting from voting by mail to voting in person, as the findings in Virginia suggest.

Conversely, the relative increase in mail ballot returns among Democrats might mean the party’s voters are particularly enthusiastic about the upcoming election. But this pattern is also consistent with these Democrats returning their mail ballots faster to address concerns about Postal Service slowdowns.

Observing who casts early in-person votes over the next several weeks will help test these competing narratives. Still, we won’t have a clear picture of voter enthusiasm until we see who turns out on Election Day.

Beyond that, our findings underscore the need for caution when interpreting early voting data and election-night results.

Analysts often rely on voting patterns from past elections as key benchmarks to assess how each party is performing on election night. But if more Democrats vote in person, or get those mail ballots in faster, the timing of when Democratic votes are reported and counted could change in important ways. Thus, what may seem to be either a Democratic over- or under- performance on election night could instead be the reflection of the election landscape shifting once more.

World.title: MAHA fractures deepen as some RFK Jr. followers turn into harsh critics
World.content:
Some supporters of the “Make America Healthy Again” movement have begun to publicly turn against their leader, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and the Trump administration as a whole as they demand tougher crackdowns on food dyes and pesticides.

A scorecard released Thursday by MAHA activists, including former members of Kennedy’s 2024 presidential campaign, claims the Trump administration broke more than 85% of its promises to MAHA on food, agriculture and environmental health. The makers of the scorecard include Dave Murphy, a former fundraiser for Kennedy’s campaign, and Charles Eisenstein, Kennedy’s former chief speechwriter.

NBC News is first to report on the scorecard, which offers a window into how MAHA views the administration, and Kennedy himself, ahead of the midterm elections. It accuses the Trump administration of doling out favors to the chemical industry, pointing to its decision to approve new pesticides and hire industry lobbyists and executives.

“We’re asking the Trump administration to deliver on even the most basic promises they’ve made to the MAHA movement, and we’ve seen over and over again not just a lack of interest in doing so, but a blatant slap in the face,” said former Kennedy campaign adviser Tiffany Cianci, a MAHA advocate who authored the scorecard.

About 41% of adults in the U.S. say they support MAHA ideals, according to an April poll from KFF, a nonprofit health think tank. Most are Republicans or Republican-leaning independents, according to the poll, though alignment with Kennedy or President Donald Trump wasn’t a primary reason for supporting the movement.

MAHA coalesced during Kennedy’s presidential bid in 2024, then threw its support behind Trump when Kennedy endorsed him. It brought together multiple social movements, including food safety, environmentalism and vaccine skepticism, under the umbrella of taking on big corporations whose products may contribute to chronic diseases.

But many of these advocates have become Kennedy’s harshest critics as of late, arguing that their priorities are being ignored by the Trump administration.

Covid vaccine skeptics such as Dr. Mary Talley Bowden have criticized Kennedy and Trump for allowing mRNA vaccines to stay on the market. Food safety advocates say Kennedy hasn’t put enough pressure on companies to remove synthetic dyes and other additives from their products. And advocates for reducing pesticide exposure claim Trump undermined their mission by issuing an executive order to boost the supply of the weed killer glyphosate in the U.S.

That dissatisfaction has led to infighting between Kennedy loyalists — including those appointed to key government positions — and activists faithful to their original cause.

“What started out as a hairline crack in the coalition is now widened to be a gaping fissure,” said Peter Lurie, president of the Center for Science in the Public Interest, a nonprofit advocacy group focused on nutrition and food safety.

White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said the Trump administration “has already secured extensive victories for the MAHA Agenda, including overhauling the dietary guidelines for Americans, axing artificial ingredients in our food supply, and investing in regenerative farming.”

“After years of being on the political sidelines, the MAHA coalition has found a champion in President Trump, who has made incredible strides to Make America Healthy Again,” Schuster said in a statement.

Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, said Kennedy “remains focused on delivering lasting reforms grounded in science, transparency, and accountability.”

“President Trump and Secretary Kennedy are delivering the fundamental change Americans voted for. In just 20 months, this Administration has moved at a historic pace to advance MAHA across the federal government,” she said in a statement.

Cianci acknowledged that many of the administration’s actions on environmental toxins and food additives have been outside of Kennedy’s purview. But his time in the administration has done “obvious harm” to his reputation, she said, noting that Kennedy’s career history involved suing the very pharmaceutical and pesticide companies the administration is now working with.

“To see him not speaking out on the issues that are so obviously against everything that was promised is very hard because I believe ethically it’s probably working against his own inclinations,” Cianci said.

Kelly Ryerson, a well-known MAHA advocate who goes by the moniker “Glyphosate Girl” and helped develop the scorecard, said she doesn’t fault Kennedy as much as the rest of Trump’s Cabinet because she knows “where his heart lies.”

“I know how deep the forces are in terms of corporate influence on regulators, and it’s something that he himself has criticized for years,” she said. “[But] the actions of the administration have worked really in opposition to everything that we hoped and everything that Trump promised.”

Pamela Herd, a professor of social policy at the University of Michigan, said the MAHA movement was always vulnerable to conflict because it consists of unusual bedfellows: liberal moms who feed their kids organic produce, fringe doctors who falsely claim that vaccines cause autism and Trump supporters who want to remove corporate influence from the federal government.

Over time, though, MAHA’s main goals have solidified. A March poll from Politico suggests that removing ultra-processed foods from American diets and limiting exposure to PFAS, microplastics and pesticides were key priorities for people who self-identified as part of the movement.

“What the MAHA movement has always been especially interested in is chemicals,” Lurie said.

Much of Cianci’s scorecard focuses on actions taken by the Environmental Protection Agency and Agriculture Department — agencies Kennedy does not oversee. For instance, it considers the EPA’s decisions to weaken mercury emissions standards and roll back drinking water limits for certain PFAS as broken promises.

Phasing out food dyes

Several of the promises that were “partially kept,” according to the scorecard, come directly from Kennedy-led agencies like the Food and Drug Administration.

For instance, the FDA asked food companies to voluntarily phase out certain dyes and banned two others that were not widely used. It also proposed a requirement for food manufacturers to notify the FDA when they determine that an additive is “generally recognized as safe.” The rule would not remove the additives already in food or prevent manufacturers from adding more, however.

Lurie said Kennedy campaigned on fixing these issues, but “never took into account the practical aspects on the ground: What do the regulations actually look like? What authority do these agencies actually have?”

The scorecard does not mention an action Kennedy has touted often: his January overhaul of the federal dietary guidelines, which encourages Americans to eat more protein and cut out ultra-processed foods.

It also does not address Kennedy’s vaccination policies. Both Kennedy and Trump have attempted to reduce the number of universally recommended vaccines for children. And Kennedy last year fired the longtime members of a federal vaccine advisory committee, replacing them with vaccine skeptics. (A federal judge temporarily blocked the change, which is still being challenged in court.)

“If you’re going to pick one thing that RFK was successful at, it’s very much how he has influenced government policy on vaccines,” Herd, the University of Michigan professor, said.

Kennedy reassured anti-vaccine activists last month that they have “a strong and steadfast friend at the White House.”

But as tensions mount, many MAHA supporters insist the movement does not need a political affiliation. Ryerson said MAHA voters will likely sit out the upcoming midterm elections.

“The disappointments with Obama and Biden are similar to the disappointments with Trump,” she said. “The difference with this administration is that we are promised something very, very different in a very real way, so I think that that burn feels especially raw.”

World.title: Affording America: How a single mother in Chicago turned to gig work to survive
World.content: Jade Crossfrench is a single mother supporting three children with a day job selling insurance. But that isn't enough to provide for her family. For over a year she's been making extra money as a gig worker, doing DoorDash food deliveries around Chicago, often with her kids sitting in the back seat of the car.Sept. 30, 2026

World.title: Trump says Nobel committee not awarding him Peace Prize leaves ‘indelible stain’ on Norway
World.content:
President Donald Trump lamented that the Norwegian Nobel Committee chose not to award him with its annual Peace Prize on Friday, telling rallygoers the decision leaves “an indelible stain on the country of Norway.”

Speaking at a rally in Syracuse to boost New York Republicans, Trump listed off all of the accomplishments he believes have earned him the right to win the Nobel Peace Prize, including efforts to end or prevent conflicts in Africa and Asia and for having “saved more lives than anyone in history.”

Earlier Friday, the committee awarded the prize to Navi Pillay, an 85-year-old South African legal pioneer who led a United Nations panel that concluded Israel committed genocide in Gaza.

“I’ve never heard of the person,” Trump said. “I know a lot of people. I never heard of this particular person, but congratulations, anyway. … The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn’t.”

South African lawyer Navanethem "Navi" Pillay at the Nuremberg Forum following the announcement of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. Daniel Karmann / Picture alliance via Getty

“And this is an indelible stain on the country of Norway and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” Trump continued. “The Nobel Peace Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are antidemocracy and really enemies of civilization, and we will not forget Norway, that you didn’t give this prize with the greatest record in history.”

The president added that he should have received eight Nobel Peace Prizes for his efforts because he claimed to have ended eight ongoing conflicts. The president did not mention the war in Ukraine, which has raged on through his presidency as his administration has failed to bring the conflict to an end. And in the Middle East, the president earlier this year launched an ongoing war with Iran.

President Donald Trump takes the stage to speak during an election rally in Syracuse, N.Y., on Friday. Alex Wong / Getty

Trump said the committee’s choice to award the prize to Pillay “is just another sign of how Norway and all these others are ripping off our country.”

Throughout his second term, the president has made clear his ambition to secure a Nobel Peace Prize, and his allies have said he deserves it for efforts to end the war in Gaza in addition to other conflicts. Earlier this year, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, the 2025 winner, offered to share her prize with him as she sought his support for her efforts in Venezuela after the Trump administration removed President Nicolás Maduro from power.

After learning of her award at a law gathering in Germany on Friday, Pillay joked to the crowd: “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.”

The president was in Syracuse to boost the candidacy of GOP gubernatorial nominee Bruce Blakeman and state Republicans. He shouted out Saritha Komatireddy, the Republican nominee for state attorney general too, before attacking sitting state Attorney General Letitia James, a Democrat he has often clashed with.

“And on Election Day, New Yorkers should tell both [Gov. Kathy] Hochul and that disgusting Letitia dog — she’s a dog — you’re fired, get the hell out of here.”

Letitia James, New York's attorney general. John Lamparski / Bloomberg via Getty

The Trump administration has so far failed multiple times in its efforts to prosecute James, who spearheaded an investigation into his business dealings that led to a state judge ruling he had conspired to manipulate his net worth and ordering him to pay a fine of more than $350 million. The fine was later thrown out on appeal by a state court.

“Donald Trump is in Syracuse supporting the only attorney general candidate who clerked for Brett Kavanaugh, the man who ended Roe v. Wade,” a James campaign spokesperson said in response to the president’s comments. “The contrast is crystal clear and we welcome it.”

World.title: Vehicle driven by ICE agents in Texas hits and injures man, sheriff says
World.content:
A vehicle driven by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents hit and injured a man in the greater Houston area on Saturday, the Harris County Sheriff's Office said.

"The incident appears to have occurred while ICE authorities were conducting an enforcement action in the area," the sheriff's office said in a statement.

During a press conference, Major McConnell of the Harris County Sheriff's special investigation bureau said the sheriff's office was called to the scene around 7:20 a.m.

ICE agents were headed south in pursuit of a wanted suspect, McConnell said, and the suspect drove west in an eastbound lane. The suspect bailed out of his vehicle and went on foot, he said.

The driver and passenger fled and ICE agents attempted to capture them both, he said. While trying to capture the passenger, the ICE agent hit him with his vehicle.

The victim was taken to a local hospital. McConnell said it appears the man has a broken leg. McConnell said the victim is a 48-year-old male and is currently in the custody of ICE at the hospital.

In a statement provided to CBS News Saturday, an ICE spokesperson said that agents were "conducting a targeted enforcement operation" to arrest Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, a Mexican national and undocumented immigrant.

During the operation, ICE agents observed Mendoza-Cervantes and a second Mexican national and undocumented immigrant, identified as Miguel Parra-Hernandez, enter a vehicle and drive away.

According to the ICE spokesperson, when they attempted to stop the vehicle, the two subjects stopped and ran away on foot.

During the ensuing chase, Parra-Hernandez "ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck."

The ICE spokesperson said that Parra-Hernandez was taken to an area hospital with injuries believed to be non-life-threatening.

Mendoza-Cervantes escaped and remains at large, ICE said.

In its statement, ICE alleged that Mendoza-Cervantes had four prior arrests for drunken driving charges, as well as an arrest for charges of unlawful possession of a firearm. ICE did not confirm if he was convicted of any of those allegations. ICE stated that an immigration judge had issued him a final order of removal. The agency spokesperson also said that he had been previously deported twice.

World.title: Gunman charged with killing officer, wounding another in West Philly
World.content:
The man accused of shooting two police officers, killing one and injuring another, early Saturday morning in West Philadelphia is identified as 35-year-old Eric Lewis, according to District Attorney Larry Krasner.

Lewis faces a slew of charges in the shooting death of 40-year-old officer Shane Seiber. Police Commissioner Kevin Bethel identified the fallen officer as a 10-year veteran of the force with two children. His wife and other relatives were by his side at the hospital, he said.

"He fought valiantly, but he lost his life today," said Bethel during a mid-morning news conference. "I want to say I appreciate all of the calls and all the support we received when we left out of [the hospital] this morning.

"We had an immense amount of hope."

According to Krasner, Lewis shot the two police officers and opened fire on nine other officers around 1 a.m. on the 100 block of North 52nd Street in West Philadelphia. Lewis is charged with homicide of a law enforcement officer, murder, attempted homicide of a law enforcement officer, possession of an instrument of crime, reckless endangerment and more.

Krasner added that the nine other officers who were fired at weren't struck by gunfire.

Lewis is being held without bail and will have a preliminary hearing soon, Krasner said.

"Thoughts and prayers — I hate when people say that — thoughts and prayers. My thoughts and prayers, but our deeds with these charges are what I'm looking forward to at this point," Councilmember Curtis Jones said during an afternoon news conference.

What led to the Philadelphia police shooting

Police initially received a call about a man with a gun on the porch at the West Philly home. When officers arrived, they approached and came under heavy gunfire, Bethel said.

Mayor Cherelle Parker said two of the officers were "badly wounded." They were rushed into surgery at Penn Presbyterian Medical Center.

Bethel said Seiber was shot three times. The other officer, a 33-year-old father of five, was shot 12 times, said Bethel, adding that "he's not out of the woods yet."

Seiber had recently completed SWAT training and hoped to be transferred to that unit, police sources told CBS News Philadelphia.

After the initial gunfire, more officers — including a SWAT team — were called to the scene and closed in on Lewis, who allegedly fired at the responding officers multiple times.

Lewis was eventually arrested after police pulled him from a tree and took him into custody.

Pennsylvania state Rep. Amen Brown, who lives a few blocks away, said Lewis was hiding in the tree for hours. Brown said he was on the scene to see the suspect being taken into custody.

The suspect lives in the neighborhood and has "an extensive criminal record," Brown said. While Lewis was being arrested, he allegedly said he wished he had killed more officers, Brown added.

Police recovered three guns from the scene — two handguns and a shotgun. One of the handguns had been taken from one of the officers who was shot, according to Bethel.

Lawmakers react to Philadelphia police shooting

Parker said the incident is a reminder of the dangers police officers face on the job and urged the public to pray for the officers.

"I want to be very clear, I am grateful for their service and the reason is because for nights like tonight. We think of them as law enforcement officers, but I see mothers and fathers, sons and daughters, brothers and sisters," Parker said.

"Beyond the fact that this is incredibly tragic, it feels even more tragic because the community has been working so hard here to make things safer," Councilmember Jamie Gauthier said during an afternoon news conference.

Parker also called upon Pennsylvania state leaders to consider bills to address mental health and substance abuse to help improve public safety.

"We are ... [seeking] legislation that will expand involuntary commitment laws to cover not only severe mental illness, but substance use disorder and any kind of mental and/or behavioral challenge that could interfere with Philadelphia's ability to keep itself safe," Parker said.

"I don't apologize for it."

In a statement, Gov. Josh Shapiro said he ordered U.S. and state flags to fly at half-staff in honor of Seiber.

"Our law enforcement officers are the very best of us," Shapiro said. "They put their lives on the line every day, running towards danger to keep their fellow Pennsylvanians safe, not knowing if they will return home. We owe them our deepest gratitude."

Pennsylvania U.S. Sen. John Fetterman posted on X that "we're hoping for a full and speedy recovery for the other officer.

"It's a stark reminder of the dangerous job our law enforcement has in keeping us all safe — and why we should always be grateful for their service," his post read.

World.title: House candidate who reported rape on campaign trail details why she came forward
World.content:
In the days since U.S. House candidate Bernadette Greene-Placentia publicly came forward alleging she was raped over the summer while repairing a campaign sign, she says women have been reaching out to her to share their own stories.

"The humbling thing is that so many – hundreds and hundreds of women from around the world — have taken the time to write me and tell me their own story," Greene-Placentia told CBS News in an interview. "I would say about 70% of them have acknowledged that they never reported it, and they are thanking me for being in the public eye and talking about it and giving voice because they didn't feel like they had a voice when they went through the same thing."

Greene-Placentia, a Democrat, is facing freshman Republican Rep. Abe Hamadeh on the ballot in November in Arizona's 8th District, located in the Phoenix suburbs. The district is rated as solidly Republican by Cook Political Report.

The reported sexual assault happened amid a heated campaign season, as concerns about political violence swirl. At a rally in September, an armed man lunged at Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, and at a town hall earlier this year, a man lunged and sprayed vinegar at Rep. Ilhan Omar.

Greene-Placentia, who had been a long-haul trucker, told CBS News that "we are not a well-funded campaign," and she and her staff were usually the ones putting up campaign signs or fixing them.

"I took pride in being able to, you know, do these things myself because we are a grassroots campaign, so it wasn't unusual," she said of fixing signs at all hours.

She said that a "little after midnight" one night in August, she was repairing some supplies when she was hit on the back of the head. When she regained consciousness, she said she realized she was on the ground, and a "man was on top of me, and then I felt pain down there." She said that man "climbed off," and then another man assaulted her.

"At that point, I remember I started, like, moving around and kicking," she said. "He said, 'You know, just not worth it.' And they left. I don't know how long I stayed there."

Greene-Placentia said she drove straight home, and she said she believes police have footage of her driving home.

A police report from the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office says the incident occurred on Aug. 14 between 2 a.m. and 3 a.m., and she reported the incident on Aug. 31.

The Maricopa County Sheriff's Office said in a statement earlier this week that it was investigating the incident but could not comment further.

Greene-Placentia said she told her husband and staff the next day, but she didn't want to talk about it at first.

Greene-Placentia said Friday that she realized she wanted to come forward while she was telling her own personal story on the trail. She said she was talking about how her father died while waiting to get care with the Department of Veterans Affairs and she found out six months later that her mother had been rationing her insulin.

"I was asking them, 'Do you think anybody's gonna fight harder than me?'" Greene-Placentia said. "And then in the back of my head, I'm like, 'Well you're telling these folks that you're gonna fight for them, but what about all the women that are victims of sexual assault? Are you not gonna fight for them? That kind of makes you a hypocrite, Bernadette.'"

Greene-Placentia's story was first published on Wednesday in the Phoenix New Times. Since then, her opponent, Hamadeh, called it a "disturbing story," and he was calling "upon authorities to investigate these serious allegations thoroughly, including finding all possible camera footage of the time and place in order to prosecute the crime to the fullest extent of the law."

Greene-Placentia said that she wants to tell women who come up to her that she understands what they are going through.

"As women, we want to take responsibility for everything and blame ourselves, and that is a societal problem we've got to get away from," Greene-Placentia said.

World.title: 8 killed, including 2 children, in mass shooting in Erie; suspect also dead
World.content:
A mass shooting in a residential area of Erie, Pennsylvania, left nine dead, including the suspected shooter, police said.

According to CBS affiliate Erie News Now, police were called to Perry Street around 5 p.m. on Friday after witnesses reported seeing a man firing a gun before he entered a home.

Two women were found dead in the street, and more victims were found dead inside the home.

Police said that the suspect was also found dead with an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.

On Saturday morning, police confirmed the death total and said that all of the deaths occurred before their arrival. They also said that no additional shots were fired after police arrived, and that during their response, sounds heard were flash-bangs associated with their tactical response.

The scene in Erie as of Saturday morning. KDKA Photojournalist Bryce Lutz

Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said that a tragedy of this magnitude is difficult to put into words.

"There are no words that can adequately express the magnitude of the loss of life here," he said. "Out of respect for the victims and their loved ones, I will not discuss the specific details of what our officers encountered today. Our investigators are working diligently as we speak to establish the full circumstances of what occurred. We will not speculate about a motive or any information that could compromise this investigation."

The City of Erie government and Erie Mayor Daria Devlin released a joint statement on social media reiterating that there is no longer a threat to the public.

"Tonight, a terrible tragedy occurred near 7th and Perry Streets in Erie, resulting in multiple deaths," the statement read. "We understand that this news brings deep shock and sorrow to our residents, and we want to assure the public that the situation has been contained. The shooter is deceased, and there is no ongoing threat or danger to the public at this time. Our thoughts are with the victims, their loved ones, and everyone impacted by tonight's tragedy."

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro issued a statement on Saturday morning.

"I've spoken with Mayor Devlin and offered my Administration's full support following the tragic mass shooting in Erie last night — killing nine of our fellow Pennsylvanians," Governor Shapiro's statement read. "My heart breaks for this family. Lori and I are praying for their loved ones and the entire Erie community."

KDKA-TV has reached out to law enforcement officials in Erie and will bring you the latest updates on KDKA.com and on KDKA-TV.

Editor's Note: This story has been updated to reflect that the total number of people dead includes the suspected shooter.

World.title: Trump says Ukraine needs new president, blames Zelenskyy for diesel prices
World.content:
President Trump said Saturday that it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting the current leader, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has not done enough to end his country's war with Russia.

"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does," Mr. Trump told reporters as he was leaving the White House for a trip to Tennessee.

He also blamed Ukraine's recent strikes on Russian oil refineries for contributing to high diesel prices before the midterm election, despite the ongoing war in Iran.

"He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel," Mr. Trump said.

Mr. Trump also suggested that if he had been U.S. president in 2022, Russia's invasion of Ukraine "would have never started."

"There was no reason that the war with Ukraine and Russia started," he said. "It started due to incompetence."

Zelenskyy, Mr. Trump said, has "lost 30% of your country and you've had over a million people go between the two of them, over 2 million people killed. That's a war that should have never started. And I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president."

President Trump speaks to members of the media as he departs the White House on the South Lawn on Oct. 10, 2026, in Washington, DC. Aaron Schwartz / Getty Images

Ukraine's foreign minister said Saturday that Zelenskyy had the backing of the Ukrainian people and deserved support.

"He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide," Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga said of Zelenskyy in a post on X. "Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well. He deserves support."

The American president's comments came hours after Zelenskyy offered pointed criticism of a new diesel deal between the U.S. and Russia. He said the deal would help bankroll Moscow's war in Ukraine.

According to Mr. Trump's announcement on Friday, Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."

"Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Mr. Trump's shocking announcement was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month that aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel Russia's war against Ukraine.

The Treasury Department announced Friday that it would temporarily waive sanctions on Russia's energy sector to "allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market."

In a lengthy post online reacting to the deal on Friday, Zelenskyy said Russia would repay it "with further terror and perfidy." He cast it as an investment in the war, allowing it to be prolonged.

"It plays into Russia's hands — allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world," he said.

Russian strikes kill at least 20 in Ukraine

Meanwhile, Russian strikes killed at least 20 people, including three children, in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, officials said on Saturday.

Russian aerial bombs hit residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, Mykhailo Semikin, the head of the regional military administration, said Saturday. At least 18 people were wounded.

A man talks on the phone while sitting on the rubble of a residential building destroyed by a Russian airstrike in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. AP Photo/Kateryna Klochko

Missiles also struck Kyiv in a daytime attack Saturday. Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said four people were wounded.

Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow's full-scale invasion. Ukraine is struggling to counter escalating Russian bombardments that have killed more than 60 people over the past four days.

Rescue workers clear the rubble of a residential building destroyed by a Russian airstrike in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. AP Photo/Kateryna Klochko

"Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia," Zelenskyy wrote Saturday on X.

He said the attacks show Moscow understands "any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities," adding that "different signals are needed."

World.title: Man attacked by tiger in England after entering enclosure at wildlife park
World.content:
A man sustained serious injuries Saturday after entering the tiger enclosure at a wildlife park in northern England, police said.

The incident occurred at the Yorkshire Wildlife Park near the city of Doncaster at about 1:35 p.m., South Yorkshire Police said in a statement. The tigers remained inside the enclosure and there was no danger to the wider public, the force said.

The Yorkshire Ambulance Service said it dispatched two ambulances, an air ambulance and a doctor to attend the scene. Authorities didn't immediately release information about the victim's injuries.

"We are working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened,'' the wildlife park said in a statement posted on its website.

Yorkshire Wildlife Park began operations in 2009, with its "Land of the Tigers" attraction opening in 2011.

The attraction is a purpose-built two-acre reserve for endangered Amur tigers, also known as Siberian tigers. The enclosure includes a 300-meter raised walkway that allows visitors to watch the big cats roam through woodlands and grasslands or playing in a waterfall pool, the park says on its website.

Visitors to several zoos and wildlife parks around the world have tried to enter tiger enclosures. A woman was caught in 2024 jumping over a fence and taunting a tiger at the Cohanzick Zoo in New Jersey. In 2016, a zookeeper was fatally attacked by a Malayan tiger at a Florida zoo when she entered the enclosure for the tigers' night house, a medical examiner's investigation found.

Several years earlier, in 2012, a man jumped from an area near the monorail in the Bronx Zoo over two fences, including an electrified one, in one bound to get into the tiger enclosure, police said. He was severely injured in what appeared to be a suicide attempt, police said.

World.title: Christa Pike discharged from the hospital and back in prison
World.content:
Christa Pike discharged from the hospital and back in prison

toggle caption i Tennessee Department of Correction/AP

Christa Pike was released from a local hospital and is back in prison, at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center in Tennessee, her attorneys Luke Ihnen, Randy Spivey, Stephen Ferrell and Kelly Gleason said in a statement on Saturday.

"She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances," the attorneys said.

They also said Pike is receiving medical care at the prison and they are tracking her recovery.

Pike had been hospitalized for several days after her botched execution last month, in which she received and survived two doses of the sedative pentobarbital.

NPR reported on the Sept. 30 execution attempt, in which Pike was strapped to a gurney and administered the barbiturate that is normally used in the U.S. executions. Shortly after the first dose was administered, Pike said her arm was burning and asked whether it was supposed to feel that way. She then said, "Please try up on my shoulder higher."

Sponsor Message

Spivey, who witnessed the execution attempt, previously told NPR that after a second dose Pike became unconscious but continued breathing and making choking sounds. "It "went on for so long," he said. He has called Pike "a survivor."

Judge I'Ashea Myles of the Davidson County Chancery Court in Nashville ordered the prison officials to preserve all evidence, such as messages, connected to Pike's failed execution.

Pike was on death row for a murder she committed when she was 18 years old. She and her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, in 1995, tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow classmate in the Knoxville Job Corps. Shipp received life in prison without parole for his part in the murder.

NPR's Scott Neuman contributed to this report.
