World.title: Spanish PM Sánchez launches campaign with housing as key theme
World.content:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez kicked off his election campaign for the 29 November election in Dos Hermanas, Seville, where more than 5,000 people gathered to hear him speak.

 

The choice of that town is no coincidence, as it is the largest city in Andalusia where the Socialists remain in power following the most recent regional elections.

It was there in 2017 that Sánchez began his bid to secure the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party's (PSOE) general secretariat. His campaigns in 2019 and 2023 also began in what Alejandro Moyano, deputy secretary for Organisation of the PSOE in Andalusia, describes as the party's "lucky city".

The Socialists have a long way to go to win back voters after losing the last series of elections: the 2022 Andalusian poll, the 2023 local and general elections, the 2024 European vote and the Andalusian elections earlier this year.

Sánchez paid tribute to Maricarmen Abascal, who has become a symbol of Spain's housing protests, saying that "the social cause bears the name of an 87-year-old woman". He also repeated one of her phrases: "What I have suffered, I don’t want anyone else to go through".

The prime minister described his political opponents as a bloc that has spent eight years spreading "messages of fear". By referring to the fable of 'The Boy Who Cried Wolf', Sánchez drew his own conclusion: "They are the wolf."

He summed up the dilemma facing the People's Party (PP) as "susto o muerte" ("fright or death"): if they are in opposition they hurl insults, and if they govern they make cuts.

Opposition leader and People's Party president Alberto Núñez Feijóo also launched his pre-election campaign in Madrid on Saturday. In his speech, he pledged to give his all for those in attendance and for the millions of Spaniards seeking change.

The People's Party presdient launched a sharp attack on Sánchez, arguing that he (Feijóo) does not come "from the saunas or the sewers" but from a background in management: from presenting and balancing budgets, maintaining public services and stepping up in good times and in bad.

After Sánchez called an early general election for 29 November, 2,769,645 voters holding a Spanish passport and residing abroad have been called to vote. This represents an increase of more than 19%, or 444,335 more voters than in the 2023 election, underscoring the impact of the so-called "Grandchildren's Law."

Since 2023, Spain's overall electoral register has grown by 1.26 million people, while 1.6 million young people have reached voting age and become eligible to cast their vote for the first time.

World.title: Left-wing primary: more than half of registered voters have already voted, say organisers
World.content:
After a first day disrupted by a cyberattack that slowed the voting process, the French centre-left primary is back on track, organisers said.

 

By midday on Saturday, 87,841 ballots had been cast, representing 62.6% of the 140,282 registered voters. At 7 p.m. on Friday, only 20,000 people had managed to vote.

Turnout will be crucial in gauging the success of this primary, which is held entirely online, as well as an indicator of the legitimacy the winning candidate will carry into the race for the Élysée Palace.

Other political forces are already well entrenched in the presidential race, notably the far-right with Marine Le Pen, and the far-left led by Jean-Luc Mélenchon.

Although he was not invited to take part in the primary, Mélenchon has remained a central figure in televised debates leading up to the vote. Discussions have focused on the possibility of an alliance with La France Insoumise in the legislative elections that will follow the presidential contest, as well as disagreements about endorsing the Insoumise candidate in the second round if the centre-left fails to qualify.

Speaking to Euronews, Rachel Garrat-Valcarcel, political journalist and author of the newsletter "Blocs & Partis", believes that a turnout of "at least 80%" would be necessary for the primary to be considered a success for its organisers, the Socialist Party and Place publique, the party of MEP Raphaël Gluksmann, regarded as the favourite.

But in her view, a high turnout alone would not be enough. To "very possibly" generate momentum, she argues, Glucksmann would have to win "by a very wide margin in the first round".

Five candidates in the running

Buoyed by the 14% won by his list in the 2024 European elections, Raphaël Glucksmann is facing several challengers in this primary, including Ségolène Royal, a prominent Socialist figure and former presidential candidate in 2007, Olivier Faure, the current Socialist Party (PS) leader, and MPs Jérôme Guedj and Emmanuel Maurel.

Before the cyberattack disrupted the ballot, the campaign had already been rocked by several controversies. Socialist MP Philippe Brun was excluded from the primary on September 16, following accusations of "violence" against a former staffer.

The debates have also been marked by heated exchanges, with Ségolène Royal going so far as to label Raphaël Glucksmann a "political intern".

The €15 fee charged to non-members of the PS and Place publique, reduced to €10 for those on lower incomes, has also drawn criticism. Critics argue the fee could favour Glucksmann's supporters, who are perceived as more affluent.

The result was initially expected on Saturday evening, but voting has been extended until Sunday at 6 p.m.

World.title: Pope Leo condemns death penalty, Vance vows not to watch Hasan’s execution live
World.content:
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth’s announcement of the execution by firing squad of Fort Hood gunman Nidal Malik Hasan continues to fuel controversy. Former US Army Major Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people and wounding another 32, is expected to be put to death in a live-streamed execution, most likely on 3 December.

 

Pope Leo XIV has also intervened in the debate, without commenting directly on the case. Marking the World Day Against the Death Penalty on 10 October, he declared on Saturday that capital punishment is “inadmissible”.

In a post on X, the US-born Pope cited the revised Catholic teaching on capital punishment introduced by Pope Francis, according to which the death penalty attacks the inherent dignity of a human being.

“The common good can be safeguarded and the demands of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment,” reads the post published on Leo’s account, @Pontifex. “Effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens and at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption.” The post ends with the hashtag #nopenadimorte.

The Pope did not refer to either the planned execution or the botched lethal injection in Tennessee that recently reignited the debate over the death penalty in the United States. However, his post came just hours after his top deputy, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, had explicitly stated that the planned public execution in the United States was “unacceptable” and that it was “unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle”.

In 2018, Pope Francis amended official Catholic teaching to declare the death penalty “inadmissible” in all circumstances.

Previously, the Catechism of the Catholic Church, the official compendium of Church teaching, stated that it did not rule out recourse to capital punishment “if this were the only possible way to defend effectively human lives against an unjust aggressor”.

The head of the US bishops’ conference, Archbishop Paul Coakley, expressed “shock” and “great sorrow” at the Pentagon’s plans. “In no way can Hasan’s actions be condoned, but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered,” he said in a statement on Friday. “The public execution even of those who have done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and represent a stain on the conscience of its people,” he added.

Vance will not watch the execution if it is broadcast

Although he has not opposed Hasan’s execution, US Vice-President JD Vance has said he will not watch the live broadcast and has even questioned whether the Pentagon’s plan for a public execution will actually go ahead.

According to Vance, the planned method of execution is distracting attention from the seriousness of Hasan’s crimes. “This is a man who carried out, in my view, the worst terrorist attack on American soil since 11 September,” the US vice-president said, adding: “The people he was supposed to care for, the Army soldiers he was meant to treat for mental illness and other problems, he struck at their moment of maximum vulnerability and mowed these people down right where they lived.”

“Whatever controversy there is over the method of execution, I hope people do not forget that this is a man who brutally murdered many innocent people,” he continued.

President Trump is a staunch supporter of the death penalty. In the first nine months of 2026, 30 executions have been carried out in the United States. The Pentagon said on Monday that the president had approved the execution of Major Hasan.

World.title: Cristiano Ronaldo suspended by Portuguese FA for leaving training camp
World.content:
The Disciplinary Board of the Portuguese Football Federation has opened disciplinary proceedings against Cristiano Ronaldo for walking out of the national team’s training camp in Copenhagen, Denmark.

 

Before the match against Denmark, the captain clashed with coach Jorge Jesus (JJ) after being left on the bench and not brought on in the previous game against Norway, despite what he had been promised. According to Ronaldo, Jorge Jesus had assured him he would play for 30 minutes.

Feeling that JJ had gone back on his word, Cristiano Ronaldo walked out on the national team on 30 September, posting a message on his Instagram account announcing his decision and promising that, “in due course”, he would tell “the truth to all Portuguese people” about the reasons behind his sudden departure.

Until the captain made that public statement, the football world struggled to ignore the controversy that had erupted within the squad. The players, however, did everything they could to stay out of the affair, avoiding media questions and ultimately delivering the national team’s four best performances in recent years.

Under coach Jorge Jesus, Portugal won all four matches, qualified for the next phase of the Nations League and climbed back to fifth place in the world rankings, pushing Brazil down to sixth.

In the letter Ronaldo posted on social media to explain why he had left the national team camp, he apologised to the squad, his teammates and the Portuguese people. He also said he was willing to return to the team and took “responsibility” for walking out, adding that he was prepared to face the disciplinary consequences.

According to the Disciplinary Board (CD), Cristiano Ronaldo has therefore been provisionally suspended while the case, classified as “urgent”, is processed.

“Disciplinary proceedings have been opened against Cristiano Ronaldo dos Santos Aveiro by decision of the Non-Professional Section on 9 October 2026, with the aim of determining whether the facts reported on 7 October 2026 have any disciplinary implications. Without prejudice to the automatic preventive suspension to which he was subject until the proceedings were opened, a non-automatic preventive suspension has been imposed on the player, and the case has been given urgent status,” reads the statement released by the CD.

According to sports website MaisFutebol ( source in Portuguese), the disciplinary proceedings began “after two complaints were filed against Ronaldo: one by the Federation’s own board and another by third parties outside the FPF”.

Cristiano Ronaldo has been suspended for 20 days under paragraph 2 of Article 40-A of the Federation’s Disciplinary Regulations.

The suspension ends on 30 October, which could mean the captain will be available to rejoin the squad in time for the national team’s November fixtures, adds MaisFutebol.

Ronaldo could face a severe punishment for leaving the training camp. The federation’s disciplinary regulations stipulate that any player who, without justification, “leaves or fails to attend” a training session, a match, or a national team activity “shall be sanctioned with a suspension of between one and six months”, in addition to a fine.

Ronaldo informed the federation that he was leaving, but it remained unclear whether the decision would be deemed justified under the regulations.

“I have already apologised, but I know that actions must have consequences. Anyone in the world of football, just like me, knows that, regardless of one’s status, the rules are the same for everyone,” Ronaldo wrote in the letter in question.

The federation said on Saturday that the case is before the disciplinary inquiry committee (CD) and that the information gathered will remain confidential until it reaches a conclusion.

World.title: Evacuations and injuries reported at Riyadh airport after another alleged Houthi attack
World.content:
The Riyadh international airport was attacked once again on Saturday, in what is reported to be a missile strike by Yemen’s Houthis, according to a diplomatic source.

 

"Dozens of people were injured, most of them Saudi nationals," a source at a hospital in the Saudi capital said, adding that at least five of the injured were treated in an intensive care unit.

The attack comes two days after three people were killed in a Houthi-claimed attacks on Riyadh's international airport on Thursday.

While Saudi authorities have not confirmed a new attack or evacuation of the airport, several witnesses said people at the King Khalid International Airport were being evacuated on Saturday, as the airport called on passengers to check their flight status.

One witness reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board, while another witness said they saw a strike that had wounded people.

"I was on gate 403" at the domestic terminal, one witness said. "I saw 401 hit, I saw injured in front of my eyes. Everyone was running."

The US, Canadian, German and Spanish embassies in Saudi Arabia warned citizens to avoid the airport following reports of the attack.

According to flight-tracking site Flightradar24, all flights to Riyadh have been either diverted or cancelled.

Meanwhile, Kuwait Airways said it cancelled two flights in and out of the Saudi capital, citing a "security situation".

"Kuwait Airways announces that flight KU775 from Kuwait to Riyadh and flight KU776 from Riyadh to Kuwait have been cancelled today, Saturday, October 10, 2026, due to the closure of the airport as a result of the security situation," read a statement posted online.

Several airlines, including Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines, had already suspended flights to and from Saudi airports following the attack on Thursday. The Houthis had warned global airlines about facing possible consequences for continuing to operate in Saudi airspace.

Saudi Arabia's airports, oil facilities and tankers are often the target of Houthi attacks, as fighting in Yemen between the rebel group and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces continues to escalate.

World.title: Houthi war risks dragging Israel and Turkey into Horn of Africa standoff
World.content:
The escalating clash between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia now threatens to ignite the already tense rivalry between Israel and Turkey in the Horn of Africa. This week, Turkey threw its military weight behind Saudi Arabia, while Somaliland – a self-declared state recognised only by Israel – is urgently seeking Israeli military support.

Advertising

Somaliland, a breakaway state from Somalia, is calling on Israel to provide military hardware. “We need air defence systems,” Mohamed Osman Fadal, a senior foreign affairs adviser to Somaliland’s president, said in a Middle East Eye interview this month.

Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi made a similar request last month for Israeli military support.

Last December, Israel became the first nation to recognise Somaliland, which declared independence from Somalia in 1991. Because of its close ties to Israel, Somaliland now fears it could become a target for the Houthis, who operate from Yemen just across the Gulf of Aden and have previously targeted Israel.

“The Houthi threat is growing; it’s a major issue,” said Gallia Lindenstrauss of the Institute for National Security Studies at Tel Aviv University.

“Access to the Red Sea and Somaliland’s location just across from Yemen are very important, and I think this is where Israel recognises that it’s difficult to deal with the threat only from afar, and it’s important to have allies in the Horn of Africa,” she added.

Israel, which is in the midst of an election campaign ahead of the 27 October vote, has not commented on the request. But Lindenstrauss predicts a favourable response. “Obviously, if you look at the location, there should be some military support," she said.

Turkey’s backing for Somalia

Yet Somaliland’s call for military aid is fuelled by more than just anxiety over the Houthis. Somalia’s government is still intent on reclaiming Somaliland, branding it a rogue state. At the same time, Turkey has stepped up its military support for Somalia, deploying F-16s and advanced drones in January, and running its largest overseas military base to train Somali troops.

Somaliland president makes 'historic' visit to Israel

“Turkey has strong defence cooperation with Somalia; Somaliland sees that as an issue for them. It sees them as a potential future threat down the road. And so that’s why they’re calling for Israeli security support,” explained Horn of Africa analyst Omar Mahmood of the International Crisis Group.

“I think what’s happening is both sides, Somalia and Somaliland, are drawing external actors into their local dispute,” added Mahmood. “So it’s elevating what has been an unresolved but a local dispute for quite some time into something broader, something more regional.”

Tensions between Turkey and Israel have also been mounting, fuelled by Israel’s ongoing wars in Gaza and Lebanon and Ankara’s vocal support for Hamas. Both nations now see each other as an increasing threat.

“There is a security dilemma evolving between Turkey and Israel,” warns Lindenstrauss. “What Turkey does for its security, Israel sees as threatening. What Israel does for its defences in [Syria] is seen as threatening.”

Soli Ozel, an expert on Turkey at the Institut Montaigne in France, warns that because Somalia holds such strategic value for Turkey, any Israeli military involvement in Somaliland could dangerously escalate the situation.

“They may consider the deployment of Israeli missiles in Somaliland another destabilising factor,” said Ozel. “But I don’t think that the F-16s or the drones would be used against Somaliland, honestly; at least for the moment, I wouldn’t expect that to happen.”

Lebanon becomes latest battleground in Turkish-Israeli tensions

Containment, not conflict

Ozel argues that while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan are trading increasingly bellicose rhetoric, both countries are engaged in a high-stakes battle of containment rather than conflict.

“The theatrics and the realities of Turkish-Israeli relations may not be exactly the same,” explained Ozel. “I don’t think they will fight, but they are both showing their colours, right? Israel sent missiles to Somaliland; the Turks send F-16s and drones in order to set limits to what the other party will do.”

Turkey is preparing to expand its military footprint in the region. This week, Turkey and Pakistan pledged armed support to Saudi Arabia against the Houthis under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed in August, a pact binding the three nations to mutual defence.

While the specifics remain unclear, Lindenstrauss notes that despite rising friction between Turkey and Israel, both countries may still find common cause in confronting the Houthis.

“I think the recognition that the Houthis are not something that is seen as only Israel’s problem, and it’s not just a minor proxy of Iran, but it’s a major problem that many states have to join together to deal with. I think that’s actually good news,” said Lindenstrauss.

Turkey warns it could be Israel's 'next enemy' as tensions escalate

Yet Mahmood cautions that as clashes in the Red Sea escalate, Israel’s possible deployment of military hardware to Somaliland points to a worrying new trend.

“Horn actors need to realise that while they’re inviting external actors in to support their own ambitions locally, to get one step over their political adversaries, they risk turning their theatre into a wider proxy battleground. And so certainly, I think there’s a risk that those types of tensions can spill over,” he warned.

World.title: Podcast: AI in France, translators fight back, musicians' mentor
World.content:
Artificial intelligence is everywhere in France but who's using it, and how? We also look at its impact on translators and how they're striving to keep humans at the helm. And Nadia Boulanger – the pioneering French composer and conductor who taught generations of musical greats.

Advertising

AI is widely used in France, despite many peoples' misgivings. Tech consultant Frederic Cavazza says adoption is being driven by individuals, rather than a coherent or systemic approach. That results in a paradox: the technology is everywhere, but guidance and confidence in it is lacking. (Listen @2'40'')

One field that is heavily impacted by generative AI in France – and the non-English-language world – is translation. Low-cost translation agencies are increasingly using machines to deliver first drafts and relying on humans for ungratifying, poorly paid "post-editing". But translators are fighting back. The En chair et en os collective and the recently-launched STEF union for translators in publishing marked last week's World Translation Day with symbolic strike action. They gathered to find collective ways of keeping humans at the heart of the translation process, including an initiative to "sabotage" the post-editing system. (Listen @17'50'')

The story of French musician Nadia Boulanger, a talented composer and the first woman to conduct some of the world's top orchestras. Today she is best remembered for teaching an extraordinary number of the 20th century's most famous musicians, from Aaron Copland to Philip Glass, Burt Bacharach and Quincy Jones. (Listen @10'30'')

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

World.title: Saudi Arabia: 12 killed, hundreds injured in Riyadh airport attack
World.content:
Officials said at least 12 people were killed in a strike on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh. The airport had already been targeted multiple times this week.

At least 12 people were killed and hundreds were injured in an attack on Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia on Saturday.

"King Khalid International Airport was targeted by an attack, amid continued attacks targeting civilian aviation facilities in the kingdom," the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said in an initial statement.

Hours later, the authority announced that 12 people had been killed, including four Saudis, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese national.

At least 309 others were injured in the attack, the aviation authority said, adding that "all injured individuals are receiving the necessary medical care at several hospitals."

Operations at the airport had been suspended until further notice.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen also announced that "a projectile" had also landed near King Fahd International Airport in the eastern city of Dammam.

What do we know about the Riyadh attack?

A Saudi official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told the Associated Press that many people were wounded after a missile hit a passenger terminal.

The AFP news news agency also reported that a number of people were injured, citing a local medical source who also spoke on the condition of anonymity.

"ER doctors are being called to hospitals across Riyadh," the source told AFP. "We were told we are dealing with a 'serious emergency situation'. Injured are being moved to hospitals across Riyadh."

Ambulances were seen outside the passenger terminal Image: Social Media/REUTERS

Several Western embassies in Riyadh, including those of Germany, the United States, Canada and Spain, urged citizens to avoid the airport.

The US embassy said it was "aware of attacks" at the airport. Spain's embassy referred to a "new attack" by the Houthi rebels in Yemen while Canada's embassy warned of "ongoing military activity."

What did the Houthis say?

The Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen did not immediately claim responsibility for the attack.

However, after the attack, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree retweeted his own post from a day earlier in which he said that only pre-approved humanitarian flights would be allowed to land at Riyadh airport.

In the retweet on Saturday night, Saree wrote: "A reminder."

When asked about the attack, US President Donald Trump said the US would soon decide whether to join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.

"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision," Trump told reporters at the White House. "We move very quickly."

Can Yemen's government turn the tide against the Houthis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Strikes hit Riyadh airport earlier this week

Fighting has intensified between Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed government in Yemen.

The Iran-backed Houthis have been launching strikes on targets in Saudi Arabia, including several this week on the airport in Riyadh that killed four people, injured several others, and damaged planes.

Etihad Airways and Qatar Airways canceled multiple flights between their ​respective hubs and Riyadh, with some cancellations extending into Monday. Kuwait Airways also cancelled its flights on Saturday.

King Khalid Airport was hit earlier this week in an attack claimed by Yemen-based Houthi rebels Image: Social Media/REUTERS

Last month, Houthi rebels made advances on important strategic locations along Yemen's Red Sea coast, with a Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces seeking to take back those gains.

The Houthis have responded by launching attacks into Saudi Arabia, which represents a significant escalation in their multi-year conflict with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government after a peace deal unraveled in July.

The Saudi-backed government in Yemen last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, especially those around the Bab al-Mandab strait.

World.title: Money, networks and bias: Why women struggle to win seats in US politics
World.content:
The US is holding Congress and state governors elections. At all levels of US politics, women are underrepresented — but they may win some historic victories in the midterms on November 3.

Around 51% of the population of the United States is female, but that is not reflected in the make-up of the US Congress, where only 28.4% of the members are women . Nevertheless, with 152 women in total sitting in the House of Representatives and Senate, the number is higher than it has ever been in the history of the United States. The number of female governors of the 50 US states is also currently higher than ever before: Some 14 of them — 28% — are women.

There are a number of reasons why there are still comparatively few female representatives in the US Congress. "Some of them are structural: There are rules and processes in place in our political system that make it harder for any newcomers to break in," says Kelly Dittmar, director of research at the Center for American Women and Politics (CAWP) at Rutgers University. "Historically, women were newcomers."

Seats in the Senate only come up for election every six years. Members of the House of Representatives serve two-year terms, but there is no limit to the number of times they can stand for reelection, so in theory they can stay in office for decades.

Also, as Dittmar points out, election campaigns in the US are very expensive. Women have historically been less able to access networks of rich donors — who, like many party leaders, are still most likely to be men. Leading male politicians are also more likely to recruit men to stand as new candidates. Finally, cultural biases also play a role: "Stereotypes and expectations about what women can and should do."

The elections on November 3 will decide whether more or fewer women will sit in the US Congress over the next two years. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate are up for election in the midterms. And in 36 states, the citizens will also decide who will move in to the governor's villa.

Amy Klobuchar is already a leading Democrat in the Senate Image: Nathan Posner/Anadolu/picture alliance

House of Representatives: Female Democrats outnumber female Republicans three to one

125 of the 435 representatives in the House are women. As in the Senate, and also with the gubernatorial posts, they are not evenly distributed between the two parties: There are more women among the Democrats than among the Republicans. At present, there are 95 women sitting as representatives for the Democrats, and 30 for the Republicans.

"There is a far less robust support infrastructure for women within the Republican Party," says Dittmar. She comments that organizations that specifically recruit, train, and fund women candidates are almost all either on the Democrat side, or non-partisan. Besides, she adds, "A lot of the [Republican] party leaders don't see an electoral incentive or pressure" to recruit more women. Diversity is more important to Democrat voters, who place greater value on seeing women among their elected representatives.

The Republicans currently have a majority in the House of Representatives, which means that they also get to appoint the Speaker or majority leader. At the moment, the position is held by Mike Johnson. Only one woman has held this powerful post to date: Nancy Pelosi, who was the Democrats' Speaker from 2007 to 2011, and again from 2019 to 2023.

Peggy Flanagan wants to become the first Native American woman to join the US Senate Image: Stephen Maturen/Getty Images/AFP

US Senate: Even higher bar for women

Women currently constitute 27% of the US Senate – 16 Democrats and 11 Republicans. Each of the 50 states is represented by two senators. The term of office is longer in this chamber of the US Congress, and the majority of the officials here represent many more voters than the representatives in the lower house.

According to Dittmar, it's even harder for women to win a seat in the Senate. "With the Senate, it's an opportunity and timing issue," she says. Each seat comes up for election every six years. There are 100 in total, and every two years only a third of them are available. Little opportunity, then, for women who have not previously sat in the Senate to advance. A state-wide senatorial election campaign is also more expensive than the equivalent campaign for a seat in the House of Representatives — and studies indicate that female candidates are generally less wealthy than their male counterparts.

For one senatorial candidate, the November midterms could prove historic. If the Democrat Peggy Flanagan wins in Minnesota, she will be the first Native American woman to sit in the US Senate. Flanagan is Ojibwe, otherwise known as Chippewa, an indigenous people from the Great Lakes region spanning the US and Canada.

Flanagan currently holds the post of lieutenant governor of Minnesota. Polls suggest that her chances are good. She has a slight lead over her rival, the Republican Michele Tafoya, previously a sports reporter and advisor to conservative politicians.

Keisha Lance Bottoms is vying to become the first ever female black governor Image: Elijah Nouvelage/Getty Images/AFP

First black woman state governor?

Ten of the current 14 female governors are Democrats, while four are Republicans. Six of the 14 are standing again, including Sarah Huckabee Sanders, the governor of Arkansas, who was President Trump's press secretary during his first term in office.

For the first time in US history, it is possible that a Black woman may be elected state governor. In Minnesota, the Democrat Tim Walz — Kamala Harris's vice-presidential candidate in the 2024 election — is not standing for reelection. The main rivals for his seat are the Democrat Amy Klobuchar and the (Black) Republican Lisa DeMuth. Meanwhile, the Black Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms is running for governor of the state of Georgia.

Kelly Dittmar doesn't think DeMuth will win in Minnesota — the state is regarded as solidly Democrat. And Klobuchar is well known among the people there; she has represented Minnesota in the US Senate since 2007.

But in Georgia, according to Dittmar, it's a different story: "That race is considered a toss-up, 50-50." Dittmar believes that Bottoms "absolutely has a chance to be the first Black woman governor." Former President Barack Obama is her most prominent supporter, while President Trump has declared his support for the Republican candidate, Rick Jackson.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Eritrea urges UN deterrence measures against Ethiopia
World.content:
Eritrea has officially requested UN Security Council assistance over the conflict in Tigray. Both Eritrea and Ethiopia accuse each other of fueling regional instability.

In the ongoing struggle for control of Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, both Ethiopia and Eritrea have appealed to the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) for assistance.

On Friday, citing Article 51 of the UN Charter, Ethiopia's Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said his country was making use of its right to exercise self-defense measures against Eritrea.

Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of deploying infantry and mechanized units in recent weeks and supporting, financing, arming and directing insurgent groups.

On Saturday, Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh, who rejected Ethiopia's accusations, responded in a letter, writing, "Eritrea requests the UN Security Council to forcefully condemn Ethiopia's deplorable declaration of war against Eritrea... and take the requisite deterrent measures," asking the international body to invoke Chapter VII of ​the ⁠UN Charter, which allows measures ⁠from ​sanctions to military action.

Saleh said Ethiopia's actions could cause, "huge devastation to the peoples of both countries and destabilize the region."

The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ethiopian troops regaining ground lost to TPLF rebels

Last month, Tigrayan rebel groups announced they had joined forces to oust Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, swiftly launching major attacks on Ethiopian government forces and seizing regional airports.

Since then, Ethiopian troops have driven back Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) militants and taken control of large parts of the region, including the capital, Mekelle.

Recent fighting, which broke a 2022 peace agreement, and this weekend's exchange of accusations only deepen the growing rift between Ethiopia and Eritrea, who were allies in a bloody 2020-2022 border war that saw them team up against TPLF rebels.

The developments also come as Ethiopian PM Abiy Ahmed reiterates his landlocked country's need for access to the Red Sea — a demand he repeated on Monday — and which Eritrea regards as a direct threat to its sovereignty.

World.title: Trump slams Zelenskyy, says Ukraine should elect new president
World.content:
President Trump has criticized Volodymyr Zelenskyy for not making a deal with Russia to end the Ukraine war. Trump also warned Kyiv against targeting Russian oil refineries that will supply the US with diesel fuel.

US President Donald Trump on Saturday said it's time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting that current Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not done enough to end Ukraine's war with Russia.

Speaking at the White House, Trump said, "I suggest they get a new leader who can make a [peace] deal," adding that "for some reason [Zelenskyy] never does."

Trump claimed Zelenskyy has "lost 30% of your country and you've had over a million people go between the two of them, over 2 million people killed. That's a war that should have never started. And I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president."

Independent estimates put the percentage of Ukrainian territory under Russian control at 20%, with British defense officials recently stating that about half a million Russian soldiers had been killed in the war and that there were no reliable recent estimates about how many Ukrainians had died.

In his remarks, the US president also warned Kyiv against targeting Russian oil refineries.

Trump said he had told Zelenskyy to "do what you want" against Russia but "don't hit refineries."

"He better damn well stop," Trump added.

Donald Trump blames Ukraine for record US diesel prices To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump again helping Putin, chiding Zelenskyy

Trump's calls for Zelenskyy to be replaced follow attacks leveled at the embattled ally on Friday, and Zelenskyy's condemnation of a US scheme that will fill Russia's state coffers and could allow Moscow to step up attacks.

Trump has been trying to deflect blame for rising fuel prices caused by his war with Iran onto Ukraine for the past several weeks and has publicly lambasted Zelenskyy for Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil infrastructure.

As US voters grow angrier and November midterm elections — which will determine the balance of power for the last two years of his presidency — near, Trump has repeatedly sought to pin blame for rising costs on Zelenskyy.

On Friday, Trump tried it again, claiming of the Ukrainian leader, "He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel."

Trump's statement came just after he had reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin — who launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022 and has illegally occupied Crimea since 2014 — to lift US sanctions on Russian diesel exports.

How Russia turned sanctions into a diesel deal To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Russia welcomes Trump's call for Zelenskyy's ouster, EU mulls response

Trump's call for Zelenskyy's replacement has been well received in Moscow, with Kremlin special economic envoy Kirill Dimitriev posting on X, "President Trump joins the many who believe that Ukaine needs leadership actually focused on peace, not Zelenskyy's warmongering."

Ukraine and its allies are still reeling after being blindsided by the announcement of the US-Russia diesel agreement on Friday.

Trump's call for Zelenskyy's removal came just hours after Russian attacks killed 20 people in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region on Saturday.

Zelenskyy commented on X, "Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia."

World.title: 'Ragebait' is the 2026 German Youth Word of the Year
World.content:
Already named the 2025 Oxford Word of the Year, "rage bait" has also been widely adopted in German slang.

The 2026 Youth Word of the Year, "Ragebait," was announced on Saturday at the Frankfurt Book Fair by publisher PONS Langenscheidt.

The "Jugendwort des Jahres," or German Youth Word of the Year, is an annual campaign that documents the popularity of new slang expressions.

"Ragebait" (in English: rage bait) refers to social media content that is deliberately designed to make people angry, frustrated or morally outraged.

It aims to drive engagement, since the algorithms of platforms like Instagram, TikTok and X reward high-energy interaction. A post that generates a heated debate through angry comments, or that is widely shared due to the emotional reaction it provokes, counts as high engagement, which leads the platforms to push the content to more feeds.

Shortlist also included 'Peak' and 'Crashout'

"Ragebait" was on a shortlist of three words for the 2026 Youth Word of the Year, alongside "Peak" and "Crashout."

All three terms are borrowed from English, demonstrating once again the language's significant influence on German youth culture.

Around one million young people, aged 11 to 20, have voted since August 28 for their favorite term.

"Ragebait" obtained 36.5% of the votes, followed by 33.8% for "Peak" and 29.7% for "Crashout."

"The close result shows that all three terms have a firm place in the vocabulary of generations Z and Alpha," said Artur Raiser, marketing manager at PONS Langenscheidt, in a press statement. "'Ragebait' held a slight lead from the start," but only by a narrow margin throughout the voting period, he added. "It remained an exciting race for us at the publishing house, too, until the very last moment."

Peak crash out

"Crashout" (used by young Germans as "crashout gehen," or "going crash out") originally comes from the English "to crash out," which traditionally means to fall asleep very quickly due to exhaustion.

But in newer internet slang, popularized on gaming and social media platforms, "crashing out" means having an intense emotional breakdown, losing control of one's temper or reacting with sudden, uncontrolled anger or stress. It is often used with a touch of humor, to emphasize that the reaction might be somewhat exaggerated.

As for the other shortlisted word, "Peak," it refers to something that is the absolute best. In German youth slang, it functions like an adjective: "That was peak football" or "that is peak comedy."

PONS Langenscheidt, a publishing company that specializes in language reference works, has been selecting the German Youth Word of the Year since 2008 — originally via a jury, and since 2020 through an online vote. Offensive, racist or discriminatory terms are not permitted. The multi-stage public nomination and voting process for next year's word will start in the summer of 2027.

"Das crazy" was selected last year, while "Aura" was the Youth Word of the Year 2024.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Germany sticks to Russia sanctions after Trump diesel deal
World.content:
10/10/2026 October 10, 2026 Germany 'committed' to further Russia sanctions

Germany has not purchased Russian oil since 2023 [FILE May 2024] Image: Alexander Ryumin/TASS/dpa/picture alliance

Germany on Saturday said it would continue pursuing sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine, coming a day after US President Donald Trump announced a temporary US sanctions reprieve on Russian diesel.

"The federal ⁠government ⁠has taken note of the US decision relating to Russian diesel deliveries," government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said in a statement.

"The federal government ​remains committed to the decisions on ​sanctions against ‌Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions," the statement added.

Germany's "support for Ukraine in its struggle to defend itself remains unfailing ... Diplomatic efforts for a peaceful solution continue," he added.

After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Moscow has been subject to round after round of sanctions packages led by the US and EU.

Russian crude and other oil products have been subject to EU sanctions since 2023, and Germany has not imported any oil or oil products from Russia since then.

A spokesperson for Economic Affairs Minister Katherina Reiche said Saturday that "Germany stands fully behind the sanctions packages."

"Our supply is diversified in this area; we are independent of Russian oil," the spokesperson said.

Germany remains Ukraine's largest financial backer in Europe. During a visit to Kyiv last weekend, Chancellor Friedrich Merz reiterated Germany's unwavering support for Ukraine.

In what amounts to a major reversal in US policy, Trump on Friday said he would temporarily lift US sanctions to allow Russia to "immediately" supply over 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to US and global markets.

The move comes as diesel prices reach record levels after the war in Iran launched by the US and Israel sent diesel prices skyrocketing around the world. In the US, the high prices are putting political pressure on Trump's Republicans ahead of the midterm elections in November.

However, despite Trump's claims on social media, it remains unclear how much Russian fuel will reach global markets amid domestic fuel shortages as Ukraine continues to target refineries.

World.title: Operations Plan Germany: How the Bundeswehr trains for NATO collective defense
World.content:
How prepared is Germany for national defense? The answer lies in the Operations Plan Germany. Military exercises such as "Red Storm Charlie" are designed to put these preparations to the test in realistic scenarios.

In a residential district of Hamburg at midnight, the streets are quiet and deserted. Suddenly, the silence is shattered: Several helicopters circle the night sky, and flashing blue lights illuminate the darkness. A long convoy of vehicles moves through the streets. Soldiers stand atop armored Bundeswehr vehicles, their machine guns at the ready. For local residents, it is an unusual, perhaps even unsettling sight in an otherwise peaceful port city.

"Red Storm Charlie" is the name of the exercise that brought parts of Hamburg, northern Germany's largest city, to a standstill for three days. The Bundeswehr, police, and civilian organizations were jointly testing how well prepared they are to respond in a crisis.

The scenario centers on a deteriorating security situation on NATO's eastern flank. NATO troops, represented in the exercise by Bundeswehr soldiers, arrive at the port of Hamburg, Germany's largest seaport, before moving eastwards through the Hanseatic city.

Acts of sabotage and demonstrations, also included in the scenario, hamper their advance. With around 1,700 participants, including 500 soldiers, the exercise held in late September 2026, was the largest of its kind to date.

"Red Storm Charlie" forms part of a classified strategy known as the "Operationsplan Deutschland " (Operations Plan Germany). Through this document, the Bundeswehr is preparing for the possibility of a Russian attack on NATO territory. The Operations Plan Germany is an integral element of NATO's broader defense planning and is closely aligned with the Alliance's overall defense framework.

NATO members in Kyiv: 'We stand unwavering with Ukraine' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In the event of war or a major crisis, not only the city of Hamburg but Germany as a whole would assume a pivotal role as a logistics hub for hundreds of thousands of NATO soldiers, weapons, and pieces of heavy equipment. "This is a highly detailed and strictly classified plan that specifies exactly where NATO allies would arrive in Germany, including which ports they would use and which routes would be required for their transit across the country," security expert Aylin Matlé of the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) told DW.

Germany as a transit country for NATO troops

The Baltic states are widely regarded as the region where NATO considers a Russian attack most likely. In such a scenario, the alliance would concentrate large troop contingents from its 32 member states there. To reach the region, soldiers from southern and western Europe would need to pass through Germany. "In concrete terms, this means that around 800,000 soldiers and 200,000 vehicles would have to move through our country within six months. Those are the calculations," says Marcel Bohnert, a Bundeswehr officer who contributed to the first version of the Operations Plan.

Speaking to DW in a personal capacity rather than as a representative of the Bundeswehr, Bohnert explained: "We must ensure that soldiers can use our roads and ports safely. That is why we take care of all their needs: We arrange accommodation, provide food, ensure their security, and guide them through our transport network."

The plan also covers transport in the opposite direction, from east to west, including the evacuation of wounded soldiers and civilians fleeing the conflict. Its development was commissioned by Bundeswehr Inspector General Carsten Breuer in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. As Germany's highest-ranking military officer, Breuer is far from alone in his concern that Russia could target additional countries. Germany is already confronting a wide range of Russian hostile activities, from cyberattacks to acts of sabotage directed against the Bundeswehr.

German spy chief warns of rising Russia threat To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Defense Minister Pistorius: 'Moscow is testing our response'

A new dimension of the threat emerged with the attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August. An explosive-laden drone was deployed there and failed to detonate only through luck. The German government holds Russia responsible. "The threat is becoming more tangible. It is serious, acute, and increasingly visible. This is exactly what the Russian president wants. Moscow is testing our response," Defense Minister Boris Pistorius of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) told the Bundestag on September 23.

The Bundeswehr is also addressing this threat through the Operations Plan Germany, which is continuously being refined and updated. Lessons learned from exercises such as "Red Storm Charlie" are incorporated into the plan. According to Bohnert, the plan also serves as a deterrent: "We hope to discourage Russia from further aggression by demonstrating our strength through the rapid build-up of military capabilities and the highly organized, swift deployment of forces to the borders."

Roads and bridges need upgrading

How well prepared is Germany for its role as a military logistics hub? Matlé identifies one major vulnerability in the country's ageing and, in some cases, deteriorating infrastructure. Germany, she argues, must address the maintenance and repair of the bridges, roads, and transport routes required for troop movements "far more quickly and comprehensively." "Some of this infrastructure dates back to the Cold War and was not designed to accommodate heavy loads or military equipment."

A further challenge lies in striking the right balance between confidentiality and public involvement. To guard against acts of sabotage, sensitive details such as the precise transit routes for NATO troops must not fall into Russian hands. At the same time, the plan can only succeed through close cooperation between the Bundeswehr and civilian society, including local and regional authorities, the police, and relief organizations. "Parts of the plan must be publicly accessible because we need support from society, as well as from ministries and governments, to make it work," said Bohnert.

Could the AfD pass on sensitive information?

The debate over the confidentiality of the more than 1,000-page document recently resurfaced after the far-right Alternative for Germany(AfD) emerged as the strongest party in recent elections in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Security experts expressed concern that the party, which is classified in part as right-wing extremist and is regarded as Russia-friendly, could pass information from the plan to Moscow if it were to assume the office of state premier. The Defense Ministry rejected these concerns, noting that no federal state is given access to the complete document. Instead, the sensitive sections of the Operations Plan are shared only in excerpts and strictly on a need-to-know basis.

According to observers, however, the growing number of hybrid threats is underscoring the need for secrecy. During the "Red Storm Charlie" exercise in Hamburg, accredited journalists were not informed of routes or locations until the very last moment because of concerns over potential disruptions and acts of sabotage.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Taiwan to boost military spending to 'deter war' with China
World.content:
President Lai Ching-te ⁠said in a National Day speech that his country is boosting defense spending to 'deter war' with China. It comes after US President Donald Trump asked Taiwan to pay for US protection.

Taiwan plans to boost defense spending to deter war, President Lai Ching-te said on Saturday, as China steps up military pressure to assert its claim over the self-governed island.

Lai's government has allocated a record NT$1.1 trillion ($34.5 billion) for defense spending in 2027, equivalent to more than 3% of GDP.

Taiwan's 23 million people face the threat of a Chinese attack. Beijing claims the island as part of its territory and has not ruled out using force to bring it under its control.

"Our aim in increasing investment in national defence is not to provoke, but to deter war," President Lai Ching-te said in a speech marking Taiwan's National Day.

Successive governments have increased military spending as Taiwan strengthens its defenses against a potential Chinese invasion and seeks to demonstrate to the United States its commitment to defending itself.

Lai says China must respect Taiwanese people's right to exist

"We do not seek hegemony, nor do we seek to dominate others," Lai said in his annual address outside the Presidential Office in Taipei, attended by thousands of people, including foreign diplomats.

He warned that peace could not be taken for granted, accusing China of using military and grey-zone activities to change the status quo across the Taiwan Strait.

Lai welcomed talks between the United States and China but stressed that Beijing must respect "the right of the people of Taiwan to exist."

Officials in Washington and Taipei have repeatedly said US policy on Taiwan remains unchanged under President Donald Trump, although some of his remarks have raised concerns in Taipei.

US arms deal in focus as Taiwan awaits Trump's approval

Trump raised concerns in May when he suggested that US arms sales to Taiwan could be used as a bargaining chip in negotiations with Chinese President Xi Jinping, following their meeting in Beijing.

Taiwan is awaiting Trump's approval of $14 billion in weapons sales, including the US-made Patriot air defense system.

At a high-profile summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington in September, trade and artificial intelligence dominated the agenda. One of the most contentious issues, Taiwan, was discussed only behind closed doors.

Ahead of Lai's speech, Taiwanese fighter jets and two Chinook helicopters carrying giant Taiwan flags flew over the capital.

Facing China's much larger military, which continues to expand its arsenal with advanced weapons, including stealth fighter jets, aircraft carriers and a vast array of missiles, Taiwan is increasing defence spending and modernising its armed forces.

Lai said Taiwan's resolve was about more than its survival in the face of "authoritarian expansion" in his National Day speech Image: Chiang Ying-ying/AP Photo/picture alliance

Washington remains Taipei's most important security backer

China's Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Lai's speech. Beijing has never renounced the use of force to bring Taiwan under its control, calls Lai a "separatist" and has rejected his offers of talks.

Democratically governed Taiwan faces growing military and political pressure from China, which claims the island as its territory despite strong objections from the government in Taipei.

The United States welcomed Lai's commitment to maintaining peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait. A senior US administration official said that, referring to China, "a routine speech is no justification for aggressive or coercive actions."

The United States switched official diplomatic relations from Taipei to Beijing nearly 50 years ago, but Washington is Taipei's most important security backer.

Saturday's celebrations marked the 115th anniversary of the 1911 revolution that toppled China's Qing dynasty and paved the way for the founding of the Republic of China.

The dispute between China and Taiwan dates back to the Chinese civil war, when nationalist leader Chiang Kai-shek fled to the island in 1949 after his forces were defeated by Mao Zedong's communists.

World.title: Sánchez se centra en vivienda y ataca al PP por dudar del voto por correo: “Estos son los de cuantos menos voten, mejor”
World.content:
Pedro Sánchez ha arrancado en el auditorio Los del Río de Dos Hermanas (Sevilla) su primer mitin de la larga campaña electoral ante unas 5.000 personas, según el PSOE. Los socialistas han dejado definitivamente atrás las invocaciones a la llegada de la derecha y la extrema derecha. Ya gobiernan juntas en cuatro comunidades. Ya están ahí, así que hay poca novedad. A lo que sí ha apelado el presidente del Gobierno y candidato a la reelección es a Maricarmen Abascal, la mujer de 87 años que falleció el pasado miércoles días después de haber sido desalojada de la que había sido su casa durante 70 años.

“La causa social lleva el nombre de una mujer de 87 años y honraremos ese ejemplo de vida cuando afirmó: ‘Lo que yo he sufrido, que no lo sufra nadie más”, ha dicho Sánchez, que se ha mostrado convencido de que el desbordamiento de la sociedad es lo que procurará “una mayoría progresista”. Y se ha comprometido a reforzar los decretos ley de la vivienda tras las elecciones, dando por hecho que ganará.

01:30 Sánchez, sobre los que ponen en duda el voto por correo: “Ahora son los de ‘cuantos menos voten, mejor” El presidente del Gobierno y secretario general del PSOE, Pedro Sánchez, en Dos Hermanas (Sevilla), durante el primer mitin de precampaña electoral. Foto: PACO PUENTES

Sánchez se ha referido al “bulo” de que el voto por correo en España no es seguro. “¿No os parece un poco raro?”, se ha preguntado el líder socialista, quien cree que tras esa duda lo que el PP manifiesta es “miedo porque van a perder”. En un intento de ser pedagógico, Sánchez ha afirmado que el voto por correo lo utilizan los trabajadores que están de guardia en domingo o los que “viven fuera” o “las personas desvalidas” que ni pueden desplazarse por sí solas. “Estos de ‘los que puedan hacer que hagan’ [una frase de José María Aznar] son los de ‘cuantos menos voten, mejor”.

En su opinión, el PP y Vox llevan ocho años lanzando “mensajes de miedo” y están siempre con la “fábula de Pedro y el lobo. El lobo son ellos; yo, en todo caso, un perro que no tiene amo”.

Una simpatizante de Pedro Sánchez sostiene un cartel con su imagen, este sábado en Dos Hermanas (Sevilla). PACO PUENTES

Antes del mitin, el PSOE ha publicado en redes un vídeo de campaña donde se recogen todos los insultos dirigidos al presidente del Gobierno y candidato socialista a la reelección. Feijóo, Abascal, Tellado, Milei, Trump, Díaz Ayuso, entre otros, aparecen profiriendo graves acusaciones contra el líder socialista. Un cartel con las palabras “Pedro Sánchez, hijo de puta” cierra la primera parte del vídeo. ¿Por qué nos insultan?”, se preguntan. “Nos insultan porque somos el Gobierno de la gente que pone en su sitio a los de arriba”, responden. El PSOE ya convirtió en suya la expresión “PerroSánchez” a su favor, y ahora pretende hacer lo mismo con los insultos, en un video que evoca el difundido por los socialistas en la campaña de 1996, en el que se veía la imagen de un amenazante perro dóberman con el que el PSOE quería alertar de lo que ocurriría si el PP de José María Aznar llegaba a La Moncloa, como finalmente ocurrió. Sánchez ha justificado en algunas ocasiones determinadas decisiones de las que renegaba en el pasado apelando a que había que hacer “de la necesidad virtud”. Más o menos es lo que pretende hacer ahora. El lema electoral en estos primeros días es “La fuerza de la gente”.

Sánchez ha apelado al triunfo de la política frente a la “mala educación” y ha asegurado que estas elecciones son de “susto o muerte”, porque si el PP sigue en la oposición, seguirá con los insultos y, si gobierna, “recortan”. Tanto el candidato como la secretaria general del PSOE andaluz y vicesecretaria federal, María Jesús Montero, han hecho repaso de la gestión del Gobierno (subida de las pensiones, SMI, reforma laboral, crecimiento económico) y han advertido de la propuesta de Vox de implantar un sistema mixto de pensiones.

Menos de 24 horas después de anunciar el pasado lunes la disolución de las Cortes y la convocatoria de las elecciones para el 29 de noviembre, la secretaría federal de Organización comunicó al PSOE andaluz que Sánchez abriría la campaña en Dos Hermanas por deseo expreso del presidente del Gobierno. Después de perder el poder en todas las capitales de provincia andaluzas, esta ciudad es la más grande que gobiernan los socialistas en Andalucía. Sánchez arrancó aquí en 2017 su carrera interna para recuperar la secretaría general del PSOE, tras su dramática salida en 2016. En Dos Hermanas inició la campaña de 2019 y de nuevo eligió esta ciudad en la de 2023. “El presidente tiene un especial vínculo emocional con Dos Hermanas”, comentó días atrás la secretaria general del PSOE de Andalucía, María Jesús Montero.

Pedro Sánchez, junto a María Jesús Montero y Francisco Rodríguez. PACO PUENTES

La elección de esta ciudad de 146.522 habitantes para arrancar la campaña tiene mucho de simbología porque pretende invocar a las remontadas de Sánchez en momentos difíciles. Y es una manera de lanzar el mensaje de que el PSOE andaluz, en sus horas más bajas, aún tiene músculo para llenar los recintos. El sitio escogido es el auditorio Los del Río, con capacidad para 3.386 personas sentadas, aunque dispone de una gran extensión de césped y puede llegar a albergar hasta 4.526 personas, según recoge la web de la Junta. “Es una ciudad talismán y queremos llevar al presidente en volandas”, afirma el secretario adjunto de Organización del PSOE andaluz, Alejandro Moyano. Para llenar el auditorio, han tocado el cornetín en las ocho provincias andaluzas, con la contratación de un centenar de autobuses. Pese al esfuerzo, este acto palidece con los que antaño se celebraron en el velódromo nazareno, donde el PSOE llegó a reunir a 20.000 personas para escuchar a Felipe González, Alfonso Guerra o José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, todos hoy fuera de juego por distintos motivos.

El PSOE andaluz afronta otro reto seis meses después de las autonómicas de mayo ―donde obtuvo el peor resultado de su historia en unas autonómicas). Lleva perdidas las cinco últimas elecciones —andaluzas de 2022; municipales de 2023; generales de 2023; europeas de 2024 y andaluzas de 2026— y está por ver si conseguirá quebrar esa curva descendente. En 2023, los resultados en Andalucía y Cataluña fueron claves para apuntalar a Pedro Sánchez. Aportaron 21 y 19 escaños, respectivamente. En esta ocasión, Andalucía elige 60 diputados, uno menos por la pérdida de población en Cádiz que gana Madrid. El pasado mayo, el PP aventajó al PSOE en Andalucía en 19 puntos, lo mismo que hace cuatro años en autonómicas. Pero en las generales ese margen se estrecha mucho. Ocurrió en 2023, cuando los socialistas lograron recortar, movilizaron más de medio millón de votos y se quedaron a tres puntos. Ese es el objetivo también ahora.

World.title: Las ‘telecos’ se tambalean ante la entrada de Starlink en el mercado móvil
World.content:
Las acciones de las operadoras en Europa y EE UU se hunden en Bolsa tras confirmarse la compra de licencias de espectro por SpaceX para convertir a su filial en operador móvil

Las acciones de las principales compañías de telecomunicaciones registraron notables descensos en los mercados de renta variable a ambos lados del Atlántico, tras el anuncio de que SpaceX, la firma de servicios aeroespaciales fundada por Elon Musk, ha adquirido una cartera de licencias de espectro de baja frecuencia en Estados Unidos por valor de unos 8.000 millones de dólares (7.140 millones de euros). La operación permitirá a su filial de conectividad satelital, Starlink, prestar servicios de telefonía móvil directa a terminales convencionales.

Al cierre de la última sesión en Wall Street, los títulos de T-Mobile US cedieron un 12,4%, mientras que las acciones de Verizon Communications y AT&T cayeron un 9,8% y un 10,2%, respectivamente. El movimiento a la baja se trasladó con fuerza a los parqués europeos. Deutsche Telekom encabezó los descensos en el continente con un retroceso del 8,94%, penalizada por su participación mayoritaria en T-Mobile US. En la Bolsa de Madrid, Telefónica perdió un 4,61% hasta los 3,25 euros por acción, situándose cerca de sus mínimos anuales. Por su parte, la británica Vodafone cedió un 4,86% en Londres y la francesa Orange bajó un 2,50% en París.

El detonante de las ventas masivas en el sector ha sido la transacción acordada por SpaceX con el fondo de inversión Grain Management. Mediante este acuerdo, la compañía aeroespacial pasa a controlar licencias en la banda de 800 megahercios (MHz), una frecuencia utilizada tradicionalmente por la infraestructura terrestre de antenas para ofrecer cobertura de telefonía móvil de amplia cobertura y capacidad de penetración en interiores.

La transacción se suma a una serie de movimientos corporativos e inversión en capital ejecutados por la firma de Elon Musk. SpaceX, que levantó 86.000 millones de dólares (76.800 millones de euros) en su oferta pública de venta (OPV) del pasado junio y cotiza con una valoración superior a los 2 billones de dólares, fortalece así la capacidad operativa de Starlink. La filial opera actualmente una red de banda ancha por satélite de órbita baja con presencia en más de 160 países.

En una comunicación remitida al mercado tras obtener la autorización del regulador de telecomunicaciones de Estados Unidos (FCC), SpaceX detalló que la división Starlink Mobile combinará su constelación de satélites Gen2 con despliegues en infraestructura terrestre. La combinación de la red no terrestre con el nuevo espectro de baja frecuencia en la banda de 800 MHz busca resolver dos de las principales limitaciones históricas de la tecnología satelital: la menor densidad de tráfico admitida y la interrupción de la señal en espacios cerrados o dentro de edificios.

La FCC aprobó recientemente el plan de la compañía para poner en órbita hasta 15.000 nuevos satélites de segunda generación. Esta ampliación operativa refuerza la capacidad de red del grupo, que el año pasado ya adquirió licencias de espectro inalámbrico a la firma EchoStar por 17.000 millones de dólares. Según los datos del comunicado corporativo, la nueva arquitectura convertirá a la división en el primer operador comercial en integrar espectro terrestre y satelital en un único servicio móvil.

Pese a la reacción positiva de la cotización de SpaceX, que avanzó más de un 1% tras conocerse la transacción, diversos análisis de mercado han señalado los costes de capital y el endeudamiento asociados a la expansión del grupo. Para desplegar la infraestructura terrestre complementaria necesaria y ejecutar sus proyectos de inteligencia artificial, SpaceX prevé captar 40.000 millones de dólares de financiación adicional, estructurados en 10.000 millones de dólares en préstamos bancarios y 30.000 millones en emisión de deuda, destinados en parte a la adquisición de chips de procesamiento avanzado.

Un mercado aún reducido

El avance de las tecnologías de conectividad satelital directa al móvil (Direct to Cell) modifica el escenario competitivo para las operadoras tradicionales a escala global. Hasta la fecha, los servicios satelitales mantenían un uso residual en la mayoría de los mercados desarrollados. En España, el informe más reciente de la Comisión Nacional de los Mercados y la Competencia (CNMC) contabiliza cerca de 100.000 conexiones activas por satélite, una cifra reducida respecto al total de líneas móviles en el país. Sin embargo, el organismo regulador español advirtió de la creciente concentración del segmento en torno a operadores globales como Starlink

En el mercado español, la tecnología de satélite directo al móvil opera actualmente en fase piloto. Durante los incendios forestales registrados en julio de 2026 en Ávila, Madrid y Toledo, Starlink activó de forma puntual servicios de mensajería y emergencia en zonas sin cobertura terrestre, en colaboración con operadores locales como Movistar y MásOrange.

El despliegue comercial masivo del servicio Starlink Mobile requerirá el cumplimiento de los marcos regulatorios locales y el uso de terminales compatibles con el estándar 3GPP Release 17 y módems de última generación. Los dispositivos de fabricantes como Apple (a partir de la serie iPhone 13), Samsung (serie Galaxy S21 y posteriores) y Google (serie Pixel 9) cuentan con la arquitectura de hardware requerida para la conexión directa con redes no terrestres.

World.title: Las cajas de ahorro islámicas están de moda en Turquía
World.content:
Sus sucursales se han multiplicado en los últimos años, especialmente en las capitales de provincia del interior de Turquía, donde ocupan los puestos de honor de las principales avenidas. Sus lustrosos y modernos escaparates prometen hacer realidad los sueños de sus clientes: adquirir una casa, un automóvil o una tienda “sin necesidad de créditos” o “sin pagar intereses”. Son las Empresas de Financiación mediante Ahorro (TFS, en turco), una suerte de cajas de ahorro islámicas basadas en los principios de las finanzas islámicas, como el rechazo a los intereses —aunque esto, como mucho en las finanzas islámicas, tiene truco— y la mutualización del riesgo: un grupo de ahorradores aporta cuotas mensuales a un fondo común y, por turnos o por sorteo, cada miembro recibe el capital solicitado para adquirir la propiedad elegida.

Algunas, como Eminevim o Fuzul, se han convertido en grandes grupos empresariales. Comenzaron su existencia como sociedades de ahorro colectivo creadas durante los años noventa por empresarios del entorno del islamismo político deseosos de financiarse fuera de unos bancos controlados por la —entonces dominante— élite laica del país. Otras quebraron o fueron liquidadas, pues operaban en un vacío legal. Su historia cambió en 2021, cuando el Gobierno del conservador Recep Tayyip Erdogan endureció los requisitos de solvencia, profesionalizándolas y poniéndolas bajo el control de la Agencia de Regulación y Supervisión Bancaria. Pero sobre todo, su verdadera explosión se ha dado desde que, en 2023, Mehmet Simsek fue nombrado ministro de Finanzas con el mandato de reducir una tasa de inflación que había llegado a superar el 100% interanual. Aplicó el manual más ortodoxo e instó al Banco Central a elevar el precio del dinero, lo que ha supuesto que los bancos restrinjan los créditos y eleven los intereses de sus préstamos hipotecarios por encima del 40% anual (la inflación sigue sin bajar del 30%). “Debido a las medidas de macroprudencia financiera, se ha hecho muy difícil acceder a créditos bancarios. Aunque, al inicio, las TFS se dirigían a personas de bajos ingresos, ahora les interesan a trabajadores de cuello blanco e incluso a gente de ingresos altos que no puede acceder a créditos bancarios”, explica Ahmet Büyükduman, analista financiero.

Una comisión fija por adelantado

Frente a los elevados intereses que demandan los bancos —y que implican que se termine pagando casi cuatro veces el capital inicial en préstamos a diez años—, las TFS cobran una comisión fija por adelantado, equivalente a entre el 7% y el 10% del capital solicitado. La pega es que solo se puede acceder a la casa, el automóvil o el negocio que se va a adquirir cuando se ha aportado al fondo el 45% de su valor, lo cual puede ocurrir pronto —si se adelanta parte del capital o se eligen cuotas de pago mensuales elevadas— o tardar varios años. La TFS, luego, hipoteca el bien hasta que el cliente ha terminado de pagar los plazos, pero entretanto puede hacer uso de él. Otro de los problemas es la protección de los ahorros contra la inflación galopante, ya que la cantidad solicitada por un cliente al inicio del programa puede haberse convertido en insignificante cuando llega a ejecutarla. Así que las TFS han tenido que establecer programas de inversión de estos ahorros en oro, bonos del Estado acordes con las finanzas islámicas (sukuk) o fondos.

De los apenas 370.000 usuarios que las TFS tenían hace tres años en Turquía se ha pasado a más de 1,5 millones en la actualidad, y su tamaño en activos se ha multiplicado por diez hasta superar los 9.000 millones de euros. Aun así, apenas suponen una fracción de la banca tradicional, y es que muchos turcos mantienen cierta suspicacia: por el carácter islámico de este sistema y porque algunos lo acusan de ser un esquema piramidal, debido a la necesidad de que lleguen nuevos ahorradores para mantenerse. Pero Büyükduman atribuye estas críticas a falta de información: “También los bancos pueden quebrar si los depositantes se retiran”. Para este experto, lo más importante es que estas entidades “promueven el ahorro antes de ofrecer un préstamo” y permiten a personas que trabajan en sectores informales acceder a financiación.

World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The United States has announced sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), escalating Trump’s war on the international tribunal.

“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate,” US secretary of state Marco Rubio said in an announcement.

The Trump administration has previously pledged to dismantle the court “brick by brick” and has sanctioned 13 current and former staff members, but this is the first time it has levied sanctions against the institution itself.

Ahead of the announcement, prime minister Rob Jetten said the Netherlands will protect the ICC “stone by stone”.

Foreign minister Tom Berendsen said the country would stand behind the court. “The announced sanctions against the International Criminal Court are an undesirable new escalation,” Berendsen said in a statement. “I deeply regret this new step.”

The sanctions will cut the court off from any US company or organisation, including providers of financial and technology services.

The announcement came hours after South African jurist Navi Pillay, who has served as a judge at both the ICC and the International Court of Justice in The Hague, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

Trump has long coveted the prize, telling reporters earlier this week that he deserved the award for what he said was ending eight wars.

World.title: Russia wants NL to hand over ICC judges
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Russia has asked the Netherlands to hand over nine International Criminal Court (ICC) officials who were convicted in absentia last year.

The prosecutor’s office in Moscow requested the extradition of the court’s president, Tomoko Akane, and other staff members for their involvement in the arrest warrant of Russian president Vladimir Putin.

The ICC issued the warrant for Putin’s alleged involvement in “the war crime of unlawful deportation of children” from occupied Ukraine.

The ICC has also issued an arrest warrant against Maria Alekseyevna Lvova-Belova, Russia’s commissioner for children’s rights.

In December, a court in Moscow convicted Akane and others in absentia, sentencing them to prison terms ranging from 3.5 to 15 years.

Japan, Akane’s home country, said the request was regrettable. “Measures targeting individuals connected to the ICC are unjust and unacceptable,” Masanao Ozaki, the country’s deputy chief cabinet secretary, said.

The United States has also sanctioned 13 staff members, including Akane, over the investigation into alleged Israeli war crimes in Gaza.

World.title: Unions call regional transport strike, threaten weekly walkout
World.content:
Regional bus services across the Netherlands will be heavily disrupted on Wednesday, after the FNV and CNV unions called a nationwide 24-hour strike in a dispute over a new pay and conditions deal.

If Wednesday’s strike does not shift the employers, the unions say they will hold an action day every week, and will only announce the dates shortly beforehand. Earlier this month they said they were considering weekly strikes in the run-up to Christmas.

Some 13,000 workers, mainly bus drivers, are covered by the public transport collective agreement, which expired on July 1. Staff at Arriva, EBS, Qbuzz, Keolis, Transdev and RET’s regional services are involved. City transport in Amsterdam, Rotterdam and The Hague is not affected.

Talks broke down after eight rounds of negotiations. This week an ultimatum to the employers’ organisation VWOV expired without a response.

“Employers are holding on to drastic cuts in working conditions,” FNV negotiator Marijn van der Gaag said in a statement. “In doing so, they are forcing their staff to take action.”

The unions say employers want to reduce sick pay, add more unpaid breaks to shifts and give staff less say over their rosters. Rosters are currently fixed about eight days in advance, and employers want to cut that to four days or less, Van der Gaag said.

The FNV wants a 6% pay rise. The CNV is calling for 9.5% over two years, as well as better arrangements for older workers and faster access to permanent contracts.

“We will not let employers sabotage the action by drawing up emergency rosters at the last minute,” CNV negotiator Niels Rook said, explaining why dates will not be announced in advance.
