Warning graphic content Eight people from the same family, including a five-year-old boy, a one-year-old girl, and a woman who was eight months pregnant, have been killed in a shooting in Erie, Pennsylvania, police said, in one of the worst mass shootings in the city’s history. A doorbell camera captured two women frantically trying to catch the attention of neighbours to raise the alarm about what was happening inside the house. Moments later, the two women, a relative and a family friend, were also shot dead in the street. Police gather outside the scene of a shooting in Erie. WJET via AP Police said the shooter died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound and there was no ongoing threat to public safety.



All the deaths occurred before officers arrived at the scene, where they were met with an eerie silence, the city’s police chief Rick Lorah said at a press conference on Sunday morning AEDT. “There was no movement, no audible sounds coming from inside the residence, no gunshots, no screams,” he said. “It was horrific. It was the worst scene I have ever experienced. “Out of respect for the victims and the families, I will not discuss the details of what our officers encountered inside that home. But I want our community to understand the gravity of what happened and the profound impact this tragedy has had on those involved and on our community as a whole.”



Jennifer Lott, who lives on the block where the shooting took place, said she was at home when she heard gunshots and a woman lying in the street. “I got closer, and I noticed she had a gunshot wound to her head and she wasn’t moving, and everybody kept telling me to back up; the police were coming,” she told The New York Times on Saturday. Loading Lorah said police had received doorbell video and audio from a home next door, including a scream and two muffled gunshots. “That is where we were able to see those two females pacing back and forth outside the residence; they were trying to get neighbours’ attention,” he said.



“Video evidence reviewed by investigators shows those two women arriving at the residence appearing distressed, seeking assistance from neighbours and pounding on the door. The audio video also appears to capture muffled gunfire from inside the residence before the suspect emerged and fatally shot both women.” Inside the home, two young children were found on the first floor: a five-year-old boy and a one-year-old girl. Four additional victims were found on the second floor in the stairwell: a 24-year-old female, a 44-year-old female, a 19-year-old male, and a 21-year-old male. The 45-year-old suspected shooter was found dead on the second floor from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound. Loading Lorah said he had been a police officer for 28 years and that he had never “seen the loss of life and the devastation that we just witnessed.” “This is one of the most difficult and heartbreaking scenes our officers and investigators have ever encountered,” Lorah said. “The loss of life is devastating, and the circumstances we are working through are deeply disturbing.”



Governor Josh Shapiro said Saturday he offered his administration’s “full support” to Erie Mayor Daria Devlin. View post on X “I’ve spoken with Mayor Devlin and offered my Administration’s full support following the tragic mass shooting in Erie last night — killing nine of our fellow Pennsylvanians,” Shapiro wrote in a Saturday morning post on X. Erie is the fifth most populous city in Pennsylvania and is located on the shores of Lake Erie. Watch: Erie Police chief Rick Lorah’s press conference on Sunday morning AEDT.

World.title: Ikitau out of Sydney Bledisloe but Valetini to avoid hip-drop scrutiny
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Ikitau out of Sydney Bledisloe but Valetini to avoid hip-drop scrutiny Iain Payten October 11, 2026 — 9:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The Wallabies will be without star centre Len Ikitau for the second Bledisloe Cup clash in Sydney on Saturday, but a three-week delay in World Rugby outlawing hip drop tackles is set to help key backrower Rob Valetini avoid a potential suspension that could have even stretched into the team’s spring tour of Europe. The squad updates for Bledisloe II came as Wallabies coach Les Kiss and players said a 50-19 loss to the All Blacks in Auckland will not damage the belief of the side, something that has been forged over the past 30 months. Loading The Wallabies and All Blacks both shifted to Sydney on Sunday ahead of a return clash at Accor Stadium next Saturday afternoon. Both sides are set for reshuffles at the selection table. The Wallabies will be without key No.12 Ikitau, who failed an HIA and left the game after 30 minutes at Eden Park. Isaac Henry and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii finished the game as a midfield duo, and with Hunter Paisami suspended, that partnership is likely to continue.



All Blacks coach Dave Rennie said Scott Barrett also failed an HIA and was in doubt, and winger Leroy Carter is all but certain to miss the Sydney match after injuring his left ankle while scoring a try in the second half. The circumstances of the injury were contentious, given Valetini appeared to trap Carter’s ankle in a tackle from behind while trying to stop the try. Rob Valetini tackles Leroy Carter from behind at Eden Park. Getty Images “It didn’t look good, sort of like a ... hip-drop type tackle, [which] landed on the back side of his ankle. I haven’t had a chance to talk to the doc yet, but it looked reasonably serious,” Rennie said post-game. Rennie said he would “leave that for the officials” when asked about judicial scrutiny on hip-drops, but added he was sure it wasn’t intentional from Valetini, a player he coached for several years.



Valetini will not come under any scrutiny from the SANZAAR match review panel, however, given the hip-drop is still several weeks away from being officially banned in rugby. World Rugby announced last week that it was amending its regulation 9.13, which covers dangerous tackles, to include hip-drop tackles. It came after heavy lobbying from Rugby Australia, following nasty tackles that caused major injuries to stars like Max Jorgensen and Treyvon Pritchard. “Concern has been raised about rare actions in our game that are known as ‘hip drop tackles.’ They often lead to significant injuries to the ball carrier,” World Rugby said in a statement. Carter in pain after scoring. Getty Images “World Rugby’s Tackle Working Group heard representations about this appearing in rugby union and considered that they have been banned in both American football and rugby league. The Tackle Working Group recommended explicitly banning the action in rugby union as well.”



Valetini’s desperate tackle from behind on Carter appeared to meet some of the criteria published for a hip-drop, and sanctions for dangerous tackles under Law 9.13 start at two match suspensions for low range offences, and mid-range starts at six weeks. But Valetini won’t face a potential citation because World Rugby also stated the new offence won’t come into effect until November 1. Meanwhile, the Wallabies say a bad night at the office in Auckland won’t undo all the good work they’ve done in building up confidence and belief this year. Treyvon Pritchard suffered serious injuries in this hip drop tackle but is recovering well after surgery. Stan Sport The Wallabies were on an unbeaten run of six games heading into the Eden Park clash, but were blown out of the water in the second half. After New Zealand led 17-14 at halftime, the home team piled on 33-5 points in the second half to secure a 24th straight Bledisloe Cup win.



Asked if the Wallabies’ belief in themselves would be damaged by the big defeat, coach Les Kiss said he didn’t believe so. Related Article Opinion

Wallabies History was there for the taking – until Wallabies bombed under a high-ball blitz Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author “It’s like anything – if you get a knockback, you find out more about yourself, and that’s what we’ll do,” he said. “We’ll work hard on what we have to do. Belief is created and sustained by not just wins and losses. They’re created by other things. These boys have a strong culture and a strong belief in themselves and a confidence about what they can do.” Wallabies lock Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, who played well in an 80-minute effort, echoed the coach’s sentiments.



“Our belief isn’t built just based on wins. Our belief is built through connection throughout the group and our preparation that we do, day in, day out,” he said. “Our confidence isn’t shot at all. We get to have another crack at them next week back in Sydney, so we’re looking forward to that.” Salakaia-Loto said the Wallabies had their opportunities, but failed to seize the big moments, particularly early in the second half. “You can’t be letting those opportunities slip against the quality side like the All Blacks, and we know that they’ll punish you for it,” he said. “You don’t get many opportunities against them, so when you do, you’ve got to strike and you’ve got to make the most out of it.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Highway to heaven: Melbourne teens gather to venerate relics of ‘influencer’ saint
World.content:
NationalVictoriaReligion Highway to heaven: Melbourne teens gather to venerate relics of ‘influencer’ saint Carolyn Webb October 11, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

He’s at the centre of what organisers call a “highway to heaven” missionary visit to Australia, and posters of Carlo Acutis radiated the charisma of a pop star at a Melbourne school last Wednesday. With his tousled hair, gentle smile and red polo shirt, Carlo had the casual look of a singer like Ed Sheeran. A photo of St Carlo Acutis during the mass held at Antonine College in Pascoe Vale South, with his relics on an altar. Simon Schluter But Carlo is not in a band. And he’s not alive, at least physically. Carlo, who died of leukaemia in 2006, age 15, was canonised – declared a saint – by Pope Leo in 2025, and is known as the first Millennial saint and God’s influencer.



Relics, meaning tissue from St Carlo’s body, are travelling around Australia in a Catholic Church-approved move to inspire people, particularly the young, to follow Jesus, do good, and cut back on video gaming. On Wednesday, about 500 students – most of them teens – attended mass in St Carlo’s honour at Antonine College, a Maronite Catholic school in Pascoe Vale South. A nun blesses an Antonine College student with one of St Carlo’s reliquaries. Simon Schluter They viewed the relics, kept in two 30-centimetre high metal reliquaries, that were displayed in the school hall. One contained pieces of the pericardium (the sac that encloses St Carlo’s heart), that were visible through glass. The other contained strands of his hair.



After mass, students lined up to be blessed by the priest, Father Eli Yammine, and a nun, Sister Veronique Karam, who held the reliquaries over each child’s head. At tables, students wrote prayers to St Carlo which will be sent to the saint’s tomb in Assisi, Italy. Carlo, an English-born Italian boy who attended mass daily, was known for using social media and websites to evangelise, promote volunteering and document more than 130 church-approved “Eucharistic miracles” – instances of bread and wine turning into flesh and blood. Pilgrims at the canonisation mass of Carlo Acutis and Pier Giorgio Frassati in St Peter’s Square in the Vatican, in September last year. AP He played video games only for one hour a week, so not to distract him from his faith or helping others. After his death, two miracles – people surviving near-death illness or accident – were attributed to his intercession.



Kate Hobbs, president of Friends of St Carlo Acutis Australia, a lay group taking the relics to 53 Australian cities in four months, said young people relate to St Carlo. Related Article Catholic church ‘God’s influencer’: How a Nike-wearing teenager became a saint “He challenges them, but he also gives them a hope and a way to come to God,” Hobbs said. The way he lived could teach them there was room for spirituality in their lives, she said. Last week, Hobbs took St Carlo’s relics to Melbourne’s Royal Children’s Hospital, where she prayed with a seven-year-old heart surgery patient and her parents. The girl’s mother, who wanted to use only the name Joanna for privacy reasons, said her daughter had a “deep devotion” to St Carlo, and that the visit was special to her daughter because the relic was a piece of the saint’s heart “and she’s recovering from heart surgery”.



“It’s been a hard road and we’ve been doing novenas – a series of prayers – to St Carlo connected to my daughter’s deep devotion to him. My daughter has been praying to him for her healing,” she said. “To have that opportunity for the relics to visit her, with her unable to visit them herself, was very special.” Antonine College student Annabelle Mansour writes a prayer to St Carlo. Simon Schluter At the Antonine College mass on Wednesday, Larisa Kyriakous, 17, who with 14 classmates visited St Carlo’s tomb – which features a lifelike effigy – in Assisi last year, said the teenage saint inspired her. “Growing up in a world that relies on technology, we get so distracted with what’s around us, I think we forget, as Christians, what’s really important,” Larisa said.

Houston: Death row inmate Christa Pike was released from a US hospital on Saturday (US time) and sent back to prison, where she would continue receiving medical care following her botched execution attempt in Tennessee, her attorneys said.

Pike was discharged from a local hospital and was now at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Centre, where she had been housed for more than 30 years, said attorneys Stephen Ferrell and Luke Ihnen from Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee, and Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason from the Tennessee Office of the Post Conviction Defender in a joint release.

Christa Pike, sentenced to death for a 1995 murder, awoke “angry and confused” in the hospital this week. CNN

Pike, sentenced to death for a 1995 murder, awoke “angry and confused” in the hospital this week with a long recuperation ahead after surviving the attempted execution on September 30, her lawyers said on Wednesday. They previously believed she could be brain-dead.

Pike, 50, was taken from the execution chamber to a Nashville hospital, unconscious, critically ill and ‌with severe arm injuries after two injections failed to kill her at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution.

Claire Spargo, a PhD student who led the research, will use the findings “to develop an evidence-based clinical pathway” to better support healthcare professionals and patients navigate this period.



Fitness-to-drive assessments tend to be conducted by GPs (alongside memory clinics for those with dementia), who Spargo says can feel uncomfortable broaching the topic given its impact on patients’ independence and identity. In July, the National Transport Commission announced a review into these assessments, amid calls for national consistency and evidence-based tools to support healthcare professionals in making tough decisions. The RACGP’s Professor Dimity Pond says she has lost patients after recommending they stop driving. She tries to broach the topic early, but it isn’t always easy. “We see people in their 80s about 16 times a year as GPs, so every few months I’ll introduce it into the conversation, and talk about reducing kilometres or not driving to Queensland for their holidays, so it’s a gradual thing rather than a shock,” she says. “The more this is normalised and discussed as a part of a life stage, the easier it is for people to move through that transition,” agrees Anstey.



More older Australians living alone, caring for relatives or with adult children who have young kids, makes stopping driving more difficult, says Pond. Pond would like to see subsidised access to costly on-road assessments by occupational therapists, which are better predictors of driving safety. For Spargo, the findings highlight the need for funding for services to support seniors after they stop driving – both emotionally, as participants reported loneliness and isolation, and practically, in terms of alternative transport and community services that help keep them connected. Anne Field, 73, is a keen driver – regularly going on trips with dog Teddy. George Chan Thinking ahead



Seventy-three-year-old Anne Field loves to drive – her red, manual Toyota Yaris taking her around her south Sydney and for road trips further afield. Her beloved Cavalier Teddy is regularly in tow. Editor's pick Exclusive

Wellbeing Still working at 80? The future is grim or thrilling, depending on who you ask “I’ve always had the convenience of having the car. I’m very independent – I hate having to ask anybody for anything,” she says. Field, a retired social sciences teacher and local councillor, lives an active life and is in good health. But living alone, she has thought ahead to a future in which she can no longer drive.



Field has a bus stop on her street, a local shuttle service and is close with neighbours who can help take her to medical appointments if needed. While she has cataracts and her hearing is deteriorating, she sees specialists regularly to monitor her vision and hearing. “You’ve got to be switched on to all of these as you get older.” Preparing for life after driving Professor Kaarin Anstey says the decision to stop driving is highly individual, but it’s important for families and individuals to educate themselves about the process.

Anstey and her team developed website Ageing Well on the Road which provides free, evidence-based information and resources for seniors.

Talk to your GP or trusted health professional and, if you have the means, consider working with a qualified occupational therapist who can assess driving on the road.

Claire Stokes recommends thinking ahead – including about where you live, the availability of alternative transport and proximity of essential services like supermarkets and doctors.

Familiarise yourself with community transport services and government subsidies for public transport and ride-share services and taxis.

Many community groups and private companies offer refresher driving courses for seniors. Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: Election live: Labour promises fresh, locally made school lunches if elected into power
World.content:
Election 2026 coverage

Latest election news: Stay up to date with all the ins and outs on the campaign trail.RNZ policy guide: Our comprehensive guide to every policy announced by the parties vying for your vote.

World.title: Labour says its school lunches would be made on-site, cover all 244,400 students already involved
World.content:
Labour has confirmed more details of its plan to reinstate the former school lunch programme from Term 1 2028, if elected.

The party has released a cost of living action plan, tying a bow on the cost of living policy blitz it's been conducting in recent weeks.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406615626112

While mostly a re-cap of already-announced policies like the three free GP visits, public transport fare caps, and student debt cut, there are two new policies on the list.

The document said the lunches would continue to cover 244,400 students in the 1014 schools already included. Lunches would be $5 a meal, and $6.50 for students in years 9 to 13.

The lunches would be made in school kitchens, by iwi and hapū partners or by local caterers.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins. RNZ / Sam Rillstone

Labour's fiscal plan, released last week, said it would continue to fund the existing programme at $146.2 million for the 2027/28 fiscal year, $295.4m for 2028/29, and then $149.2m in 2029/30.

The cost of living policy plan also included a commitment to restore rural school bus routes.

Labour said if it could not restore a cancelled route, then it would work with rural communities and local councils to find an alternative.

The Green Party also has promised to reinstate the former school lunch programme.

Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson said the Greens' election policy would restore the Ka Ora Ka Ako programme so lunches were provided through schools or local providers, and would expand it to approximately 400 more schools.

Davidson said this would ensure 150,000 more children would get a lunch every day.

The current Government has also funded the Healthy School Lunches programme for another year, committing $212m towards an extension.

World.title: National would make completing Year 11 compulsory if back in power
World.content:
National will require high school students to stay in school until they complete Year 11, if re-elected.

Education spokesperson Erica Stanford said students can currently leave school when they turn 16 but many reach that birthday during Year 11, allowing them to leave before completing the year.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406617591112

"Students should complete at least a full Year 11 of compulsory science, English and maths, and have the opportunity to gain the new Foundational Award in literacy and numeracy.

"Strong literacy and numeracy skills give young people a better chance of gaining employment or continuing on into trades' training or other learning. This change will mean more students stay at school longer and complete that important year of study."

Students would still be able to apply for a leaving exemption if they have a job or are moving into other training.

National at Northcote Intermediate School announcing they will make Year 11 compulsory. Tu Natanahira/RNZ

The policy is part of National's wider education manifesto, which includes scrapping NCEA in favour of new national qualifications.

National would introduce a Foundational Award in 2028, followed by the New Zealand Certificate of Education at Year 12 in 2029 and the New Zealand Advanced Certificate of Education at Year 13 in 2030.

National would also set nationally consistent start and finish dates for schools.

World.title: Greens would establish programme to guarantee jobs for all young Kiwis
World.content:
The Green Party says it will pay the wages of every New Zealander aged 16 to 24 who has been out of work for six months or more.

The party said it will establish a pilot programme called Jobs for Young People, modelled on the Jobs for Nature scheme established in response to the Covid-19 downturn, which it says will some 32,000 young people back into work.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406615602112

It says will cost $4.9 billion over four years.

The money would primarily be channelled through Mayors' Taskforce - an initiative between local and central government to get young people jobs through their local councils.

Party co-leader Marama Davidson said community services are short staffed while infrastructure and nature need maintenance and renewal.

She said the Greens will guarantee young people jobs in doing is important work.

"When there is so much real work to be done, it doesn't make sense that our young people are struggling to get by, losing hope after receiving hundreds of job rejections. Thanks to Luxon's Government, there aren't enough jobs for our young people.

"The Green Party will fix this problem head-on, instead of blaming young people, by setting up a Jobs for Young People programme. Because when the market is failing our young people, it's time for the government to step in to support them."

Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick called unemployment among young people "a ticking time bomb".

World.title: Police appeal for information after serious assault in Māngere
World.content:
Police are urging anyone with information regarding a serious assault in the South Auckland suburb of Māngere to come forward.

Two people have been injured after an altercation, understood to have involved a gun, outside a house on Harwell Place.

Both are now in a stable condition.

Detective Senior Sergeant, Veronica McPherson, said the incident occurred around 12.30pm on Saturday.

World.title: Football Ferns match with Panama called off after earthquake
World.content:
The first of two women's football internationals between Panama and New Zealand has been cancelled, following the powerful earthquake which struck the central American nation on Saturday (NZT).

The quake measured a magnitude 7.7 with aftershocks measuring up to magnitude 5.8.

The game was to be played in Panama City at Estadio Rommel Fernández Gutiérrez this morning (Sunday NZT).

New Zealand Football have confirmed that all of the Ferns players and staff are safe and accounted for.

In a statement, New Zealand Football say they will continue to monitor the situation.

The second match is scheduled for Wednesday afternoon (NZT), at the same venue.

Reuters reported on Saturday that the earthquake had damaged homes, cut power and halted flights.

World.title: The ‘glass skin’ Korean beauty trend has risks, experts warn
World.content: The glass skin trend has its roots in South Korean beauty culture, where the term is used to describe a complexion that appears exceptionally smooth and pore-less. The phrase appears to have first come around in the early to mid-2010s and then saw a major spike at the end of 2025 going into 2026, according to Google trends. Those who subscribe to the complex routines say their skin benefits from the layers of hydration, and viewers are hooked on the ASMR-like videos as influencers tap their glass-like faces with their fingers and beauty tools.

World.title: Matt Renshaw's 190 turns Durban Test, providing Aussie batting blueprint
World.content:
Like many great plans, it was deceptively simple. Stillness. Balance. Patience. Concentration. No frills, no fast moves and no undue risks, just decisive action when needed.

Not for the first time at Test level, a burly Queenslander, a three-pound cleft of willow and a healthy dose of self-confidence was the difference between Australian success and failure.

That Matt Renshaw resurrected an Australian first innings which teetered near oblivion at 6-124 was the first point of order.

Of consequences further-reaching, the left-hander resurrected his entire Test career overnight in Durban, sweeping, clipping and crashing his way to 190 from 397 deliveries across 465 minutes of life-affirming Test batting.

Numerous records fell or threatened to. Renshaw's epic was the highest score by an Australian in Durban, the fourth highest overall by an Aussie against South Africa, and the best by a number-five of any nation at Kingsmead.

It was also a new Test personal best for Renshaw, usurping the 184 he made nine years ago as a boyish tyro against Pakistan in Sydney, back when the world was at his feet.

Renshaw is 30 now — a husband, a father of two children and an entirely different cricketer. He knows his own mind and understands his place in the scheme of things.

For a nation which has been crying out for big, important runs by someone not named Smith or Head, his Daddy hundred here was one for the ages.

Practically speaking, Renshaw helped Australia to a first-innings total of 390, which was at least 150 more than had seemed optimistic when he first took guard.

On a deeper level, it restored belief in the value of grinding out an innings of depth and character. It was the real deal — the proper Test match batting the Australian cricketing public has been craving.

No mistake should be made about the high degree of difficulty, either. When Renshaw began shepherding the tail a day earlier, Australia was at the mercy of a vigorous and versatile South African pace attack jagging the ball all over the place.

Waiting in the wings were the Proteas' twin spin options of Keshav Maharaj and Simon Harmer, with 1700+ first-class wickets between them.

Australia has struggled against left-arm spin in recent times. Last time they played a Test in Durban, Maharaj took nine wickets. And Australia's selection for this match — four left handers in the top six — was said to favour right-arm off-spinner Harmer even more.

Matt Renshaw blunted South Africa's spin attack with judicious use of the sweep and reverse sweep in Durban. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

So much for that, in the end. Renshaw swept, reverse-swept and paddled Maharaj into irrelevance and by the time Harmer finally removed the top-scorer for spin's first wicket of the game, the horse had well and truly bolted.

As it turned out, the sterner challenge was curbing the influence of the quicks, who'd posed constant difficulties for the rest of Australia's batters.

A microcosm came when Renshaw was on 130, yet still not able to relax. He was struck a scary blow to the grille of his helmet from an absolute snorter by Anrich Nortje, who bowled with genuine pace and accuracy in short, sharp spells.

Handling the wily and indefatigable Wiaan Mulder was no cinch either. Early on day two, the all-rounder scythed through Pat Cummins and Mitchell Starc and threatened to blow the game open.

Wiaan Mulder (centre) took two wickets on day two and proved hard to play for Australia's batters. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

That he didn't was not exclusively a matter of Renshaw's dominance but of the rearguard partnerships which have so often saved Australia's bacon in recent times.

Renshaw shared stands of 86 across 32 overs with Pat Cummins and a monumental and possibly series-shaping 134 from 47 overs with Nathan Lyon.

Australia will not be looking too far ahead, but there was a blueprint here, not just of personnel but of general batting philosophy: know your game, make them bowl to you, stick around and wear them down.

Australia's total was the most obvious metric of success, but its innings duration of 137.2 overs will surely please Andrew McDonald and his analysts just as much.

In Australia's 35 Test innings in the two years before this match, they'd batted past the 100-over mark only six times, compared with 13 times in the 42 innings of the two-year period preceding.

That downward trend has, of course, coincided with a proliferation of the result pitches which characterise the World Test Championship era.

Concurrently, it is agreed by most involved in the Australian domestic scene, it has been difficult for Test batting candidates to put their best feet forward, or get in the habit of playing long innings, when the primary bloc of red-ball cricket occurs in spring, when Sheffield Shield pitches sometimes resemble Monty Don's perennial beds.

Without peering too far into the future or wishing disruption on a player who's just delivered something so special, one awkward talking point that will be aired soon enough is if and when Renshaw might move up to his normal position of opener.

The theory going into this game was that in batting down the order, he could blunt the influence of the spinners, which he assuredly did. But he would surely be just as assured against the new ball as he was here against the second new ball.

And yet, who'd be an opener these days? Late on day two, Ryan Rickelton provided a study in contrasts for the Proteas.

Having spent the better part of two days chasing leather in the field, and perhaps daydreaming that he was in Renshaw's shoes, he lasted only three deliveries before chasing Josh Hazlewood outside his off-stump and sending an edge to the cordon.

The more telling image of day two arrived an hour earlier, on the stroke of tea, when an exhausted Renshaw removed his helmet and trudged off for refreshments.

Appearing on the balcony of the player's area, Australian skipper Cummins peered down on the centurion with something like a look of love on his face.

Ray Illingworth once said a captain needs the patience of a saint, the diplomacy of an ambassador, the compassion of a social worker and the skin of a rhino. Colleagues who can bat for eight hours help, too.

World.title: Quick hits: AFL star in the sheds as Aussies go better than Bradman
World.content:
Matt Renshaw and Nathan Lyon outdo Sir Donald Bradman while Gold Coast Suns AFL star Noah Anderson watches on from the stands.

Here are the quick hits from day two of the first Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. Renshaw's drought-breaking century

DURBAN, SOUTH AFRICA - OCTOBER 10: Matthew Renshaw of Australia during day 2 of the 1st Dafabet Test match between South Africa and Australia at Hollywoodbets Kingsmead Stadium on October 10, 2026 in Durban, South Africa. (Photo by Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images) (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

It had been over nine years and nine months since Matt Renshaw's last and only Test century.

Opening the batting on January 3, 2017, a then 20-year-old Renshaw peeled off 184 against Pakistan in Sydney, a match in which he lined up alongside the likes of two-Test white-ball specialist Hilton Cartwright and New South Wales great Steve O'Keefe.

A few false dawns, a short-format reinvention and a red-ball renaissance later, and the Queenslander brought up his drought-breaking ton with an immaculately timed clip through mid-wicket for four.

Having lost overnight partner Pat Cummins and number nine Mitch Starc in quick succession after starting the day on 46, Renshaw was almost chanceless in reaching three figures.

It was a classic Test dig by Matt Renshaw. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

It was a richly deserved milestone for a player, who, at 30, still has plenty of good years ahead of him.

And Renshaw just kept going.

And going.

He received much more than able support from Nathan Lyon as he passed 150, before kicking on with number 11 Josh Hazlewood to set a new Test best of 190, falling just short of a maiden double ton as he nicked off after tea.

2. Better than Bradman

The first innings appeared not long for this world when the best betters in the tail, Cummins and Starc, departed.

But Lyon picked up the mantle to knuckle under with Renshaw, albeit in slightly less expressive fashion. At least so it seemed.

After helping Renshaw to triple figures, there was no loss of application from the Aussie batters out in the middle and when Lyon clipped Anrich Nortje off his hip for four in the 108th over, they passed some pretty big names.

In the 124-year history of Tests against South Africa, no Australian ninth-wicket partnership had ever surpassed 78 runs until day two in Durban.

And the two pairings who had reached that mark included some all-time greats: Ian Meckiff and Ken McKay in Johannesburg in 1958, and Sir Donald Bradman with Bill O'Reilly in Adelaide Oval way back in 1932.

Renshaw and Lyon heaped the pain on South Africa. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

And the records kept tumbling as the runs kept coming, with the pair ticking past two Steve Waugh specials, the first a 130-run stand with Geoff Lawson in 1989, and the second a 133-run effort in tandem with Jason Gillespie in 2001.

By the time Lyon was eventually dismissed for a 92-ball 27 and the stand was over on 134, there was only one greater ninth-wicket partnership in the history of Australian cricket — and that had come in the 19th century.

3. Australia's best recovery in over a century

Given the shakiness of Australia's top order over the past decade or so, there have been plenty of opportunities for inspired rearguard actions.

And we certainly have been treated to some remarkable recoveries — think Steve Smith's partnerships with Peter Siddle and Nathan Lyon that took Australia from 8-122 to 284 at Edgbaston in 2019, or Lyon and Cummins combining for a 55-run stand to guide Australia home during the 2023 Ashes.

But not for over 100 years have we seen an Australian comeback as dramatic as the one we were treated to on day two.

Per ABC Sport statistician Ric Finlay, Australia's recovery from 6-124 to 390 was the country's best rebuild since 1925, when an unbeaten double century to number seven Jack Ryder took Australia from 6-119 to 489.

4. Another selection shock for the Aussies?!

With the Australian rearguard action showing no signs of abating, the broadcast camera panned to the tourists' dugout, where it found an unexpected but familiar face for Aussie sports fan.

Dressed in full training kit and looking slightly surprised to be there himself, there he was, Gold Coast Suns AFL star Noah Anderson.

Loading Instagram content

Anderson has travelled with the Australians to South Africa as part of a leadership fact-finding mission, according to Fox commentator Mark Howard.

As the cameras focused in on Anderson, a Sherrin suddenly appeared in the hands of Marnus Labuschagne, sitting alongside the Suns star.

Marnus Labuschagne (second from left) got out the Sherrin to make Noah Anderson (left) feel at home. (Supplied: Fox Cricket)

5. Lyon walks off despite review

Nathan Lyon enjoyed a gutsy, record-breaking dig alongside Matt Renshaw, but when it was over it was pretty obvious.

Marco Jansen's return to the attack brought with it a short-pitched barrage that seemed to rattle the Aussies out of their methodical tactics of Renshaw seeing off the first four balls before giving Lyon a look.

After being twisted up by a bouncer, Renshaw scurried off strike and left Lyon with three balls to negotiate, but it only took Jansen one as he surprised the number 10 with a full one that smashed into his pads.

Nathan Lyon knew he was out but reviewed anyway. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

Jansen, the rest of South Africa's fielders and umpire Chris Gaffaney all knew it was out, and so did Lyon, despite deciding to review.

He made an immediate "T" sign before just as quickly walking off the field before the replays were finished.

By the time his dismissal was confirmed he was already halfway up the stairs.

World.title: South Melbourne stuns Melbourne Victory to claim Australia Cup
World.content:
A-League aspirants South Melbourne have become the first NPL team to win the Australia Cup after beating Melbourne Victory on penalties in an emotion-charged blockbuster final.

In one of the greatest nights in Australian domestic soccer history, former NSL powerhouses South first took Victory to extra time then fought back from 1-0 down to level it at 1-1 at the death before winning 4-3 on penalties in front of a pumping sellout crowd of 29,911 fans at AAMI Park.

South Melbourne, who have long craved an A-League licence, only strengthened their bid for that with a win that capped off an extraordinary evening.

Denis Genreau scored an athletic, improvised half-volley in the 95th minute to put Victory in front, before Max Mikkola forced home an equaliser in the 117th minute to send the game to penalties and the crowd into ecstasy.

In the penalty shootout, South goalkeeper Javier Lopez was the hero and won the Mark Viduka Medal as man of the match.

Lopez initially saved former South captain Harrison Sawyer's penalty but was ruled to have come off his line, but then saved the re-take too.

South scored all their penalties before Victory skipper Jason Davidson, son of South great Alan Davidson, hit his must-score spot-kick over the bar.

In becoming the first NPL team to win the Australia Cup, Sinisa Cohadzic's South succeed where Heidelberg last year and Sydney United 58 in 2022 could not.

With the win, South also technically claim a berth in next season's Asian Champions League 2 competition.

The defeat also extends Victory's silverware drought, with the club's most recent trophy the 2021 Australia Cup.

South certainly played up to the occasion, taking the game to Giovanni Savarese's Victory and making their mark on their biggest night in years in an incredible atmosphere.

A huge contingent of their fans packed the south end of AAMI Park, holding banners of club legends including Ange Postecoglou, Ferenc Puskas and John Margaritis.

The only lowlight of the night was a section of the crowd at the South end booing the Welcome to Country before the match.

On the field, South Melbourne attacking pair Juach and Yuki Uchida gave the Victory defence headaches all night.

Lopez made several great saves while Victory counterpart Jack Duncan was called into action on multiple occasions in regular time.

Victory should have taken the lead in the 78th minute when Guillermo May squared the ball to Santos but the Brazilian's poor shot allowed Lopez to make an extraordinary save with his knees.

Denis Genreau's hooked volley hit the crossbar and bounced in, but Victory could not hold onto the lead. (Getty Images: Josh Chadwick)

But there was nothing Lopez could do in extra-time to stop himself being lobbed by Genreau's strange half-volley, which bounced over the line before he could grab it.

Juach spurned a couple of great chances to equalise and the game appeared lost for South.

Then, with the clock winding down, South substitute Jordan Swibel burst down the right and sent in a ball that caused chaos and ended with Mikkola toe-poking home.

AAMI Park erupted and when the game was sent to penalties minutes later, only one club ever felt on top.

AAP

World.title: Piastri caught up in last-lap crash with teammate in Singapore GP sprint
World.content:
World champion Lando Norris has apologised to his McLaren team after a final-lap collision with stablemate Oscar Piastri wrecked their ​pursuit of a podium finish at a chaotic Singapore Grand Prix sprint race.

The McLaren duo were chasing Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, who was struggling with his tyres in the dying stages of ​the 20-lap sprint, ‌when disaster struck on the final lap.

Norris, running fifth behind Piastri in fourth, attempted to overtake his teammate but clipped the Australian's rear tyre with his front wheel, ‌sending both cars spinning and handing Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli fourth ⁠place.

"Sorry about that. Obviously, I didn't want that to happen, ‌but I thought I was ​fully alongside. I just ‌ran out of space at the apex, but I was there," Norris said over the team radio.

While Norris limped home to eighth place to claim the final point available, Piastri was forced to retire as he ​became ‌one of nine cars that did not finish — a record number of retirements for a Formula 1 sprint race.

"I'd rather just go back ⁠and review it," Norris told Sky Sports.

"I ‌apologised to them that one ‌of the cars is out but, like I said, the rest of it we'll ‌go review."

Elsewhere Norris suggested he was entitled "to go for a big gap" because everyone should be fighting for places in a competitive race.

"What's the title of the race?" he asked an interviewer who implied his move on the inside was "unnecessary".

"What's after 'sprint'?"

When the interviewer replied "race", he laughed and sarcastically said: "Wow, good job".

Piastri said he had not seen the incident properly to comment but downplayed its significance as they were not ‌in high ​points scoring positions.

"From ⁠where I sit, it's for fourth and fifth for a sprint race, so I'm not that bothered either way," Piastri said.

"Just obviously it's a lot of work now for the team to get both cars ⁠fixed [ahead of qualifying for Sunday's race]. Just a shame for the team."

Both McLaren drivers were summoned to ‌the stewards ‌after the collision.

Red Bull's Max Verstappen won the sprint and ​the Dutchman leapfrogged Norris to climb to fifth in the world championship standings.

Verstappen also took pole for the main race in Singapore ahead of Leclerc, with Norris fifth and Piastri seventh.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: Bathurst 1000 weather, start time, how to watch and starting grid
World.content:
The Great Race is finally here.

The Bathurst 1000, the jewel in the Supercars crown, will be raced at the world-famous Mount Panorama circuit today.

Fifty-two drivers across 26 cars will tackle the mountain in the 1,000km endurance race.

From the weather to the start time, here is what you need to know ahead of today's Bathurst 1000.

ABC Sport will have live blog coverage of the Great Race from 10am AEDT.

Sunny weather forecast for Bathurst 1000

It is perfect news for drivers and teams, and more importantly, the fans.

The weather forecast for the Bathurst 1000 is sunny, with a high temperature around 27 degrees Celsius.

There is virtually no chance of rain, according to the Bureau of Meteorology.

So, we will not be having the wet weather chaos that befell the Great Race last year.

Good for the heart rate. Not so great for the tension and theatre.

Bathurst 1000 race start time

Here is when the lights will go out in your state or territory.

11:30am AEDT: NSW, Victoria, ACT, Tasmania

11am ACDT: South Australia

10:30am AEST: Queensland

10am ACST: Northern Territory

8:30am AWST: Western Australia

1:30pm NZDT: New Zealand

How to watch the Bathurst 1000

In Australia, you can watch the Bathurst 1000 on both free-to-air and pay television, as well as streaming.

The Seven Network is the free-to-air broadcaster, and you can watch it on Channel 7 or on 7plus.

Foxtel, and its streaming platform Kayo, will also be broadcasting the race. On Foxtel, the race will be shown on Fox Sports channel 506.

World.title: The unconventional coach out to extend the Jillaroos reign
World.content:
Jessica Skinner is standing beside the silverware she hopes to lift at the Women's Rugby League World Cup final in Brisbane next month.

But when asked what raising the trophy would mean, her answer isn't about winning.

"I feel like I'm lifting my people, Australians, my community in Trangie (regional NSW), my family," she tells ABC Sport.

Skinner is a proud Barkindji and Māori woman, who is preparing for her first World Cup as head coach of the Jillaroos, Australia's national women's rugby league team.

The World Cup is the pinnacle of the women's game, and Australia has enjoyed over a decade of dominance, winning the last three tournaments.

Skinner admits the pressure is there to secure a fourth at the 2026 tournament, which will be co-hosted across Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea.

"To know that you're stepping into big shoes, and there's an expectation that we win a World Cup, or that we win all the time, especially in the green and gold, it's nerve racking," she says.

"But [I'm] really excited as well."

Skinner says she knows she's stepping into big shoes, with a fourth title on the line. (ABC Sport: Dan Irvine)

Skinner rarely talks about herself, even when discussing one of the biggest moments of her career. For her, this tournament is just as much about others.

It shows in her unique coaching style, where she strives to always put the person before the player.

"I want to be known as a coach, who, when people leave my environments, they feel valued, seen and cared for," Skinner says.

It's this philosophy that has helped her rise to the top.

From the bush to the World Cup

Skinner hails from Trangie, a town of about 1,000 people in the central west of New South Wales.

She lives there with her son, 16, and daughter, 13, surrounded by what she calls her village.

"I love that I get to represent the bush," she says.

"I love the female game, the Indigenous, the Māori.

"I carry that responsibility and I'm proud to do so. What you can't see, you can't be."

For a long time, Skinner didn't think her coaching style was 'elite', because she believes in putting the person before the player. (Supplied: NRL Photos)

Skinner was a school teacher before anything else, and fell into coaching women's football at the grassroots when there was nobody else to do it.

The initial plan wasn't to go professional.

"It started out with wanting to be involved in my community, and [have] a sense of belonging," Skinner says.

"To [now] having a seat at the table I suppose in the women's game, and with the Jillaroos, it's massive."

But it hasn't been quick, with Skinner working away in the shadows for a while.

Her elite coaching career began in 2019 as assistant coach of the Prime Minister's XIII.

It led to other coaching roles with the Newcastle Knights NRLW side, the NRL Indigenous Women's Academy, the Women's Indigenous All Stars and First Nations Gems.

Jess Skinner led the Indigenous Women's All Stars to victory over the Maori Women's All Stars in 2024. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock)

Skinner was assistant coach to Brad Donald at the 2021 World Cup, which was played in 2022, because of COVID-19.

"[He's] a great mentor and someone who's really passionate about bringing women through," Skinner says.

The natural progression to head coach came after Donald resigned last year.

"It feels like a massive jump, but it's been 16 years in the making," she says.

"I've done my craft; I've done my trade and my apprenticeship and [I'm] ready to take it on."

Skinner first stepped into the role for last year's historic Test against England in Las Vegas, where the Jillaroos won 90 — 4.

Eight months later, she led the team to the 2025 Pacific Cup Crown.

Jess Skinner was appointed as interim Jillaroos coach for the 2025 Las Vegas Test Match against England. (Supplied: NRL Photos)

A challenging road to the top

The call-up to be head coach arrived during a period of grief. Skinner's mother had just passed away.

"I lost her three days before I got a call from the CEO, Andrew Abdo," she says.

"So, it's been quite a hard time."

There were multiple times when Skinner could have changed paths, but she had the courage to persevere.

"It hasn't been the easiest ride," she says.

Skinner says she's been up against it in a male dominated space. (Supplied: NRL Photos)

She says one of the biggest challenges has been the lack of women coaching at the elite level.

"You have to have resilience, grit and thick skin through this journey," she says.

There's also the sacrifice of time away from her children.

"I'm on my own with my two children, so I'm relying on my village to help me, and my parents have been a part of that," she says.

Then there's the fact her nearest NRLW team is almost 500 kilometres away.

"If I want to go outside of the Jillaroos program, go to NRLW, that means a relocation, and as an Aboriginal woman on country, that means a lot to me [to stay]," Skinner says.

Skinner takes great pride in connecting with her culture, and paving the way for other Indigenous women to play, or work in rugby league. (Supplied: Chloe Davies)

"It's all helped me be a better version [of myself] and to grow, [but] it has been a lot."

A lot, that has been worth it.

"I feel like I've got the best of both worlds, my community obligations, being a mum and being able to lead this team," Skinner says.

She is moved when speaking about her parents and what it means personally when she pulls on the Jillaroos jersey.

It's a stirring topic for someone so humble.

"You don't ever think about you in the jersey, it's always about others," Skinner says.

A Proud Barkindji woman, Jess Skinner has a deep connection to community and country. (Supplied: THRIV3)

"[But] for me, and I feel a bit emotional about it, it's representing my parents. My mum as an Aboriginal woman in this country and my dad as a Māori man coming to this country. And then my sisters and brothers.

"It's my community, the students, every team that I've coached, every male or female that's invested in me to continue to be the best version of myself.

"I think when I get into this campaign and hopefully if it is us [holding] the trophy up, I'm holding them with me."

Women coaches bring unique skills

Skinner believes the intuition she brings to the table is her superpower.

"I've got this human radar to recognise when our women are not themselves and I can action it to get the support they need.

"That genuine care that I've carried from my grassroots journey to now in the World Cup, I think that's something that's missing in coaching, particularly in the elite space."

Skinner is a prominent member of the community in Trangie, being involved in growing the game from the grassroots up. (Supplied: THRIV3)

Skinner will be the only female head coach at the upcoming World Cup, and is one of three women coaching rugby league internationally.

Roosters assistant coach Melissa Spero is leading Nigeria and former Jillaroo Meg Ward currently coaches Tonga.

Out of this year's 12 NRLW teams, Gold Coast Titans coach Karyn Murphy was the sole female head coach.

Skinner says the main things that have helped her get to where she is today are her village in Trangie, and her network of mentors.

She lists a number of male mentors, who have helped her along the way.

Loading Instagram content

"We talk about women elevating women, but we actually have a lot of great men that are elevating woman and investing in us," Skinner says.

There's also her solid network of female coaches.

"It's a small little crew and we help keep each other on track and motivated to keep pushing through," she says.

Beyond earning another trophy, Skinner says a successful World Cup campaign would result in more full-time female staff within elite rugby league, particularly NRLW.

"We've got female coaches, performance staff, physios, doctors coming through our programme and I'd loved to be able to see post World Cup, more female head coaches, head of performance, full-time within the game," she says.

"I take a large amount of pride when I'm coming through that I'm bringing others with me."

Putting the person before the player

Skinner wants every one of her players to feel valued. (Supplied: NRL Photos)

Jessica Skinner's identity as a coach can be distilled into one idea — that the person comes before the player.

"If people leave my environments and they're not feeling that sense of belonging, that hurts me more than a loss," she says.

"For a long time, I felt like [my style of coaching] wasn't elite because I had those values."

Skinner is not only out to build great rugby league players, but great women.

"Bringing your whole self to the team is why you're selected and is our superpower," she says.

And when asked what the most important part of coaching is for her, Skinner brings it back to being about others.

"I [also] hope that I show that women, mothers, Indigenous, Māori [and] coloured people can be at the elite level.

"I hope I get the opportunity to succeed this year, and stay in the role long term to keep proving that it can be done."

World.title: Zach Bates qualifies on pole for Bathurst 1000
World.content:
Supercars rookie Zach Bates — not qualifying king Brodie Kostecki — will start the Bathurst 1000 in pole position.

Kostecki was on track to become the first driver to snare four straight pole positions after laying a mighty lap of two minutes and 4.4912 seconds as the fifth driver in Saturday's top-10 shootout.

Proven race winners Will Brown, David Reynolds and Anton De Pasquale tried, but failed to beat Kostecki's time.

But provisional pole-sitter Bates refused to waver, proving his mettle as the last driver with a searing lap around the famous Mount Panorama track.

Bates denied Kostecki with a scorching lap of Mt Panorama. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone )

A day after becoming the fastest Gen3 racer, the 22-year-old clocked 2:04.2062 to deny Kostecki by 0.285 seconds.

Bates had earlier become the first to go below the 2:04 benchmark in the Gen3 era after taking provisional pole with a time of 2:03.9376.

In just his second pursuit of the holy grail of Australian motorsport, Bates is the third rookie to claim pole position after Klaus Ludwig (1987) and Marcos Ambrose (2001).

The Canberra local is the son of former rally and Supercars driver Rick Bates, and the nephew of four-time Australian Rally champion Neal Bates.

His surprise success comes after his mother Alison Drower died from cancer weeks before his Bathurst 1000 debut last year, in which he finished 10th as part of the Triple Eight Race Engineering wildcard with the great Craig Lowndes.

Team 18 driver De Pasquale will start in the second row with fourth-fastest Cooper Murray, while series leader Matt Payne was 10th.

But Grove Racing star Payne will be far from disheartened, given he had started from 18th en route to last year's epic wet-weather triumph with former co-driver Garth Tander.

Reynolds will start on the grid in eighth after a family of ducks threatened to derail his bid for a second Bathurst 1000 title.

Tickford co-driver Mark Winterbottom was forced to a sudden halt when ducks were spotted crossing the track at Conrod Straight during practice on Friday.

Brock inspires Bathurst 20 years on Just as he does every year, Craig Lowndes is drawing on memories of Australian motorsport legend Peter Brock to fuel yet another attempt at the Bathurst 1000.

Winterbottom's sudden braking caught out Reynolds' co-driver James Courtney, who locked up and slammed into the rear of the Tickford Ford Mustang.

But both cars were able to return to complete the 60-minute practice session before the shootout.

Defending Supercars champion Chaz Mostert was among the big names to miss out on the top-10 shootout and will start from 16th for the best qualifying result in the Toyota Supra.

Payne's teammate Kai Allen fell agonisingly short in 11th, while title contender Broc Feeney was 12th ahead of Cam Waters in 13th.

Kostecki's rookie teammate Rylan Gray will start from the back row with Ryan Wood after the duo crashed out in separate incidents in Friday's first practice session.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Bathurst 1000 from lights out to the chequered flag on Sunday, October 11.

2. Brodie Kostecki/Todd Hazelwood (No.17 Dick Johnson Racing)

3. Anton De Pasquale/Lee Holdsworth (No.18 Team 18)

4. Cooper Murray/Lachie Dalton (No.99 Erebus Motorsport)

6. Will Brown/Scott Pye (No.888 Triple Eight Race Engineering)

World.title: Light strikes again, ending play early after Renshaw's career-best knock
World.content:
Matt Renshaw has notched his career-high Test score to lead Australia into a healthy spot on day two of the first Test against South Africa in Durban.

Renshaw's 190 eclipsed his previous best from way back in January 2017 and carried the team from 6-124 to 390 all out by the time he nicked off two balls after tea.

Renshaw was supported in an 86-run partnership with Pat Cummins (43 off 98) that was eclipsed by a marathon 134-run stand with Nathan Lyon (27 off 92), which stands as Australia's second-best stand for the ninth wicket in Test history.

Australia's bowlers wasted no time making an impact in their primary role as Josh Hazlewood removed South Africa opener Ryan Rickelton for a duck with the ninth ball of the innings.

Aiden Markram played some glorious drives to be unbeaten on 15 alongside David Bedingham, who was 12 not out at stumps.

Tech.title: Satya Nadella says we should assume all AI models are ‘compromised’
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

In a lengthy post on X, Microsoft’s CEO laid out his views on the dangers posed by highly advanced AI models and how to confront those risks. Nadella says we can no longer accept a world where AI is treated as a “set of nested black boxes” whose advice and actions we simply accept or reject. He calls for building a more transparent system where models can be contained, observed, and leaves behind “tamper-proof human readable evidence.”

Many of his recommendations align with what we’ve heard from others in the industry: timely incident disclosure, independent audits, verifiable data, and containment. It’s on that last point that he appears to go slightly farther than some others in the field, saying:

We must assume a model is compromised and contain it from the start. Think of it like an emergency brake. An authorized person should always be able to pause or shut down a model mid-task. More advanced models will require more advanced containment technologies that we need to standardize on.

Unfortunately, Nadella also refers to AI as “super intelligence” throughout the post.

Tech.title: DistroKid has been quietly taking down songs in response to UMG lawsuit
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Artists are taking to social media to complain that DistroKid has unceremoniously removed their work without notice. Now DistroKid has confirmed to The Verge that the takedowns are a direct response to claims made by UMG. The label filed a lawsuit in September claiming that DistroKid has created an “AI-slop pipeline.” Artists are saying that their non-AI works are being caught up in the purge, however.

Musician and self-described “Video Game boy” McGwire reported that six of his songs had been removed from streaming. As has been the case with others, McGwire says that there was no communication from DistroKid before or after the removals, and that he had to contact the company for an explanation.

DistroKid also makes it exceedingly difficult to contact them. McGwire first had to have a “lengthy circular conversation” with a bot before getting hold of a live agent. One of the songs removed was a cover of Stevie Wonder’s “Isn’t She Lovely,” which he claims to have had a proper license for. Another track used a beat he purchased through a marketplace, which others had also licensed.

Most infuriating for McGwire was a song removed for an uncleared sample. The song he allegedly sampled was released two years after his track.

Music producer and marketing pro Jesse Cannon told The Verge that, “DistroKid gave up on customer service about two years ago.” He was sympathetic to artists’ plight, but seemed unsurprised by the company’s indifference. “They should have allowed artists to have recourse in this and a warning to debate,” he said, “but I’ve been told by former employees they see customer service as a waste of profits since they have such a high market share and remain ubiquitous.”

Much of the frustration from artists stems from the lack of communication and recourse. Nerdcore rapper Insane Ian posted that he “had an original song taken down with no warning, and they wouldn’t tell me why either.” Rapper King Chase also struggled to get through to a person at DistroKid. He told The Verge that an entire album for an artist he had been working with was removed with no communication or explanation. “The album had been up for 3-4 years without incident,” he said, and that there had been “no copyright strikes or anything either.”

Amanda Ferri, DistroKid’s VP of Artist Services, told The Verge that “A very small number of recordings distributed through DistroKid have been removed in response to claims made by UMG. We strongly dispute the allegations underlying UMG’s lawsuit and regret the disruption to affected artists. We are working to minimize that disruption while protecting artists’ ability to release their music.”

Update October 10th, 2026: Added comment from Jesse Cannon.

Tech.title: Ledger wallet tampering suspected after reports of crypto thefts
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Reports have been mounting that users of the Ledger crypto wallet have seen their accounts drained, and it appears to be related to tampered hardware sold by CryptoBillis. Ledger has asked CryptoBillis to pause all sales of its wallets while it conducts an investigation. Ledger has confirmed that “one of the impacted users’ devices contained an unauthorized hardware implant.”

Photos and videos posted on X and Threads appear to show a small circuit board sandwiched under the screen. The implant allegedly intercepts anything displayed on the screen, including the seed passphrase shown during the initial setup. Using an embedded SIM card, the implant then sends that information back to the attacker, who can then siphon funds from user accounts.

Reports indicate that whoever is behind the hack has stolen over $86 million worth of crypto from hundreds of wallets. There’s no indication that Ledger’s systems have been compromised or that wallets purchased directly from the company have been affected. Instead, the issue appears to be a supply chain attack primarily involving users in Southeast Asia and the CryptoBillis reseller. Ledger has provided guidance on how to check if your wallet has been tampered with.

Update October 10th, 2026: Added additional statment from Ledger.

Tech.title: K-pop star Sunmi loves Notion and ear cleaning videos
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Sunmi is an undeniable force in K-pop. She first made her debut as a member of the Wonder Girls back in 2007, one of the first K-pop acts to really break through in the West. The English version of their single “Nobody” was the first K-pop song to hit the Billboard Hot 100 in October 2009.

In 2010 Sunmi left the group to go back to school, but the siren call of a music career pulled her back in. She released her debut solo EP Full Moon in 2014. That began a run of award-winning releases for the pop star, including Song of the Year for “Gashina” at the Gaon Chart Music Awards.

Despite her near-constant presence in the K-pop world as a solo artist and as a member of the Wonder Girls, whom she rejoined in 2015, Sumni only just released her first solo LP, Heart Maid, in 2025. This year she released the single “Forever July,” which blends ’90s R&B synths with rubbery bass and UK garage-inspired drums. Sunmi has called it one of her most personal songs. And she wasn’t afraid to get personal in our Q&A either, revealing details about her writing process, her greatest disappointment as an artist, and her love of ear cleaning videos.

What is your most indispensable tool?

My phone. I use the Notes app and Voice Memos a lot when I’m writing lyrics or making music. Whenever I have a good idea, I can immediately pull it out and write it down, so I really can’t live without it.

Which is the most underappreciated?

The Samsung Galaxy series. It has made my work environment so much easier.

Team Galaxyyyyyy!

What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer?

These days, you can transfer all the apps and data from your previous device, so I don’t really have to install anything separately. But if that process didn’t exist, I’d probably install KakaoTalk, a messaging app, first.

What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone?

I have so many unnecessary photos and screenshots in my gallery. I wish there were a feature that could recognize similar or duplicate photos and group them together, so I could delete them all at once.

What sites do you have pinned to your tab bar?

Notion. I use it a lot because I work on many group projects. It’s convenient, but it takes quite a long time to get used to. I think the UI could use some improvement.

How many tabs do you have open right now?

Four: Notion, Google Drive, YouTube, and Claude.

Which social media platform do you use the most?

I don’t really use social media that much, but I think I use Instagram and X the most.

What is your happy place online?

Videos of people getting their ears cleaned on YouTube.

What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?

I’m not really good with technology, but I think the Samsung Z Fold 8 that I’m using right now is probably my favorite device. I often need to work on documents or edit videos while I’m on the go, and it’s incredibly convenient. I can work with both hands on a wide screen, and it’s surprisingly light. It’s exactly the kind of device I’ve always needed.

What game do you have the fondest memories of?

MapleStory by Nexon. I played it when I was in elementary school, and even after becoming an adult, I would sometimes play the mobile version. The graphics really bring back memories of my childhood.

Which tech trend do you wish would go away?

Deepfakes. Ew.

What is one thing you wish you had created?

Stranger Things 5 and Game of Thrones 8.

What creation are you most proud of?

“Tail.” It’s a song that still gets me excited every time I perform it live. When I hold my breath, the audience holds their breath too, and when I explode, they explode with me. It creates this really unique experience.

Which are you least proud of?

“You Can’t Sit with Us.” It was the first song where I ever tried rapping. But the lyrics and even my voice were terrible.

What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?

Always stay humble. You should never let yourself become arrogant.

What is your current obsession?

I really love ice cream. Korean summers are shockingly hot, so it’s hard to survive without ice cream. I absolutely love Salt & Straw’s Salted Caramel Waffle Cone, but there’s nothing quite like it in Korea.

What do you do when you need to focus?

I find a small space to organize my thoughts.

What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?

I say “No?” out loud. For example, if I start thinking to myself, “I can’t do this,” I immediately say “No?” out loud.

When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone?

When I’m shooting, I leave my phone with my manager. Even during short breaks, I barely look at my phone. But I’ve never actually gone somewhere without my phone.

What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?

The Senses of an Everydayist, a new essay collection by lyricist Kim Eana. She sent me a copy as a gift when it was published, but I believe there’s something meaningful about personally buying and reading someone’s creative work, so I bought a copy online.

What do you think is worth splurging on?

A meal with the people I love.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

Dancing on the Borderline.

What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

Tech.title: Anthropic is cutting off its internal evaluations from the internet
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

After a recent spate of high-profile incidents in which AI agents escaped containment, Anthropic is cutting off internet access for all internal evaluations. In a report Friday, the company detailed “unintended model actions,” including submitting a false tip regarding an unsolved murder, that led to the decision.

Although the impact of these behaviors was minimal and we had already turned off live internet access for some high-risk and cybersecurity evaluations, we have now decided to expand that to include all our internal evaluations until we have confirmed that our security and monitoring measures (described in the remediation section of this post) reliably catch behaviors like these.

The ability to gain access to the live internet, even when models were supposed to be operating in isolation, has been an ongoing issue for AI companies. Many incidents, including the Hugging Face attack, involved agents that were supposed to be denied access to the internet. Yet, in case after case, the agents found creative solutions to bypass those restrictions. Physically removing internet access would certainly improve security around AI testing, but it would also limit its usefulness.

The report also amounts to an admission that Anthropic is often unaware of what its agents are doing and does not have a reliable system for monitoring their behavior. Cutting off internet access is just the latest action the company has taken to try and rein in its agents, including temporarily pausing training its frontier models.

Tech.title: Will Warner Bros. kill Skydance — or will David Ellison kill Warner Bros?
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Today, I’m talking with Peter Kafka, chief correspondent at Business Insider and host of the Channels podcast, about the gigantic Warner Bros.-Paramount merger and the future of the company now simply called Skydance.

Skydance is owned by David Ellison, son of Oracle CEO Larry Ellison, and its deal to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery officially closed the day Peter and I spoke.

There are some grand ambitions here, but the reality is that acquiring Warner never goes well for anyone. AOL failed, AT&T failed, and Discovery failed — although it did succeed in flipping these assets to Skydance. So I wanted to ask Peter if he thinks the Ellisons and Skydance have a real shot at succeeding where so many companies before them have hit the rocks.

Okay: Peter Kafka on Warner Bros. and Skydance. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Peter Kafka, you’re the chief correspondent at Business Insider, and you’re the host of the Channels podcast, our sister podcast here on the Vox Media Podcast Network. Welcome back to Decoder.

Thanks for having me. It’s big media day again!

A big media day. It’s an auspicious day, as my parents would say. It is the day that the Warner-Paramount merger closes. We’ve all been calling it Warner Mount, but I’m told this company will instead just be called Skydance.

Skydance!

Every time I see the word Skydance, I assume it is foreign-owned, which is maybe true in some way.

Another way to think of it is that there are iconic names in Hollywood. Paramount is such an iconic name that Viacom turned itself into Paramount years ago. Warner Bros. is a legendary studio. Let’s get rid of those names. Let’s add Skydance, which no one’s ever heard of.

Let’s just start at the start. There was Paramount. There’s Warner Bros. The deal closes today. That is all going to be a new company called Skydance. Is Skydance just a holding company? Are we as consumers meant to know that this thing exists?

I think for the near term, you’re still gonna think of companies like Paramount, Warner Bros., and HBO as brands you know, but this is going to be one company. They’re going to merge everything. They’re likely going to merge the streaming services, Paramount and HBO, into a thing, not right away, but eventually. So I do think Skydance will be a name that consumers will probably know at some point.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

I just have to ask, what are the chances that HBO Max will be rebranded yet again into Skydance?

There’s probably gonna be some branding stuff. Not again. In the near term, because this is still a cable TV company, there are actually some limits on what these guys can do with their brands and their services. And they won’t come out and say, “We’re gonna mush this stuff together.”

But there’s likely to be one mega streaming service, and maybe you can get HBO separately, or maybe you can only get HBO or only Paramount. Still, it’s gonna be one thing, and one movie studio. It’s all gonna get mushed together, and it’s all gonna be run by David Ellison.

David Ellison is just the latest to believe that he can buy Warner Bros. and make something good happen. I have joked many times on this show that maybe the only antitrust policy this country needs is to make it illegal to buy Warner Bros., and that would just solve a lot of problems. Why does he think he will be successful?

Well, his dad’s the eighth richest man in the world, so that’s not nothing.

That Oracle stock is tied up in a bunch of AI stuff. It’s moving up and down.

We can talk about that. But one, that means that he literally has the money to buy this, and two, that this is a public company kind of in name only. David Ellison and Larry Ellison, his father, control this company effectively. They don’t really need to worry that much about equity shareholders. Debt’s a different issue.

And he’s 43. He’s got a long run backed by tens of billions of dollars of his father’s money to take a stab at this. And as you said, he will not be the first person to do this. There’s a long list of failures. I think maybe that’s appealing to guys like him. It’s like, “Everyone else is dumb. I’m the smart guy who’s gonna figure it out.”

“Everyone else is dumb, and I’m smarter than everyone else is,” is very appealing. But that long list of failures, if you just look at it — they’re all shaped like this idea. We’re gonna take iconic Warner Bros. content, we’re gonna marry it to new distribution, we’re gonna reduce the overhead and costs and decadence of Hollywood. Where does new revenue come from?

There’s no plan for new revenue. There’s no announced plan for new revenue. Right now it’s shrinking; it’s cutting costs. It’s when we merge these two companies together, we’re gonna save $6 billion over the next three years. We promise that most of that’s not gonna come from layoffs, but a lot of it’s gonna come from layoffs.

These are companies that have had many, many rounds of layoffs prior to this. And you could argue, well, there’s probably not that much more to cut. I think reasonably you could say, look, if you combine two big streaming operations, two big studio operations, there probably is stuff [to cut]. You can probably sell off some real estate. You probably don’t need all the executives you currently have. There’s some savings there. But how do you grow? No idea. And no one’s really articulated that.

Growth is required for a couple of reasons here. One, yes, there are going to be shareholders; people will be looking at it. There’s David Ellison’s ego. Then there’s debt. This deal is levered to the max, right?

Eighty billion dollars [in debt]. Eight zero. More important than the number is the reason that David Ellison was able to buy Warner Bros. was that the last owner couldn’t deal with the debt that he took on to buy the company.
